    Algorithms Deep Dive — Sorting, Searching, Recursion, Graphs, DP, Greedy, Strings & Math¶

    Format: samjhaane ke liye Hinglish (roman script), aur jo aap interviewer ke saamne bolenge wo English mein — > **Interview answer:** blockquotes mein. Saara code Python mein hai.

    Ye document un logon ke liye likha gaya hai jinke paas formal CS/DSA background nahi hai. QA/SDET ho, Playwright + pytest likhte ho, aur ab senior QA / SDET / software engineering interviews ke liye algorithms seriously seekhne hain.

    How to Use This Document¶

    Video dekh kar algorithm samajh mein aa jata hai — aur video khatam hote hi udd jata hai. Wajah simple hai: video mein aapko result dikhaya jata hai, derive nahi karwaya jata. Aap dekhte ho ki merge sort O(n log n) hai, par aapne khud kabhi ginn kar nahi nikala ki log n levels kyun bante hain.

    Isliye is document mein har algorithm ke saath ye 10 cheezein hamesha aayengi, isi order mein:

    # Section Isme kya milega
    1 Kya hai Ek plain sentence mein idea + ek real-world analogy, code se pehle
    2 Kyu hai Pichhle algorithm mein kya kharabi thi jiski wajah se ye banana pada
    3 Kaise kaam karta hai Mechanism, ASCII diagram ke saath
    4 Poora dry run Chhote input par step-by-step trace, table mein, har pass ke baad ki state
    5 Code Python, aur neeche har line ka numbered explanation
    6 Complexity derive karke Best / average / worst time, space + recursion stack — ginn kar, maan kar nahi
    7 Stability, in-place, adaptive Teenon ka matlab aur kisi ko farak kyun padta hai
    8 Kab use karna hai / kab nahi Practical situations
    9 Kitne tareeke se optimize Har known improvement aur wo kya deta hai, kya leta hai
    10 Interview answer English mein, bolne wala jawab + cross-questions

    Padhne ka sahi tareeka¶

    1. Dry run ko skip mat karna. Wahi asli seekhne wala hissa hai. Ho sake to paper par khud saath saath trace karo — table ko haath se bharo.
    2. Code pehle padho, phir line-by-line explanation. Jo line samajh na aaye, uska number dhoondh kar neeche padho.
    3. Complexity derivation ko rat-ta mat maaro. Ek baar summation ya recursion tree khud bana lo, phir wo kabhi nahi bhoolega.
    4. Interview answer ko zor se bolo. Likh kar samajhna aur bol kar samjhana do alag skills hain, aur interview mein doosri wali test hoti hai.

    Notation jo baar baar aayega¶

    Symbol Matlab
    n Input ka size — array mein elements, graph mein vertices, string mein characters
    V, E Graph ke vertices aur edges ki sankhya
    O(f(n)) Upper bound — "isse zyada bura nahi hoga"
    Omega(f(n)) Lower bound — "isse behtar ho hi nahi sakta"
    Theta(f(n)) Upper aur lower dono — "exactly itna hi"
    log n Base 2 ka log, jab tak alag se na likha ho
    Amortised Ek operation kabhi kabhi mehnga, par lambe chalte average sasta

    Part 1: Sorting Algorithms¶

    Sorting sabse purana aur sabse zyada padha jaane wala topic hai, aur iski wajah sirf ye nahi hai ki data ko order mein lagana zaroori hota hai. Asli wajah ye hai ki sorting ke andar poori algorithm design ki alphabet chhupi hui hai: comparison, swapping, invariants, divide and conquer, recursion, partitioning, heaps, counting, radix — sab kuch. Agar aapne das sorting algorithms ko sach mein derive kar liya, to graph aur DP aadhe se zyada aasan ho jaate hain, kyunki wahan bhi wahi mental tools lagte hain.

    Sorting Fundamentals¶

    Kya hai¶

    Sorting matlab ek collection ke elements ko kisi defined order (chhote se bade, ya bade se chhote, ya kisi custom rule) mein rearrange karna.

    Real-world analogy: Aapke haath mein taash ke 13 patte hain. Aap unhe kis tarah lagate ho? Zyadatar log ek-ek patta uthate hain aur pehle se lage hue patton ke beech uski sahi jagah par ghusa dete hain. Wo insertion sort hai — aapne wo bina padhe hi khud invent kar liya tha. Doosra insaan poore haath mein se sabse chhota patta dhoondh kar bahar nikaalta hai, phir bacche hue mein se sabse chhota — wo selection sort hai. Teesra insaan patton ko do dher mein baant kar dono dher alag alag lagata hai aur phir dono ko merge karta hai — wo merge sort hai. Yaani teenon algorithms insaan ke natural behaviours hain; hum sirf unhe formalise aur measure kar rahe hain.

    Kyu hai — sorting ka fayda kya hai¶

    Sorting apne aap mein manzil nahi hai, ye doosri cheezon ko sasta banane ka tareeka hai:

    Sorted hone ke baad kya sasta ho jata hai Unsorted cost Sorted cost
    Kisi element ko dhoondhna O(n) linear scan O(log n) binary search
    Duplicates dhoondhna O(n²) ya hash set (O(n) space) O(n) — bas padosi compare karo
    Median / k-th smallest O(n) quickselect ya O(n log n) O(1) — index par jaao
    Do sorted lists ka intersection O(n·m) O(n + m) two pointers
    Range query "50 se 80 ke beech kitne" O(n) O(log n) do binary searches
    Closest pair (1D) O(n²) O(n) — sirf padosi check karo

    QA context mein soch lo: aapke paas 2 lakh test results hain aur aapko har 5 second mein poochna hai "is duration se dheeme kitne tests the?". Unsorted par har baar 2 lakh scan. Ek baar sort kar lo (O(n log n)), phir har query O(log n). Ek baar ka kharcha, hamesha ka fayda.

    Teen properties jo har sort ko define karti hain¶

    Ye teen shabd har sorting interview mein aayenge. Inhe abhi acche se samajh lo, phir har algorithm ke saath sirf apply karna hoga.

    1. Stability (sthirta)

    Ek sort stable hai agar equal elements ka aapsi order input se output tak wahi rahe.

    Input  (name, marks), marks se sort karna hai:
  ("Amit", 90), ("Riya", 85), ("Karan", 90), ("Sana", 85)

Stable sort ka output:
  ("Riya", 85), ("Sana", 85), ("Amit", 90), ("Karan", 90)
   ^^^^^^ Riya Sana se pehle thi -> ab bhi pehle hai
                                     ^^^^^ Amit Karan se pehle tha -> ab bhi pehle hai

Unstable sort ka valid output (bhi sahi hai, par order badal gaya):
  ("Sana", 85), ("Riya", 85), ("Karan", 90), ("Amit", 90)

    Isse farak kyun padta hai? Kyunki stability se aap multi-key sorting kar sakte ho bina complicated comparator likhe. Agar aapko "pehle department se, phir department ke andar salary se" sort karna hai, to stable sort ke saath aap ulta karo: pehle salary se sort karo, phir department se sort karo. Department wala sort salary ka order todega nahi (kyunki stable hai), to result perfect aa jayega. Unstable sort se ye trick kaam nahi karti.

    2. In-place (jagah par)

    Ek sort in-place hai agar wo input array ke alawa sirf O(1) ya O(log n) extra memory use kare. Merge sort ko har merge ke liye poora doosra array chahiye — O(n) extra — isliye wo in-place nahi hai. Quick sort sirf recursion stack use karta hai — O(log n) — isliye use "in-place" maana jata hai.

    Isse farak kyun padta hai? Embedded systems, bade datasets, ya jab memory hi bottleneck ho. 10 GB array ko sort karna hai aur RAM 12 GB hai — merge sort ka O(n) extra aapko maar dega, quick sort bach jayega.

    3. Adaptive (haalat dekh kar tez)

    Ek sort adaptive hai agar input jitna zyada pehle se sorted ho, wo utna hi tez chale. Insertion sort nearly-sorted data par O(n) ho jata hai. Standard merge sort har haal mein wahi O(n log n) karta hai, chahe input already sorted ho.

    Isse farak kyun padta hai? Real world ka data kabhi random nahi hota. Log files time ke hisaab se almost sorted hote hain, database mein naya record append hota hai, test results execution order mein aate hain. Adaptive sorts real data par nateeje se kahin behtar chalte hain. Isi wajah se Python ka Timsort adaptive hai.

    Comparison sorts ki theoretical limit¶

    Ye ek aisi baat hai jo interview mein bolne par turant senior lagta hai.

    Agar aapka algorithm sirf comparisons (a < b) ke through decide karta hai, to wo O(n log n) se tez nahi ho sakta. Proof ka idea:

    n elements ke n! possible orderings hain (permutations).
Har comparison ka answer sirf 2 ho sakta hai: yes ya no.
Yaani har comparison decision tree mein ek binary branch hai.

Ek binary tree jiski depth d hai, usme zyada se zyada 2^d leaves hote hain.
Hume n! alag leaves chahiye (har possible ordering ke liye ek).

  2^d  >=  n!
  d    >=  log2(n!)

Stirling se: log2(n!) ~ n·log2(n) - 1.44n
  => d = Omega(n log n)

    Iska matlab: koi bhi comparison-based sort — chahe kitna bhi clever ho — worst case mein kam se kam ~n log n comparisons karega. Merge sort aur heap sort is limit ko chhoo lete hain, isliye wo "optimal" comparison sorts hain.

    Aur isi se ye bhi samajh aata hai ki counting sort / radix sort O(n) kaise ho jate hain: wo comparisons karte hi nahi. Wo elements ki value ko directly index ki tarah use karte hain, isliye ye lower bound un par lagta hi nahi.

    Interview answer: Sorting is rarely the goal in itself — it's an enabling step. Once data is sorted, searching drops from O(n) to O(log n), duplicate detection becomes a single linear pass, and range queries become two binary searches. So we pay O(n log n) once to make many later operations cheap.

    I evaluate any sort on three axes. Stability — do equal elements keep their relative order? That matters because with a stable sort you can do multi-key sorting by sorting on the secondary key first and the primary key second. In-place — does it use only O(1) or O(log n) extra memory? That matters when the dataset approaches available RAM. Adaptive — does it get faster on partially sorted input? Real-world data is almost never random, so adaptivity often dominates the theoretical numbers.

    One important theoretical point: any comparison-based sort has a lower bound of Omega(n log n) in the worst case. The argument is a decision tree — each comparison is a binary decision, you need n! distinct leaves for the n! possible orderings, so the tree depth is at least log2(n!), which is Theta(n log n). Counting sort and radix sort beat that only because they don't compare elements at all; they use the values themselves as array indices, so the bound doesn't apply.

    Cross-question: "If stability is so useful, why not always use a stable sort?"

    Because stability usually costs memory. Merge sort is stable but needs O(n) auxiliary space. Quicksort and heapsort are in-place but unstable. There are in-place stable sorts — block sort, for example — but their constant factors are bad enough that they're rarely worth it. In practice you pick stable when you need multi-key ordering or when the elements carry identity (records, objects), and in-place when memory is the binding constraint.

    Cross-question: "Is Python's sorted() stable?"

    Yes. Both list.sort() and sorted() use Timsort, which is guaranteed stable, and CPython documents that guarantee — so it's safe to rely on it. That's why the idiom sorted(records, key=lambda r: r.dept) after sorted(records, key=lambda r: r.salary) gives you dept-then-salary ordering.

    Bubble Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Bubble sort baar baar array par ghoomta hai aur har do padosi elements ko compare karke, agar galat order mein hain to swap kar deta hai. Har full pass ke baad sabse bada bacha hua element apni final jagah (array ke end ki taraf) pahunch jata hai — jaise paani mein hawa ka bubble upar aa jata hai. Isi se naam pada.

    Real-world analogy: School assembly mein bachche height ke hisaab se line mein lagne hain. Teacher line ke ek sire se chalti hai aur sirf do-do bachchon ko compare karti hai: "tum lamba ho, tum peeche jao" — swap. Aage badho, agla jodi. Ek poore chakkar ke baad sabse lamba bachcha line ke end mein pahunch chuka hoga, chahe wo shuru mein kahin bhi khada tha. Ab teacher dobara shuru se chalti hai, par ab last wale ko chhod deti hai kyunki wo settle ho chuka hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Bubble sort ka "kyu" thoda alag hai — ye kisi problem ko solve karne ke liye nahi bana, ye sabse pehla, sabse naive idea hai jo kisi ko bhi soojhega. Iski value ye hai ki:

    1. Ye correctness ka sabse aasan proof deta hai. Agar koi bhi padosi jodi galat order mein nahi hai, to poora array sorted hai. Bas.
    2. Ye baaki sab algorithms ke liye baseline hai. Jab hum kehte hain "selection sort bubble se behtar hai kyunki kam swaps karta hai", to hume bubble ka number pata hona chahiye.
    3. Interview mein iska early-exit optimisation poochha jata hai, jo "adaptive" concept ko introduce karta hai.

    Bubble ki kharabi: ye bahut zyada swaps karta hai. Ek element ko apni jagah pahunchne ke liye ek-ek step karke chalna padta hai. Agar sabse chhota element array ke end par hai, use shuru tak aane mein n-1 alag alag swaps lagenge, ek pass mein sirf ek kadam. Isi kharabi ko theek karne ke liye selection sort aur insertion sort aate hain.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Array: [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]

Pass 1 — poore array par chalo, padosi compare karo:

  [5, 1, 4, 2, 8]      5 > 1 ? haan -> swap
   ^  ^
  [1, 5, 4, 2, 8]      5 > 4 ? haan -> swap
      ^  ^
  [1, 4, 5, 2, 8]      5 > 2 ? haan -> swap
         ^  ^
  [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]      5 > 8 ? nahi -> rehne do
            ^  ^
  [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]      <- pass 1 khatam. 8 apni final jagah par LOCK ho gaya.
                |
                +-- sorted zone (size 1)

Pass 2 — ab sirf pehle 4 elements dekho (8 ko chhod do):

  [1, 4, 2, 5 | 8]     1 > 4 ? nahi
  [1, 4, 2, 5 | 8]     4 > 2 ? haan -> swap
  [1, 2, 4, 5 | 8]     4 > 5 ? nahi
  [1, 2, 4 | 5, 8]     <- 5 lock. sorted zone size 2.

Pass 3 — pehle 3 elements:
  [1, 2, 4 | 5, 8]     1>2 nahi, 2>4 nahi
  [1, 2 | 4, 5, 8]     <- 4 lock.

Pass 4 — pehle 2:
  [1, 2 | 4, 5, 8]     1>2 nahi
  [1 | 2, 4, 5, 8]     <- 2 lock. Bacha hua ek element apne aap sorted hai.

    Invariant (wo sach jo har pass ke baad hamesha true rehta hai): i passes ke baad, array ke last i elements apni final sorted position par hain aur unse chhote sab elements unke left mein hain. Ye invariant hi correctness ka proof hai — n-1 passes ke baad last n-1 elements sahi jagah par hain, aur bacha hua pehla element automatically sahi jagah par hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [5, 1, 4, 2, 8], n = 5.

    Pass 1 (i = 0, inner loop j 0 se 3 tak):

    Step j Compare arr[j] > arr[j+1]? Swap? Array ke baad
    1 0 5 vs 1 5 > 1 → haan Yes [1, 5, 4, 2, 8]
    2 1 5 vs 4 5 > 4 → haan Yes [1, 4, 5, 2, 8]
    3 2 5 vs 2 5 > 2 → haan Yes [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]
    4 3 5 vs 8 5 > 8 → nahi No [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]

    Pass 1 ke baad: [1, 4, 2, 5, | 8] — 4 comparisons, 3 swaps. 8 locked.

    Pass 2 (i = 1, inner loop j 0 se 2 tak):

    Step j Compare Bada? Swap? Array ke baad
    1 0 1 vs 4 nahi No [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]
    2 1 4 vs 2 haan Yes [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]
    3 2 4 vs 5 nahi No [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

    Pass 2 ke baad: [1, 2, 4, | 5, 8] — 3 comparisons, 1 swap. 5 locked.

    Pass 3 (i = 2, j 0 se 1 tak):

    Step j Compare Bada? Swap? Array ke baad
    1 0 1 vs 2 nahi No [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]
    2 1 2 vs 4 nahi No [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

    Pass 3 ke baad: [1, 2, | 4, 5, 8] — 2 comparisons, 0 swaps. 4 locked.

    Pass 4 (i = 3, j sirf 0):

    Step j Compare Bada? Swap? Array ke baad
    1 0 1 vs 2 nahi No [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

    Pass 4 ke baad: [1, | 2, 4, 5, 8] — 1 comparison, 0 swaps. Loop khatam.

    Total: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons, 4 swaps. Dhyaan do: pass 3 aur pass 4 mein ek bhi swap nahi hua — array to pass 2 ke baad hi sorted ho gaya tha, par plain bubble sort ko ye pata nahi chala aur usne 3 fizool comparisons kar diye. Yahi wo kharabi hai jise optimised bubble sort theek karta hai.

    Code¶

    def bubble_sort(arr):
    """Array ko chhote se bade order mein sort karta hai. In-place: original list badalti hai."""
    n = len(arr)                                  # 1
    for i in range(n - 1):                        # 2
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):                # 3
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:               # 4
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]   # 5
    return arr                                    # 6

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length ko ek baar variable mein rakh liya. len() Python mein O(1) hai (list apni length store karti hai), to speed ka fayda mamooli hai, par readability ka fayda bada hai: neeche do jagah n use ho raha hai aur ek jagah badalni ho to ek hi jagah badlegi. Agar aap yahan len(arr) inline likhte, to code chalta to sahi, bas har iteration par ek function call extra hoti.

    2. for i in range(n - 1) — ye outer loop, yaani "kitne passes karne hain". n - 1 kyun, n kyun nahi? Kyunki har pass ek element ko lock karta hai. n - 1 elements lock karne ke baad, aakhri bacha hua element automatically apni jagah par hai — usse compare karne ko koi bacha hi nahi. Agar aap range(n) likh dete to code galat nahi hota, bas ek poora fizool pass extra chalta jisme inner loop range(n-1-(n-1)) = range(0) hota, yaani kuchh karta hi nahi. Yaani range(n) likhna = ek wasted iteration.

    3. for j in range(n - 1 - i) — ye inner loop, yaani "is pass mein kitni jodiyaan compare karni hain". Do cheezein ho rahi hain:

    4. n - 1 isliye ki j aur j+1 dono valid index hone chahiye. Agar j ki max value n-1 hoti, to arr[j+1] = arr[n] — IndexError. Ye sabse common bug hai jo log bubble sort likhte waqt karte hain.

    5. - i isliye ki pichhle i passes ne last i elements pehle hi lock kar diye hain, unhe dobara compare karna waste hai. Agar aap - i hata dete to code phir bhi sahi answer deta (kyunki lock kiye hue elements already sorted hain, unme swap hoga hi nahi), bas comparisons n² ke poore ho jaate n²/2 ke bajaye — yaani 2x dheema.

    6. if arr[j] > arr[j + 1] — ye poora algorithm yahin hai. Strictly greater (>) use kiya hai, >= nahi. Ye choice stability decide karti hai: agar do elements barabar hain to > false dega, swap nahi hoga, unka aapsi order bana rahega — stable. Agar aap >= likh dete to barabar elements bhi swap ho jaate aur sort unstable ho jata, bina kisi fayde ke — bas extra swaps. Ye ek-character ka farak interview mein pooch liya jata hai.

    7. arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j] — Python ka tuple swap. Right side pehle poori evaluate hoti hai (ek temporary tuple (arr[j+1], arr[j]) banti hai), phir left side ko assign hoti hai. Isliye temp variable ki zaroorat nahi. Agar aap C-style likhte — arr[j] = arr[j+1] phir arr[j+1] = arr[j] — to dono jagah same value aa jati aur ek element gum ho jata. Isliye ya to tuple swap karo ya tmp variable use karo.

    8. return arr — Python convention ke hisaab se in-place functions None return karte hain (jaise list.sort()), par yahan arr return karna chaining aur testing ke liye convenient hai. Yaad rahe: ye copy nahi return kar raha, wahi original list return kar raha hai jo modify ho chuki hai. Agar caller ko original chahiye tha, to use pehle bubble_sort(arr[:]) bhejna chahiye tha.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Comparisons ginte hain. Inner loop pass i mein exactly n - 1 - i baar chalta hai:

    i = 0  ->  n-1 comparisons
i = 1  ->  n-2 comparisons
i = 2  ->  n-3 comparisons
...
i = n-2 -> 1 comparison

Total = (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1

    Ye ek arithmetic series hai. Iska formula derive karne ka Gauss wala trick:

    S      =  1  +  2  + ... + (n-2) + (n-1)
S      = (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1      (ulta likha)
-----------------------------------------  jodo
2S     =  n  +  n  + ... +  n  +  n        (n-1 baar)
2S     = n(n-1)
S      = n(n-1)/2

    n(n-1)/2 = (n² - n)/2. Bade n ke liye n² dominate karta hai, constant 1/2 aur -n/2 ignore ho jaate hain → O(n²) comparisons, hamesha. Chahe array already sorted ho, plain bubble sort ye saare comparisons karega hi.

    Swaps ginte hain. - Best case (already sorted): 0 swaps. Comparisons phir bhi n(n-1)/2. - Worst case (reverse sorted): har comparison par swap → n(n-1)/2 swaps → O(n²). - Average case: har jodi ke inverted hone ka chance 50% → ~n(n-1)/4 swaps → phir bhi O(n²).

    Ek aur tareeka soch ka — inversions. Ek "inversion" matlab aisi jodi (i, j) jahan i < j par arr[i] > arr[j]. Bubble sort ka har swap exactly ek inversion hataata hai (kyunki wo padosi swap karta hai). Reverse-sorted array mein n(n-1)/2 inversions hote hain, isliye utne hi swaps lagenge. Ye insight aage insertion sort ke complexity mein bhi kaam aayegi.

    Space: Sirf i, j, n — teen variables, input size se independent → O(1) auxiliary space. Koi recursion nahi, to stack bhi O(1).

    Case Time Kab hota hai
    Best O(n²) — plain version Already sorted (par plain version detect nahi karta)
    Average O(n²) Random order
    Worst O(n²) Reverse sorted
    Space O(1) Hamesha

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Bubble sort Kyun
    Stable Haan > use hota hai, >= nahi — barabar elements kabhi swap nahi hote, to unka original order intact rehta hai
    In-place Haan Sirf constant extra variables, koi extra array nahi
    Adaptive Nahi (plain version) Sorted input par bhi poore n(n-1)/2 comparisons karta hai. Early-exit version isse adaptive bana deta hai

    Kisko farak padta hai? Stability ka fayda tab hai jab aap objects sort kar rahe ho — jaise test results ko duration se sort karo par same duration wale tests apne execution order mein hi rahen. In-place ka fayda tab hai jab memory tight ho. Adaptive na hona bubble sort ki sabse badi practical kami hai, aur wahi agle section mein theek hogi.

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Aapko padhaana hai ya khud seekhna hai — sabse aasan mental model. - Array bahut chhota hai (n < 10) aur code simplicity sab se zyada matter karti hai. - Aapko sirf ye check karna hai ki array sorted hai ya nahi (ek single pass, no swaps → sorted).

    Mat use karo jab: - Production code mein — kabhi bhi. sorted() har haal mein behtar hai. - n > ~50 — insertion sort same O(n²) hote hue bhi practically 2-3x tez hai kyunki wo swaps ki jagah shifts karta hai aur nearly-sorted data par O(n) ho jata hai. - Interview coding round mein solution ke taur par — interviewer ise "didn't think about it" ka signal maanta hai. Haan, agar wo khud bubble sort poochhe to alag baat hai.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Early exit — agar ek poore pass mein koi swap na ho to break Best case O(n²) → O(n), algorithm adaptive ban jata hai Ek boolean flag, na ke barabar cost
    2 Last-swap boundary — ye yaad rakho ki last swap kis index par hua tha, agle pass mein bas wahin tak jao Partially sorted tails par kaafi passes bachte hain Ek extra integer
    3 Cocktail shaker sort — ek pass left→right, agla right→left "Turtles" (chhote elements jo end par hain) tez aage aate hain; roughly 2x kam passes Code lamba, complexity phir bhi O(n²)
    4 Comb sort — shuru mein door ke elements compare karo (gap = n/1.3), gap dheere dheere 1 tak lao Practically O(n log n) ke aas paas, turtles turant hat jaate hain Ab ye bubble sort nahi raha, ye shell sort ka cousin hai; stability chali jati hai
    5 Odd-even transposition sort — alternate passes mein sirf odd ya even index pairs Parallel hardware par har pass ke saare comparisons ek saath ho sakte hain Sequential machine par koi fayda nahi

    Inme se #1 wo hai jo aapko interview mein khud se bolna chahiye, aur wahi hum agle section mein poora likh rahe hain.

    Interview answer: Bubble sort repeatedly walks the array comparing adjacent pairs and swapping them when they're out of order. After the first full pass the largest element has bubbled to the last position, after the second pass the second largest is in place, and so on — so after i passes the last i elements are final. That invariant is the correctness argument.

    Complexity: the inner loop runs n-1, then n-2, down to 1 times, and that sum is n(n-1)/2, so it's O(n²) comparisons in every case. Swaps are O(n²) in the worst case — reverse-sorted input — and zero in the best case. Space is O(1), it's in-place, and it's stable because we swap only on a strict greater-than, so equal elements never cross each other.

    The plain version is not adaptive: it does the full n(n-1)/2 comparisons even on already-sorted input. The standard fix is a swapped flag — if a full pass completes with no swaps the array is sorted and we break, which makes the best case O(n). In practice I'd never ship bubble sort; insertion sort has the same asymptotic class but much better constants because it shifts rather than swaps, and it's genuinely adaptive.

    Cross-question: "Why does one pass of bubble sort guarantee the maximum ends up last?"

    Because once the scan reaches the maximum element, every subsequent comparison has the maximum on the left, so every one of those comparisons swaps it one step right. There's nothing that can stop it, so it travels unbroken to the end of the pass range.

    Cross-question: "Bubble sort does O(n²) swaps and selection sort does O(n) swaps. Does that make selection sort faster?"

    On memory writes, yes — selection sort is the better choice when writes are expensive, like on flash storage or EEPROM. But both do O(n²) comparisons, so asymptotically they're the same class, and on ordinary RAM the difference is a constant factor. The bigger practical winner is insertion sort, which is adaptive: on nearly sorted data it approaches O(n) while both bubble and selection stay at O(n²).

    Optimised Bubble Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Wahi bubble sort, par ek chhote se sawaal ke saath: "is poore pass mein kya maine ek bhi swap kiya?" Agar jawab "nahi" hai, to iska matlab koi bhi padosi jodi galat order mein nahi thi, yaani array pehle hi sorted hai — aur hum turant ruk jaate hain.

    Real-world analogy: Wahi assembly line wali teacher. Ek poora chakkar lagane ke baad agar usne ek bhi bachche ko idhar-udhar nahi kiya, to line already sahi hai — ab aur chakkar lagane ka koi matlab nahi. Plain bubble sort wali teacher bewakoofi se poore n-1 chakkar lagati rehti hai chahe line pehle din se hi sahi ho.

    Kyu hai¶

    Plain bubble sort ki dry run mein humne dekha tha: [5,1,4,2,8] pass 2 ke baad hi sorted ho gaya tha, par algorithm ne pass 3 aur pass 4 bhi chalaye — 3 fizool comparisons.

    Chhote array par ye 3 comparisons ki baat hai. Par socho 10,000 elements ka array jo pehle se sorted hai (bahut common — database se sorted data aa raha hai, ya aapne pehle hi sort kar liya tha aur dobara sort call ho gaya). Plain bubble sort 5 crore comparisons karega. Optimised version 9,999 comparisons karke ruk jayega. Ye 5000x ka farak hai, aur ye ek boolean variable ki keemat par mila hai.

    Yahi is optimisation ka poora point hai: algorithm ko adaptive banana — input ki halat dekh kar kaam kam karna.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Har pass ki shuruaat mein:  swapped = False

  Jab bhi koi swap ho:      swapped = True

Pass ke end mein:
  agar swapped abhi bhi False hai
      -> is poore pass mein koi padosi jodi galat order mein nahi thi
      -> "har i ke liye arr[i] <= arr[i+1]"  == definition of sorted
      -> break

    Ye kyun guaranteed sahi hai? Kyunki "sorted" ki definition hi yahi hai: har padosi jodi sahi order mein. Bubble sort ka ek poora pass har padosi jodi ko exactly ek baar check karta hai. Agar sab pass ho gaye, to array sorted hai. Ye koi heuristic ya guess nahi, ye proof hai.

    Doosra optimisation — last swap boundary:

    Pass ke dauraan yaad rakho: aakhri swap kis index par hua?  ->  last_swap

Agar last swap index 3 par hua, iska matlab index 4 se aage sab jodiyaan sahi thin
      [ ?  ?  ?  ?  | sorted sorted sorted ]
                  ^
              last_swap

Agle pass mein sirf index 0 se last_swap tak jao. Ek pass mein kai elements ek saath lock ho
sakte hain, sirf ek nahi.

    Example: [2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 1 mein sirf ek swap hoga (index 0 par), baaki sab comparisons pass ho jayenge. last_swap = 0. Ab agle pass ki range 0 se 0 hai — yaani inner loop chalega hi nahi, swapped False rahega, break. Total: 7 + 0 comparisons. Simple early-exit version 7 + 7 = 14 karta. Boundary version ne aadhe kaam mein khatam kiya.

    Poora dry run¶

    Do inputs par trace karte hain taaki dono kaam dikh jaayen.

    Dry run A — input [5, 1, 4, 2, 8] (wahi jo plain version mein tha):

    Pass 1 (swapped = False se shuru, range j = 0..3):

    j Compare Swap? Array swapped last_swap
    0 5 vs 1 Yes [1,5,4,2,8] True 0
    1 5 vs 4 Yes [1,4,5,2,8] True 1
    2 5 vs 2 Yes [1,4,2,5,8] True 2
    3 5 vs 8 No [1,4,2,5,8] True 2

    Pass 1 end: swapped = True → continue. last_swap = 2 → agla pass sirf j = 0..1.

    Pass 2 (swapped = False, range j = 0..1):

    j Compare Swap? Array swapped last_swap
    0 1 vs 4 No [1,4,2,5,8] False —
    1 4 vs 2 Yes [1,2,4,5,8] True 1

    Pass 2 end: swapped = True → continue. last_swap = 1 → agla pass j = 0..0.

    Pass 3 (swapped = False, range j = 0..0):

    j Compare Swap? Array swapped
    0 1 vs 2 No [1,2,4,5,8] False

    Pass 3 end: swapped = False → BREAK.

    Comparison: plain bubble = 10 comparisons. Early-exit + boundary = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 comparisons. 30% kam, aur ye chhota input hai.

    Dry run B — input [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (already sorted):

    Pass 1 (swapped = False, j = 0..3):

    j Compare Swap? swapped
    0 1 vs 2 No False
    1 2 vs 3 No False
    2 3 vs 4 No False
    3 4 vs 5 No False

    Pass 1 end: swapped = False → BREAK.

    Total: 4 comparisons, 0 swaps. Plain bubble sort ne 10 comparisons kiye hote. n = 10,000 par: 9,999 vs 5,00,00,000. Yahi adaptive hone ka matlab hai.

    Code¶

    def bubble_sort_optimised(arr):
    """Early-exit + last-swap-boundary ke saath bubble sort."""
    n = len(arr)                                  # 1
    end = n - 1                                   # 2
    while end > 0:                                # 3
        last_swap = 0                             # 4
        for j in range(end):                      # 5
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:               # 6
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]   # 7
                last_swap = j                     # 8
        end = last_swap                           # 9
    return arr                                    # 10

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length ek baar nikaal li. Baaki poore function mein array ki length badalti nahi, isliye ek baar nikaalna safe hai.

    2. end = n - 1 — end ka matlab hai "is pass mein j kahan tak jayega (exclusive)". Shuruaat mein n - 1, kyunki j ki max value n-2 honi chahiye taaki arr[j+1] valid rahe. Agar aap end = n likh dete, to pehle hi pass mein arr[n] par IndexError.

    3. while end > 0 — for ki jagah while isliye use kiya kyunki passes ki sankhya pehle se pata nahi hai. Ye input par depend karti hai — sorted input par 1 pass, reverse input par n-1. for i in range(n-1) likh kar break bhi kar sakte the, par while zyada honest hai: ye seedha bolta hai "jab tak unsorted region bacha hai, chalte raho". Condition > 0 hai, >= 0 nahi — agar end = 0 ho gaya to range(0) khali hai, loop kuchh nahi karta aur infinite loop ban jata. Ye classic infinite-loop bug hai.

    4. last_swap = 0 — har pass ki shuruaat mein reset. Ye reset sabse important line hai. Agar aap ise while ke bahar rakh dete, to pichhle pass ki value carry ho jati aur end kabhi ghatta nahi — infinite loop. Value 0 isliye rakhi hai kyunki wo "koi swap nahi hua" ko bhi represent karti hai: agar pass ke baad last_swap abhi bhi 0 hai to end = 0 ho jayega aur while khatam. Yaani ek hi variable early-exit flag aur boundary dono ka kaam kar raha hai — alag swapped boolean ki zaroorat hi nahi.

    5. for j in range(end) — j 0 se end-1 tak. Har iteration mein arr[j] aur arr[j+1] ki jodi. Max j = end - 1, to max index touch hoga end — jo hamesha valid hai kyunki end <= n-1.

    6. if arr[j] > arr[j + 1] — wahi strict greater-than. Stability ke liye zaroori.

    7. Tuple swap — same as before.

    8. last_swap = j — j store kar rahe hain, j+1 nahi. Ye off-by-one sochne layak hai. Agar swap index j par hua, to arr[j] aur arr[j+1] dono touch hue. Iska matlab index j+1 ke baad wali jodiyaan pakka sahi thin. Agle pass mein hume j = 0 se j = last_swap - 1 tak jaana chahiye... par actually hume j = last_swap tak bhi jaana chahiye kyunki arr[j] ki value badal gayi hai aur uske left wale se dobara compare karna pad sakta hai. Isliye end = last_swap set karte hain jisse range(end) j ko 0..last_swap-1 deta hai — yaani jodi (last_swap-1, last_swap) tak. Ye exactly utna hai jitna zaroori hai. Agar aap last_swap = j + 1 likh dete to ek extra fizool comparison har pass mein hoti (galat nahi, bas slightly slow).

    9. end = last_swap — agle pass ki boundary set. Agar is pass mein koi swap nahi hua to last_swap abhi bhi 0 hai → end = 0 → while condition fail → early exit. Agar swap hua to end chhota ho gaya → agla pass chhota. Dono optimisations ek line mein.

    10. return arr — in-place modified array.

    Ek simpler version bhi jaan lo (agar interview mein sirf early exit poochha jaye):

    def bubble_sort_early_exit(arr):
    n = len(arr)                        # 1
    for i in range(n - 1):              # 2
        swapped = False                 # 3
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):      # 4
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:     # 5
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]  # 6
                swapped = True          # 7
        if not swapped:                 # 8
            break                       # 9
    return arr                          # 10
    1. Length nikaali.
    2. Outer loop, n-1 passes maximum.
    3. swapped = False — loop ke andar, har pass ke liye fresh. Bahar rakhne se pehla swap hone ke baad ye hamesha True rehta aur early exit kabhi trigger nahi hota — optimisation silently mar jati, code phir bhi sahi answer deta. Aisa bug pakadna mushkil hai kyunki test pass ho jate hain, bas performance nahi milti.
    4. Inner loop, - i se already-locked tail skip.
    5. Strict greater-than compare.
    6. Swap.
    7. swapped = True — flag set. Note: hum sirf True set karte hain, kabhi False nahi — ek bhi swap kaafi hai batane ke liye ki array abhi sorted nahi tha.
    8. if not swapped — poora pass bina swap ke nikla → sorted.
    9. break — bahar. return bhi likh sakte the, par break se function ka single exit point bana rehta hai jo debug karne mein aasan hai.
    10. Return.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Best case — already sorted input:

    Pass 1: n-1 comparisons, 0 swaps
        last_swap = 0  ->  end = 0  ->  while khatam

Total comparisons = n - 1  ->  O(n)
Total swaps       = 0      ->  O(1)

    Ye pehla algorithm hai jiska best case O(n) hai. Isi ko "adaptive" kehte hain.

    Worst case — reverse sorted [5,4,3,2,1]:

    Har pass mein har comparison swap banti hai, to last_swap hamesha end - 1 hota hai, yaani end har pass mein sirf 1 ghatta hai — exactly plain bubble sort jaisa:

    (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2  ->  O(n²)

    Optimisation ne worst case mein kuchh nahi bachaya. Ye important hai: optimisation best aur average case ko theek karti hai, worst case ki asymptotic class wahi rehti hai.

    Average case: Random permutation par expected passes ~n, aur har pass O(n) → O(n²). Constant factor plain version se chhota hai (typically 30-40% kam comparisons), par class wahi.

    Space: n, end, last_swap, j — 4 variables → O(1).

    Case Comparisons Swaps Kab
    Best O(n) 0 Already sorted
    Average O(n²) O(n²) Random
    Worst O(n²) O(n²) Reverse sorted
    Space O(1) — Hamesha

    Nearly-sorted ka special case: Agar array mein sirf k inversions hain (k chhota), to swaps exactly k honge (kyunki har swap ek inversion hataata hai) aur passes ~k se bandhe honge. Yaani nearly-sorted par ye practically O(n·k) chalta hai, jo k chhota hone par O(n) ke kareeb hai.

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan > strict comparison — equal elements swap nahi hote
    In-place Haan O(1) extra memory
    Adaptive Haan Sorted par O(n), nearly-sorted par inversions ke proportional. Yahi wo cheez hai jo plain version mein nahi thi

    Adaptive hone ka practical matlab: QA mein aap aksar aisa data sort karte ho jo pehle se mostly sorted hai — timestamps, IDs, test execution order. Adaptive algorithm us structure ka faayda uthata hai. Yahi soch aage Timsort tak le jayegi, jo isi idea ko industrial level par le jata hai.

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Interview mein bubble sort poochha gaya ho — ye version likho, plain nahi. Ye dikhata hai ki aap best case ke baare mein sochte ho. - Aapko sirf "kya array sorted hai?" check karna ho — pehla pass hi bata dega. - Bahut chhota, almost-sorted data aur aap external library nahi use kar sakte.

    Mat use karo jab: - Random ya reverse-sorted data — worst case abhi bhi O(n²). - Production — insertion sort same properties ke saath consistently tez hai.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Early exit flag Best case O(n), adaptive 1 boolean
    2 Last-swap boundary (upar wala code) Ek pass mein kai elements lock, ~30-40% kam comparisons average par 1 integer, flag ki zaroorat khatam
    3 Cocktail shaker (bidirectional) "Turtle" problem — chhota element jo end par hai — ka fix. Passes ~aadhe Code double, worst case wahi O(n²)
    4 Comb sort (gap shrink 1.3x) Practically ~O(n log n), turtles turant fix Stability chali gayi, ab ye shell sort family hai
    5 Insertion sort par switch kar do Har case mein behtar "Ab ye bubble sort nahi raha"

    Point #5 ek asli interview insight hai: bubble sort ka har optimisation aapko insertion sort ya shell sort ki taraf le jata hai. Agar aapko bubble sort optimize karna hi hai, to sabse acchi optimisation hai use replace kar dena.

    Interview answer: The plain bubble sort wastes work: it keeps running passes even after the array has become sorted. The standard fix is a swapped flag — if a complete pass performs no swaps, then no adjacent pair is out of order, which is exactly the definition of sorted, so we can break immediately. That turns the best case from O(n²) into O(n) and makes the algorithm adaptive.

    A second, better optimisation is to remember the index of the last swap in each pass. Everything to the right of that index is already in final position, so the next pass only needs to scan up to that boundary. That can lock multiple elements per pass instead of just one, and it subsumes the flag — if the last-swap index stays at zero, no swap happened, and the loop terminates naturally.

    Neither optimisation helps the worst case. On reverse-sorted input every comparison still swaps, the boundary shrinks by one each pass, and we're back to n(n-1)/2 comparisons — O(n²). So it improves the best and average cases, not the asymptotic worst case.

    Cross-question: "Where would you initialise the swapped flag, and what breaks if you get it wrong?"

    Inside the outer loop, at the start of each pass. If you initialise it outside, the first swap anywhere sets it True permanently and the early exit never fires. The dangerous part is that the code still produces correct output — only the performance benefit silently disappears — so unit tests won't catch it. You'd only see it in a benchmark.

    Cross-question: "You store last_swap = j rather than j + 1. Why?"

    Because after a swap at index j, the value at position j has changed and may still need to move further left, so position j must remain inside the next pass's range. Setting end = last_swap makes range(end) cover j from 0 to last_swap - 1, which compares pairs up through (last_swap - 1, last_swap) — exactly the region that can still contain an inversion. Using j + 1 would be correct too, just one redundant comparison per pass.

    Selection Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Selection sort baar baar bache hue unsorted hisse mein se sabse chhota element dhoondhta hai aur use unsorted hisse ke sabse pehle position par le jata hai — ek hi swap mein.

    Real-world analogy: Aapke saamne mez par 8 books bikhri hain aur unhe height ke hisaab se shelf par lagana hai. Aap saari books par nazar daurate ho, sabse chhoti book dhoondhte ho, uthate ho, shelf par pehli jagah rakh dete ho. Phir bachi hui 7 books par nazar, sabse chhoti, shelf par doosri jagah. Aap poori nazar daurate ho (n comparisons) par haath sirf ek baar lagate ho (1 swap). Yahi selection sort ki khaas baat hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Bubble sort ki sabse badi practical kharabi thi: bahut zyada swaps. Ek element ko apni jagah tak pahunchane ke liye bubble sort use ek-ek karke sarkata hai — n positions door hai to n alag swaps.

    Selection sort ne kaha: "Compare to karne hi padenge (O(n²) unavoidable hai comparison-based mein), par swap sirf tab karo jab tumhe pakka pata ho kahan rakhna hai." Wo poore unsorted region ko scan karke minimum ka index note karta hai, aur exactly ek swap karta hai.

    Ye trade kab faayde ka hai? Jab write operation, read operation se mehnga ho:

    Storage Read cost Write cost Selection sort ka fayda
    RAM 1 unit 1 unit Mamooli
    SSD / Flash 1 unit ~10-100 units + wear Bada
    EEPROM 1 unit Bahut zyada, limited write cycles Bahut bada
    Network / remote store 1 RTT 1 RTT + risk Bada

    Aur ek theoretical baat: selection sort minimum possible swaps ke bahut kareeb hai. Koi bhi sort kam se kam n - (number of cycles in the permutation) swaps karega. Selection sort n-1 karta hai — upper bound par, par O(n) class mein, jabki bubble O(n²) mein.

    Selection sort ki apni kharabi: ye adaptive nahi hai, bilkul bhi nahi. Already sorted array par bhi wo poore n(n-1)/2 comparisons karega, kyunki use har baar minimum "prove" karna padta hai. Isi kharabi ko insertion sort theek karta hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Array ko do hisson mein socho:

  [ sorted, final positions | unsorted, abhi dekhna baaki ]
                            ^
                            i  (boundary)

Har step:
  1. arr[i..n-1] mein se minimum ka index dhoondho  ->  min_idx
  2. arr[i] aur arr[min_idx] ko swap karo
  3. boundary ek aage badhao (i += 1)

Example: [64, 25, 12, 22, 11]

i=0:  [ | 64  25  12  22  11 ]   min = 11 at index 4
      swap arr[0] <-> arr[4]
      [ 11 | 25  12  22  64 ]

i=1:  [ 11 | 25  12  22  64 ]    min of (25,12,22,64) = 12 at index 2
      swap arr[1] <-> arr[2]
      [ 11  12 | 25  22  64 ]

i=2:  [ 11  12 | 25  22  64 ]    min of (25,22,64) = 22 at index 3
      swap arr[2] <-> arr[3]
      [ 11  12  22 | 25  64 ]

i=3:  [ 11  12  22 | 25  64 ]    min of (25,64) = 25 at index 3 (khud)
      swap arr[3] <-> arr[3]  (kuchh nahi hua)
      [ 11  12  22  25 | 64 ]

i=4 ki zaroorat nahi — ek element hamesha sorted hai.

    Invariant: i iterations ke baad, arr[0..i-1] mein poore array ke sabse chhote i elements sorted order mein hain, aur wo apni final positions par hain — kabhi dobara nahi hilenge.

    Bubble sort ka invariant ulta tha (bade elements right mein lock hote the); selection sort mein chhote elements left mein lock hote hain. Dono valid hain.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [64, 25, 12, 22, 11], n = 5.

    Outer iteration i = 0 — min_idx shuru mein 0 (value 64):

    j arr[j] arr[min_idx] Chhota? Naya min_idx Naya min value
    1 25 64 Yes 1 25
    2 12 25 Yes 2 12
    3 22 12 No 2 12
    4 11 12 Yes 4 11

    Swap arr[0] (64) ↔ arr[4] (11) → [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]. 4 comparisons, 1 swap.

    Outer iteration i = 1 — min_idx shuru mein 1 (value 25):

    j arr[j] arr[min_idx] Chhota? Naya min_idx Naya min value
    2 12 25 Yes 2 12
    3 22 12 No 2 12
    4 64 12 No 2 12

    Swap arr[1] (25) ↔ arr[2] (12) → [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]. 3 comparisons, 1 swap.

    Outer iteration i = 2 — min_idx shuru mein 2 (value 25):

    j arr[j] arr[min_idx] Chhota? Naya min_idx Naya min value
    3 22 25 Yes 3 22
    4 64 22 No 3 22

    Swap arr[2] (25) ↔ arr[3] (22) → [11, 12, 22, 25, 64]. 2 comparisons, 1 swap.

    Outer iteration i = 3 — min_idx shuru mein 3 (value 25):

    j arr[j] arr[min_idx] Chhota? Naya min_idx
    4 64 25 No 3

    min_idx == i → swap ki zaroorat nahi (ya self-swap, no-op) → [11, 12, 22, 25, 64]. 1 comparison, 0 useful swaps.

    Total: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons, 3 real swaps.

    Bubble sort ne isi tarah ke input par 10 comparisons + 4 swaps kiye the. Yahan bhi 10 comparisons, par swaps hamesha <= n-1 = 4. Reverse-sorted input par bubble 10 swaps karta, selection sirf 2.

    Poora array state table:

    i Array shuruaat mein min_idx mila Swap Array baad mein Sorted prefix
    0 [64,25,12,22,11] 4 (val 11) 0↔4 [11,25,12,22,64] [11]
    1 [11,25,12,22,64] 2 (val 12) 1↔2 [11,12,25,22,64] [11,12]
    2 [11,12,25,22,64] 3 (val 22) 2↔3 [11,12,22,25,64] [11,12,22]
    3 [11,12,22,25,64] 3 (val 25) none [11,12,22,25,64] [11,12,22,25]

    Code¶

    def selection_sort(arr):
    """Har pass mein bacha hua minimum dhoondh kar aage laata hai. In-place."""
    n = len(arr)                              # 1
    for i in range(n - 1):                    # 2
        min_idx = i                           # 3
        for j in range(i + 1, n):             # 4
            if arr[j] < arr[min_idx]:         # 5
                min_idx = j                   # 6
        if min_idx != i:                      # 7
            arr[i], arr[min_idx] = arr[min_idx], arr[i]   # 8
    return arr                                # 9

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length ek baar, dono loops mein use hogi.

    2. for i in range(n - 1) — i sorted/unsorted boundary hai. n - 1 tak hi jaana hai, n tak nahi: jab i = n-1 par pahunchoge to unsorted region mein sirf ek element bacha hai (arr[n-1]), aur ek element hamesha apne aap sorted hai — usse compare karne ko koi nahi bacha. Agar aap range(n) likh dete to code sahi rehta par ek fizool iteration chalti jisme inner loop range(n, n) = khali hota. Ye "n-1 vs n" waali baat interview mein poochhi jati hai — jawab hai "the last element has nothing left to compare against".

    3. min_idx = i — assumption: abhi tak jo dekha usme arr[i] hi sabse chhota hai. min_idx ko i se initialise karna zaroori hai, 0 ya i+1 se nahi.

    4. Agar 0 se karte: arr[0] to already sorted zone mein hai aur sabse chhota hai — min_idx kabhi update hi nahi hota, aur aap sorted element ko baar baar swap karte rehte. Array corrupt.
    5. Agar i+1 se karte: aap arr[i] ko candidate hi nahi maante. Agar arr[i] sach mein minimum hai to aap galat element ko aage le aate. Wrong answer.

    6. Hum index store kar rahe hain, value nahi. Value store karte to swap ke waqt pata nahi chalta ki wo value kahan thi — dobara dhoondhna padta. Index se O(1) mein swap.

    7. for j in range(i + 1, n) — i+1 se shuru kyunki arr[i] ko humne already candidate maan liya hai (line 3), use khud se compare karna waste hai. n tak (exclusive) — poora unsorted region. Agar i se shuru karte to ek extra self-comparison hoti (arr[i] < arr[i] hamesha False) — galat nahi, bas fizool.

    8. if arr[j] < arr[min_idx] — strictly less than. Ye stability ke liye critical hai... ya theek se kahen, ye stability ko jitna bacha sakte hain utna bachata hai. < use karne se, agar arr[j] aur current minimum barabar hain to min_idx update nahi hota — yaani hum pehle wale equal element ko chunte hain. <= likh dete to hum baad wala chunte, jo equal elements ka order aur zyada todta. (Selection sort phir bhi unstable hai, par uski wajah alag hai — swap. Neeche detail mein.)

    9. min_idx = j — sirf index update. Har baar naya minimum milne par.

    10. if min_idx != i — swap sirf tab jab zaroorat ho. Agar min_idx == i to swap arr[i], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[i] hoga — no-op, par phir bhi do memory writes. Ye check un writes ko bachata hai. Practically RAM par ye chhota fayda hai, par flash/EEPROM par bada — aur wahi to selection sort ka poora selling point hai. Agar ye check hata do to code sahi rahega, bas "minimum writes" wala guarantee kamzor ho jayega.

    11. Tuple swap — arr[i] (unsorted region ka pehla) aur arr[min_idx] (unsorted region ka minimum) ki adla badli. Note karo ki arr[i] ki purani value ab min_idx par chali gayi hai — wo kahin bhi ho sakti hai unsorted region mein. Yahi jump stability todta hai.

    12. return arr — in-place modified.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Comparisons — ginte hain:

    i = 0    ->  j chalta hai 1 se n-1  ->  n-1 comparisons
i = 1    ->  j chalta hai 2 se n-1  ->  n-2 comparisons
i = 2    ->                          ->  n-3 comparisons
...
i = n-2  ->  j sirf n-1             ->  1 comparison

Total = (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2  =  (n² - n)/2  ->  O(n²)

    Ye sankhya input par bilkul depend nahi karti. Chahe array sorted ho, reverse ho, ya random — comparisons exactly n(n-1)/2 honge. Isliye selection sort ka best = average = worst = Theta(n²). Ye "Theta" likhna interview mein achha lagta hai, kyunki upper aur lower bound dono same hain.

    Swaps — ginte hain:

    Har outer iteration mein zyada se zyada 1 swap  ->  at most n-1 swaps  ->  O(n)
Best case (already sorted): min_idx hamesha == i  ->  0 swaps

    Ye selection sort ka main selling point hai: comparisons O(n²) par swaps sirf O(n).

    Bubble sort se comparison:

    Metric Bubble sort Selection sort
    Comparisons (worst) n(n-1)/2 n(n-1)/2
    Swaps (worst) n(n-1)/2 → O(n²) n-1 → O(n)
    Swaps (best) 0 0
    Memory writes Bahut zyada Bahut kam

    Space: n, i, j, min_idx — O(1). Koi recursion nahi.

    Case Comparisons Swaps Time
    Best n(n-1)/2 0 Theta(n²)
    Average n(n-1)/2 ~n-1 Theta(n²)
    Worst n(n-1)/2 n-1 Theta(n²)
    Space — — O(1)

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Nahi (standard array version) Swap door ke elements ko jump karwa deta hai, jisse equal elements ka order bigad sakta hai
    In-place Haan O(1) extra
    Adaptive Nahi, bilkul nahi Comparisons input par depend hi nahi karte

    Instability ka concrete counterexample — ye interview mein maanga jata hai:

    Input: [ 4a, 4b, 1 ]        (4a aur 4b barabar hain, 4a pehle hai)

i = 0:  unsorted = [4a, 4b, 1],  minimum = 1 at index 2
        swap arr[0] <-> arr[2]
        [ 1, 4b, 4a ]
              ^^   ^^
              ab 4b, 4a se PEHLE aa gaya!  Original order toota.

i = 1:  unsorted = [4b, 4a],  minimum = 4b (kyunki < use kiya, 4a update nahi karega)
        min_idx == 1 == i, koi swap nahi
        [ 1, 4b, 4a ]

Final: [1, 4b, 4a]  ->  UNSTABLE

    Dhyaan do ki galti comparison mein nahi, swap mein hui. 4a ko door phenk diya gaya 1 ke saath jagah badalne mein. Isi wajah se selection sort inherently unstable hai — chahe aap comparison kaise bhi likho.

    Stable banaya ja sakta hai? Haan, par cost ke saath: - Swap ki jagah rotation karo: minimum ko nikaal kar, beech ke saare elements ko ek position right shift karo, phir minimum ko i par rakho. Ab O(n) shifts per pass → swaps ka fayda khatam, aur ye basically insertion sort ban gaya. - Ya linked list use karo — wahan node ko unlink karke aage lagane mein baaki nodes hilte nahi, to stability bach jati hai.

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Writes mehngi hain — flash memory, EEPROM, ya koi bhi storage jiski write endurance limited hai. Selection sort guaranteed <= n-1 writes karta hai. - Aapko top-k chahiye, poora sort nahi — bas outer loop k baar chalao, O(n·k) mein k sabse chhote mil jaate hain. Chhote k ke liye ye heap se bhi simple hai. - Data itna chhota hai ki asymptotic farak matter nahi karta aur code ki simplicity chahiye.

    Mat use karo jab: - Data nearly sorted hai — selection sort ko farak hi nahi padta, wo poora n² karega. Insertion sort O(n) mein nikal jayega. - Stability chahiye — selection sort de hi nahi sakta. - n bada hai — n² comparisons kill kar denge.

    QA context: Agar aapko 10,000 test results mein se sabse dheeme 5 tests chahiye, to poora sort (O(n log n)) karne ki jagah selection sort ka logic 5 passes chala do → O(5n). Ya heapq.nsmallest(5, results) use karo, jo isi idea ka optimised version hai.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 if min_idx != i check Fizool self-swaps ke memory writes bachte hain Ek comparison per pass — na ke barabar
    2 Double selection — ek hi pass mein min aur max dono dhoondho, min ko aage aur max ko peeche rakho Passes aadhe (n/2), comparisons ~1.5n per pass ki jagah... net ~25% kam comparisons Code mein ek tricky edge case: agar max_idx == i to pehla swap use hila deta hai, use handle karna padta hai
    3 Heap se minimum nikalo (yaani heap sort) Minimum dhoondhna O(n) se O(log n) → poora sort O(n log n) Ab ye selection sort nahi, heap sort hai. Extra heap structure
    4 Tournament / tree selection Pehla minimum O(n) mein, baaki har minimum O(log n) mein (tournament tree ko update karke) O(n) extra space tree ke liye
    5 Rotation se stable banao Stability mil jati hai Swaps O(n) se O(n²) shifts ho jaate hain — main fayda khatam
    6 Partial sort (top-k) — outer loop sirf k baar O(n·k), poore sort se sasta jab k << log n Poora sorted array nahi milta

    Optimisation #3 ek badi seekh hai: selection sort ka bottleneck "minimum dhoondhna" hai, aur minimum dhoondhne ke liye best data structure heap hai. Selection sort + heap = heap sort. Yahi natural evolution hai, aur interview mein ye connection banana bahut acha lagta hai.

    Interview answer: Selection sort maintains a sorted prefix. In each pass it scans the entire unsorted suffix to find the minimum, then performs a single swap to move that minimum to the boundary. After i passes, the first i elements are the i smallest, in final position.

    The comparison count is fixed: n-1, then n-2, down to 1, which is n(n-1)/2 regardless of the input. So best, average and worst are all Theta(n²) — it is not adaptive at all. What it does optimise is writes: at most n-1 swaps, which is O(n), compared to O(n²) swaps for bubble sort. That makes it a reasonable choice when writes are much more expensive than reads — flash memory or EEPROM with limited write endurance.

    It is in-place with O(1) extra space, but it is not stable. The instability comes from the long swap, not the comparison: with input [4a, 4b, 1], the first pass swaps the 1 into position 0 and throws 4a to the end, so the output is [1, 4b, 4a] and the two equal 4s have swapped order. You can make it stable by rotating instead of swapping, but then you're doing O(n) writes per pass and you've lost the only advantage — at which point insertion sort is strictly better.

    Cross-question: "Selection sort and bubble sort are both O(n²). Is there any case where selection sort is asymptotically better?"

    Not in comparisons — both are Theta(n²) there. But in swaps, selection sort is O(n) while bubble sort is O(n²) in the worst case. If you measure the algorithm in memory writes rather than comparisons, selection sort is a full order better.

    Cross-question: "Why is selection sort not adaptive, when bubble sort with early exit is?"

    Because selection sort has to prove that a given element is the minimum of the remaining suffix, and the only way to prove that with comparisons is to look at every remaining element. There's no shortcut it can take from partial sortedness — nothing in a sorted prefix tells it anything about where the minimum of the suffix is. Bubble sort's early exit works because a swap-free pass is direct evidence of global sortedness; selection sort has no equivalent signal.

    Cross-question: "How would you get the 5 smallest elements from a million records?"

    I would not do a full sort. Two good options: run selection sort's outer loop only 5 times for O(5n), or maintain a max-heap of size 5 while streaming through the data for O(n log 5). In Python that's just heapq.nsmallest(5, records, key=...), which internally uses the heap approach. Full sorting would be O(n log n) — about 20 million comparisons here versus about 5 million for the partial approaches.

    Insertion Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Insertion sort array ke left mein ek sorted region rakhta hai aur ek-ek karke agla element uthakar us sorted region ke andar sahi jagah par ghusa deta hai — jagah banane ke liye bade elements ko ek position right shift karta jata hai.

    Real-world analogy: Taash ke patte. Aapke baaye haath mein pehle se lage hue patte hain, dahine haath se aap naya patta uthate ho aur baaye haath ke patton mein sahi jagah par ghusa dete ho. Aap poore haath ko dobara nahi lagate — bas naye patte ki jagah dhoondhte ho. Ye wahi algorithm hai jo har insaan bina padhe use karta hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Selection sort ki kharabi thi: wo input ki halat se seekhta hi nahi. Chahe array pehle se sorted ho, wo poore n(n-1)/2 comparisons karega, kyunki har baar use minimum "prove" karna padta hai.

    Insertion sort ne ulta approach liya: naye element ko sorted region mein daalna hai, aur sorted region mein search jaldi ruk sakta hai. Agar naya element sorted region ke last element se bada hai, to bas — wo apni jagah par hai, ek hi comparison mein kaam khatam. Isi "jaldi ruk jana" ki wajah se:

    Already sorted input:  har element sirf 1 comparison  ->  n-1 comparisons  ->  O(n)
Nearly sorted input:   har element sirf kuchh steps peeche jata hai  ->  ~O(n)

    Doosri badi baat: insertion sort swaps ki jagah shifts karta hai. Ek swap = 3 memory operations (temp = a; a = b; b = temp). Ek shift = 1 memory operation. Bubble sort ek element ko 5 positions peeche le jaane ke liye 5 swaps = 15 operations karta hai. Insertion sort 5 shifts + 1 final placement = 6 operations. Same asymptotic class, 2-3x behtar constant.

    Teesri baat: insertion sort online hai — aapko poora data pehle se nahi chahiye. Jaise jaise elements aayen, unhe insert karte jao. Selection sort ye nahi kar sakta (use minimum dhoondhne ke liye poora data chahiye), merge sort bhi nahi (use dono halves chahiye).

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    [ sorted region | unsorted region ]
                ^
                i  = wo element jise abhi insert karna hai

Step: key = arr[i] ko nikaal kar side mein rakh lo (uski jagah ab "khali" hai)
      j = i - 1 se peeche chalo:
          jab tak arr[j] > key ho, arr[j] ko ek kadam right shift karo
      jahan ruk gaye, wahin key rakh do

Example: [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3],  i = 2 (key = 4)

  [ 2  5 | 4  6  1  3 ]        key = 4, khali jagah index 2 par
    ^  ^
    sorted

  j=1: arr[1]=5 > 4 ?  haan  ->  5 ko right shift
  [ 2  _  5 | 6  1  3 ]

  j=0: arr[0]=2 > 4 ?  nahi  ->  ruk jao
  [ 2  4  5 | 6  1  3 ]        key = 4 ko khali jagah par rakh diya

    Invariant: Har iteration i ke shuru mein, arr[0..i-1] sorted hai (par ye zaroori nahi ki wo elements apni final positions par hon — aage aur elements aakar unhe right shift kara sakte hain). Ye selection sort se important farak hai: selection sort mein sorted prefix final hota hai, insertion sort mein sirf sorted hota hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3], n = 6.

    i = 1, key = 2:

    j arr[j] arr[j] > key? Action Array
    0 5 5 > 2 → haan arr[1] = 5, shift [5, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3]
    -1 — loop khatam (j < 0) arr[0] = 2 [2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3]

    Sorted region: [2, 5]. 1 comparison, 1 shift.

    i = 2, key = 4:

    j arr[j] arr[j] > key? Action Array
    1 5 5 > 4 → haan arr[2] = 5, shift [2, 5, 5, 6, 1, 3]
    0 2 2 > 4 → nahi ruko —
    — — — arr[1] = 4 [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3]

    Sorted region: [2, 4, 5]. 2 comparisons, 1 shift.

    i = 3, key = 6:

    j arr[j] arr[j] > key? Action Array
    2 5 5 > 6 → nahi turant ruko —
    — — — arr[3] = 6 (wahi jagah) [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3]

    Sorted region: [2, 4, 5, 6]. 1 comparison, 0 shifts — kyunki 6 already sahi jagah par tha. Yahi adaptivity hai.

    i = 4, key = 1:

    j arr[j] arr[j] > key? Action Array
    3 6 6 > 1 → haan arr[4] = 6 [2, 4, 5, 6, 6, 3]
    2 5 5 > 1 → haan arr[3] = 5 [2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 3]
    1 4 4 > 1 → haan arr[2] = 4 [2, 4, 4, 5, 6, 3]
    0 2 2 > 1 → haan arr[1] = 2 [2, 2, 4, 5, 6, 3]
    -1 — loop khatam arr[0] = 1 [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 3]

    Sorted region: [1, 2, 4, 5, 6]. 4 comparisons, 4 shifts — worst case for this element, kyunki 1 sabse chhota tha aur poore raste peeche gaya.

    i = 5, key = 3:

    j arr[j] arr[j] > key? Action Array
    4 6 6 > 3 → haan arr[5] = 6 [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 6]
    3 5 5 > 3 → haan arr[4] = 5 [1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6]
    2 4 4 > 3 → haan arr[3] = 4 [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6]
    1 2 2 > 3 → nahi ruko —
    — — — arr[2] = 3 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

    Sorted. 3 comparisons, 3 shifts.

    Grand total: 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 + 3 = 11 comparisons, 9 shifts.

    Summary table:

    i key Array pehle Comparisons Shifts Array baad mein
    1 2 [5,2,4,6,1,3] 1 1 [2,5,4,6,1,3]
    2 4 [2,5,4,6,1,3] 2 1 [2,4,5,6,1,3]
    3 6 [2,4,5,6,1,3] 1 0 [2,4,5,6,1,3]
    4 1 [2,4,5,6,1,3] 4 4 [1,2,4,5,6,3]
    5 3 [1,2,4,5,6,3] 3 3 [1,2,3,4,5,6]

    Dhyaan do i = 3 par: sirf 1 comparison. Selection sort us position par bhi 2 comparisons karta (poora suffix scan). Ye chhota farak nearly-sorted data par bahut bada ho jata hai.

    Code¶

    def insertion_sort(arr):
    """Sorted prefix mein har naye element ko shift karke insert karta hai. In-place, stable."""
    n = len(arr)                              # 1
    for i in range(1, n):                     # 2
        key = arr[i]                          # 3
        j = i - 1                             # 4
        while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:        # 5
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]               # 6
            j -= 1                            # 7
        arr[j + 1] = key                      # 8
    return arr                                # 9

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length ek baar.

    2. for i in range(1, n) — 1 se shuru, 0 se nahi. Kyunki ek element ka array (arr[0..0]) definition ke hisaab se sorted hai. i = 0 se shuru karte to key = arr[0], j = -1, while loop turant fail (kyunki j >= 0 False), phir arr[0] = key — yaani ek fizool iteration jo kuchh nahi karti. Galat nahi, bas waste.

    3. key = arr[i] — element ki copy side mein rakh li. Ye line critical hai. Line 6 mein hum arr[j+1] = arr[j] karte hain, aur pehli baar j+1 == i hota hai — yaani hum arr[i] ko overwrite kar rahe hain. Agar humne key mein copy na rakhi hoti to wo value hamesha ke liye gum ho jati aur arr[j] duplicate ho jata. Try karke dekho: key hata do aur arr[i] use karo — array mein duplicates aane lagenge.

    4. j = i - 1 — sorted region ke last element se peeche ki taraf chalna shuru. i - 1 isliye kyunki arr[i] khud key hai, use compare nahi karna.

    5. while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key — do conditions, aur order matter karta hai:

    6. j >= 0 pehle: agar j -1 ho gaya (yaani key sabse chhota nikla aur hum array ke shuru se bhi peeche chale gaye) to hume rukna hai. Python mein arr[-1] error nahi deta — wo last element de deta hai! Agar aap conditions ka order palat dete (arr[j] > key and j >= 0) to j = -1 par Python arr[-1] = last element uthata, usse compare karta, aur agar wo bada hua to j = -2, arr[-2]... yaani array ke end se wapas chalna shuru. Silent data corruption. Python ka and short-circuit karta hai, isliye j >= 0 pehle likhna zaroori hai. Ye ek asli, dhoonda na ja sakne wala bug hai.

    7. arr[j] > key — strictly greater, >= nahi. Ye stability deta hai: agar arr[j] == key to loop ruk jata hai aur key arr[j] ke turant baad rakhi jati hai — yaani equal elements ka original order bacha rehta hai. >= likh dete to key equal element ke aage ghus jati aur sort unstable ho jata, aur nearly-sorted equal-heavy data par shifts bhi zyada hote. Ek character, do problems.

    8. arr[j + 1] = arr[j] — shift, swap nahi. arr[j] ko ek kadam right sarka diya. arr[j] ki purani jagah ab "khali" (logically) hai — wahan abhi bhi purani value padi hai par hum use overwrite kar denge. Ye ek write hai. Swap hota to teen writes hote. Ye insertion sort ka bubble sort par constant-factor fayda hai.

    9. j -= 1 — ek aur kadam peeche.

    10. arr[j + 1] = key — j + 1, j nahi. Ye sabse common off-by-one bug hai. Loop tab rukta hai jab ya to j < 0 ho ya arr[j] <= key. Dono case mein arr[j] ki position par key nahi jaani chahiye:

    11. Agar arr[j] <= key: key ko arr[j] ke baad aana chahiye → j + 1.

    12. Agar j == -1: key sabse chhoti hai, index 0 par jaani chahiye → j + 1 = 0. ✓ Dono cases ek hi expression se handle ho gaye. Yahi elegance hai — aur yahi wajah hai ki while loop ke andar j -= 1 last mein hai, pehle nahi.

    13. return arr — in-place modified.

    Swap-based variant (kam efficient, par kabhi kabhi poochha jata hai):

    def insertion_sort_swaps(arr):
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):              # 1
        j = i                                 # 2
        while j > 0 and arr[j - 1] > arr[j]:  # 3
            arr[j - 1], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[j - 1]   # 4
            j -= 1                            # 5
    return arr                                # 6
    1. Wahi outer loop, index 1 se.
    2. j = i — yahan j us element ka current position track kar raha hai jo neeche sarak raha hai, na ki comparison target. Isliye i se, i-1 se nahi.
    3. j > 0 (j >= 0 nahi!) kyunki hum arr[j-1] access kar rahe hain — j = 0 par arr[-1] galat element uthata.
    4. Swap — 3 writes. Upar wala shift version 1 write karta tha. Isliye ye version ~2-3x dheema hai same asymptotic class hote hue bhi.
    5. Element ke saath saath position bhi peeche.
    6. Return.

    Interview mein shift version likho, swap version sirf tab jab pooche ki "bubble sort se kya farak hai" — tab ye dikhane ke liye ki ye bubble jaisa dikhta hai par jaldi ruk jata hai.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Best case — already sorted [1,2,3,4,5]:

    Har i par:  arr[i-1] > arr[i] ?  ->  nahi (sorted hai)
            while loop turant fail
            1 comparison, 0 shifts

Total = (n-1) comparisons, 0 shifts  ->  Theta(n)

    Yeh sabse important number hai insertion sort ka. O(n) best case matlab already-sorted data par ye merge sort (jo O(n log n) hi rahega) se bhi tez hai.

    Worst case — reverse sorted [5,4,3,2,1]:

    i=1: key = 4, poore sorted region (1 element) ko shift  ->  1 comparison, 1 shift
i=2: key = 3, 2 elements shift                          ->  2 comparisons, 2 shifts
i=3: key = 2, 3 elements shift                          ->  3 comparisons, 3 shifts
i=4: key = 1, 4 elements shift                          ->  4 comparisons, 4 shifts

Total = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2  ->  Theta(n²)

    Average case: Random permutation mein, har naya element apne sorted prefix mein beech mein kahin girta hai — average i/2 steps peeche. To:

    Sum over i of (i/2)  =  (1/2) * sum(i for i=1..n-1)
                     =  (1/2) * n(n-1)/2
                     =  n(n-1)/4
                     ->  Theta(n²), par worst case ka aadha

    Inversions wali derivation — ye sabse gehri insight hai:

    Insertion sort ka har shift exactly ek inversion hataata hai (kyunki wo padosi positions ko affect karta hai). Isliye:

    Total shifts = Total inversions in the input = I

Total time = O(n + I)

    Ab check karo: - Sorted array: I = 0 → O(n). ✓ - Reverse sorted: I = n(n-1)/2 → O(n²). ✓ - Nearly sorted (har element apni jagah se <= k door): I <= n·k → O(n·k). Agar k constant hai, to O(n)!

    Ye formula — O(n + I) — insertion sort ki asli identity hai. Isi wajah se Timsort chhote runs par insertion sort use karta hai: chhote chunks mein inversions kam hote hain.

    Space: key, i, j, n — O(1).

    Case Comparisons Shifts Time
    Best (sorted) n-1 0 Theta(n)
    Average (random) ~n²/4 ~n²/4 Theta(n²)
    Worst (reverse) n(n-1)/2 n(n-1)/2 Theta(n²)
    Nearly sorted (I inversions) n + I I O(n + I)
    Space — — O(1)

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan while condition arr[j] > key strict hai. Equal milte hi loop rukta hai, key equal element ke baad rakhi jati hai
    In-place Haan Sirf key ek extra variable
    Adaptive Haan, bahut zyada Time O(n + inversions). Sorted par O(n)

    Stability ka proof — trace karke:

    Input: [ 3, 1a, 1b ]      (1a aur 1b barabar)

i=1: key = 1a
     j=0: arr[0]=3 > 1a ?  haan  ->  shift  ->  [3, 3, 1b]
     j=-1: ruko  ->  arr[0] = 1a  ->  [1a, 3, 1b]

i=2: key = 1b
     j=1: arr[1]=3 > 1b ?  haan  ->  shift  ->  [1a, 3, 3]
     j=0: arr[0]=1a > 1b ?  1a aur 1b BARABAR hain, 1a > 1b FALSE  ->  RUKO
     arr[1] = 1b  ->  [1a, 1b, 3]

Result: 1a, 1b — original order bacha. STABLE. ✓

    Agar line 5 mein >= hota: 1a >= 1b True hota, ek aur shift hota, aur result [1b, 1a, 3] aata — unstable. Ek character.

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - n chhota hai (< 10-50). Yahan insertion sort merge/quick sort se practically tez hai kyunki uske constants bahut chhote hain — koi recursion overhead, koi extra array, cache friendly (memory sequential access). Isi wajah se har production sort library (Timsort, introsort, Java's dual-pivot quicksort) chhote subarrays par insertion sort par switch karti hai. - Data nearly sorted hai. O(n + I) formula ki wajah se. - Data stream mein aa raha hai (online). Aap ek-ek element aate hi insert kar sakte ho. Merge sort ya quick sort ko poora data pehle chahiye. - Stability chahiye aur memory nahi hai. Merge sort stable hai par O(n) space leta hai. - Linked list par — insertion mein shifting ki jagah pointer manipulation, par sequential search ki wajah se abhi bhi O(n²).

    Mat use karo jab: - n bada hai aur data random hai — n²/4 comparisons ka matlab n = 10,000 par 2.5 crore. - Data reverse-sorted hone ka chance hai — worst case hit hoga.

    Practical cutoff: Zyadatar libraries mein cutoff 10 se 32 elements ke beech hai. CPython ka Timsort 64 use karta hai (minrun), Java 47 use karta hai (dual-pivot quicksort mein).

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Shift ki jagah swap hatao (upar ka main version) 3 writes → 1 write, ~2-3x practical speedup Kuchh nahi. Ye default hona chahiye
    2 Binary insertion sort — jagah dhoondhne ke liye binary search Comparisons O(n²) → O(n log n) Shifts abhi bhi O(n²) — asli bottleneck wahi hai. Fayda tab jab comparison mehngi ho (strings, objects with custom __lt__)
    3 Sentinel — sabse chhote element ko pehle position 0 par le aao, phir j >= 0 check hata do Inner loop mein ek comparison per iteration bachti Ek extra pre-pass, aur array modify karna padta hai
    4 Shell sort — pehle door ke elements par insertion sort, gap ghatate jao Worst case O(n²) → ~O(n^1.3) Stability chali jati hai; gap sequence chunna padta hai
    5 2-element (pair) insertion — ek saath do elements insert karo ~10-15% kam comparisons Code kaafi complicated
    6 Library sort (gapped insertion) — array mein khali jagah chhod do taaki shifts kam hon Expected O(n log n) O(n) extra space, complicated

    Optimisation #2 par ek important baat: binary insertion sort comparisons kam karta hai par time class nahi badalta, kyunki shifting abhi bhi O(n²) hai. Interview mein agar koi kahe "binary search laga do, O(n log n) ho jayega" — ye galat hai, aur aap correct kar sakte ho.

    Binary insertion sort ka code:

    import bisect                                       # 1

def binary_insertion_sort(arr):
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):                    # 2
        key = arr[i]                                # 3
        pos = bisect.bisect_right(arr, key, 0, i)   # 4
        for j in range(i, pos, -1):                 # 5
            arr[j] = arr[j - 1]                     # 6
        arr[pos] = key                              # 7
    return arr                                      # 8
    1. bisect standard library — C mein implemented, binary search deta hai.
    2. Wahi outer loop, index 1 se.
    3. Key ko bacha liya (line 6 use overwrite karegi).
    4. bisect_right(arr, key, 0, i) — sorted region arr[0:i] mein wo index dhoondho jahan key ghusna chahiye. bisect_right use kiya, bisect_left nahi — ye stability ke liye zaroori hai. bisect_right equal elements ke baad ki position deta hai, yaani key apne barabar walon ke peeche jayegi → original order bacha → stable. bisect_left use karte to key equal elements ke aage ghusti → unstable. Yahi wo > vs >= wali baat hai, bas dusre roop mein. 0, i arguments zaroori hain — bina unke bisect poore array mein search karta, jisme unsorted region bhi hai, aur answer galat aata.
    5. range(i, pos, -1) — i se pos+1 tak ulta chalte hue shift. Ulta isliye kyunki agar seedha chalte to hum abhi tak na sarke hue elements ko overwrite kar dete. -1 step.
    6. arr[j] = arr[j-1] — ek kadam right shift.
    7. arr[pos] = key — key ko uski nayi jagah par.
    8. Return.

    Interview answer: Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix on the left. For each new element it saves the value in a temporary, walks backwards through the sorted prefix shifting larger elements one position right, and drops the saved value into the gap that opens up. That's exactly how people sort a hand of playing cards.

    The critical property is that it's adaptive. Its running time is O(n + I) where I is the number of inversions in the input, because every shift removes exactly one inversion. On sorted input I is zero and it runs in O(n) with n-1 comparisons and no shifts. On reverse-sorted input I is n(n-1)/2 and it degrades to O(n²). On random input it's about n²/4.

    It's stable because the inner loop stops on a strict greater-than — the moment it sees an equal element it stops and places the key just after it, preserving original order. It's in-place with O(1) extra space. And it's online: you can feed it elements one at a time, which merge sort and quicksort cannot do.

    This is why it's not just a teaching algorithm. Every serious sorting library uses insertion sort for small subarrays — Timsort and introsort both switch to it below a threshold — because its constants are tiny: no recursion, no auxiliary array, and sequential memory access that's very cache friendly.

    Cross-question: "Insertion sort and bubble sort are both O(n²) and both adaptive. Why is insertion sort preferred?"

    Two reasons. First, writes: insertion sort shifts, which is one memory write per step, while bubble sort swaps, which is three. That's a 2-3x constant factor. Second, early termination granularity: insertion sort's inner loop stops as soon as it finds the right position for the current element, so a well-placed element costs one comparison. Bubble sort's early exit only works at the granularity of a whole pass — it can't skip work within a pass. On nearly sorted data insertion sort is dramatically better.

    Cross-question: "Can you make insertion sort O(n log n) by using binary search to find the insertion point?"

    You reduce the comparison count to O(n log n), but not the running time. The shifting is still O(n) per element in the worst case, so total time stays O(n²). It's worth doing only when comparisons are much more expensive than moves — comparing long strings or objects with a costly custom comparator. And you must use bisect_right, not bisect_left, or you break stability.

    Cross-question: "Why does the loop condition put j >= 0 before arr[j] > key?"

    Because Python's and short-circuits and Python allows negative indices. If arr[j] > key were evaluated first, then when j reaches -1, arr[-1] would silently return the last element of the array instead of raising IndexError, and the loop could keep walking backwards from the end of the array, corrupting data. Putting the bounds check first guarantees we never index out of the intended range.

    Shell Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Shell sort insertion sort hi hai, par ek twist ke saath: pehle door-door ke elements ko compare aur sort karo (gap = kuchh bada number), phir gap ghatate jao, aur aakhir mein gap = 1 par normal insertion sort chalao. Door ke swaps se element ek hi kadam mein bahut door tak jump kar leta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Ek badi library mein hazaaron kitaabein bikhri hain aur unhe number order mein lagana hai. Aap sidha ek-ek karke jagah nahi dhoondhoge — pehle aap motey-motey groups banaoge: "1-1000 wali kitaabein is taraf, 1001-2000 us taraf". Ye motta arrangement har kitaab ko lagbhag sahi ilaake mein pahuncha deta hai. Phir aap chhote groups banate ho, phir aur chhote, aur aakhir mein har group ke andar exact order lagate ho — us waqt har kitaab apni sahi jagah se sirf 2-3 kadam door hoti hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Insertion sort ka formula tha O(n + I) jahan I = inversions. Iski problem: ek shift sirf ek inversion hataata hai. Agar sabse chhota element array ke bilkul end par hai, to use aage laane mein n-1 shifts lagenge — ek-ek kadam.

    [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Insertion sort mein "1" ko position 0 tak laane mein 8 shifts.
Poore array mein 36 inversions -> 36 shifts.

    Donald Shell ne 1959 mein poochha: "Kya hum ek move mein ek se zyada inversion hata sakte hain?" Jawab: haan, agar hum door ke elements ko swap karen.

    Gap = 4 par:  arr[0] aur arr[4] compare karo -> 9 vs 5 -> swap
[5, 8, 7, 6, 9, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Is EK swap ne kitni inversions hata di?
9 pehle 8,7,6,5 sabse aage tha (4 inversions), 5 peeche 8,7,6 ke tha (3 inversions).
Swap ke baad kaafi saari ek saath saaf ho gayi.

    Yahi shell sort ka poora idea hai: badi gap se motta order laao (kai inversions ek saath hatao), phir chhoti gap se fine-tune karo. Aur last gap = 1 hone se correctness guaranteed hai — kyunki gap-1 pass poora insertion sort hai.

    Aur ek bonus: shell sort in-place hai aur recursion nahi karta, to merge sort se memory-friendly aur quick sort se stack-friendly hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    "Gap-sorted" ka matlab: har gap distance par jo elements hain, wo aapas mein sorted hain.

    Array:  [ a0  a1  a2  a3  a4  a5  a6  a7 ]
gap = 4 se sublist banti hain:

  sublist 0:  a0, a4        (indices 0, 4)
  sublist 1:  a1, a5        (indices 1, 5)
  sublist 2:  a2, a6        (indices 2, 6)
  sublist 3:  a3, a7        (indices 3, 7)

Har sublist ko alag alag insertion sort karo.

gap = 2:
  sublist 0:  a0, a2, a4, a6
  sublist 1:  a1, a3, a5, a7

gap = 1:
  sublist 0:  poora array  -> normal insertion sort

    Ek bahut important theorem: Agar array k-sorted hai, aur phir aap use j-sort karte ho (j < k), to wo k-sorted rehta hai. Yaani mehnat waste nahi hoti — har pass pichhle pass ka fayda uthata hai aur uska structure todta nahi. Isi wajah se aakhri gap-1 pass par array itna nearly-sorted hota hai ki insertion sort O(n) ke kareeb chalti hai.

    Gap sequence shell sort ki performance decide karti hai:

    Sequence Formula Worst case Note
    Shell (original) n/2, n/4, ..., 1 O(n²) Simple, par gaps sab even → odd-even elements late milte hain
    Knuth 1, 4, 13, 40, 121... (3h+1) O(n^1.5) Practically bahut acchi, likhne mein aasan
    Hibbard 1, 3, 7, 15, 31... (2^k - 1) O(n^1.5)
    Sedgewick 1, 5, 19, 41, 109... O(n^1.33) Best known practical
    Ciura (empirical) 1, 4, 10, 23, 57, 132, 301, 701 Proof nahi, par fastest measured Experiment se nikaali gayi

Shell sort ne 0 + ~10 + 18 = ~28 kiye, aur bade array par ye farak exponentially badhta hai. n = 1000 par insertion ~250,000 shifts karta, shell ~10,000.

    Code¶

    def shell_sort(arr):
    """Knuth gap sequence (3h+1) ke saath shell sort. In-place, unstable."""
    n = len(arr)                                  # 1
    gap = 1                                       # 2
    while gap < n // 3:                           # 3
        gap = 3 * gap + 1                         # 4
    while gap >= 1:                               # 5
        for i in range(gap, n):                   # 6
            key = arr[i]                          # 7
            j = i                                 # 8
            while j >= gap and arr[j - gap] > key: # 9
                arr[j] = arr[j - gap]             # 10
                j -= gap                          # 11
            arr[j] = key                          # 12
        gap //= 3                                 # 13
    return arr                                    # 14

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length.
