    2. gap = 1 — Knuth sequence ki shuruaat. Hum upar se neeche nahi, neeche se upar build karte hain: 1, 4, 13, 40, 121... aur phir sabse bade valid gap se shuru karte hain.

    3. while gap < n // 3 — sabse bada gap dhoondho jo n/3 se chhota ho. n // 3 kyun, n kyun nahi? Kyunki agar gap n ke barabar ya usse bada ho gaya, to line 6 ka range(gap, n) khali ho jayega — pass kuchh karega hi nahi. Knuth ki recommendation hai ki sabse bada useful gap ~n/3 hai. Agar while gap < n likh dete, to pehle 1-2 passes fizool jaate.

    4. gap = 3 * gap + 1 — Knuth formula. 1 → 4 → 13 → 40 → 121 → 364 → 1093... Ye sequence isliye acchi hai kyunki consecutive gaps coprime hain (aapas mein common factor nahi), jisse alag alag passes alag alag element groups ko touch karte hain. Shell ki original sequence (n/2, n/4, ...) mein saare gaps ek doosre ke multiples hain, isliye odd aur even positions ke elements aakhri pass tak kabhi compare hi nahi hote — wahi uska O(n²) worst case ki wajah hai.

    5. while gap >= 1 — sabse bade gap se chhote tak. >= 1 zaroori hai, > 1 nahi — gap = 1 ka pass hi correctness deta hai. Agar aap > 1 likh dete to array partially sorted hi reh jata aur function galat answer deta. Ye sabse critical single character hai is code mein.

    6. for i in range(gap, n) — gap se shuru, 1 se nahi. Kyunki index 0 se gap-1 tak ke elements apne apne gap-sublist ke pehle elements hain, aur ek element ka sublist already sorted hai — unhe insert karne ki zaroorat nahi. Ye insertion sort ke range(1, n) ka exact analogue hai (wahan gap = 1 tha).

    Note: ye loop saari sublists ko interleaved process karta hai, ek-ek karke nahi. i = gap sublist 0 ka doosra element hai, i = gap+1 sublist 1 ka doosra element, etc. Ye equivalent hai aur cache ke liye behtar hai, kyunki memory sequentially touch hoti hai. Agar aap alag alag loops se har sublist alag process karte to result same hota par memory access jump-jump kar ke hoti — dheema.

    1. key = arr[i] — insertion sort jaisa hi, value bacha li kyunki line 10 use overwrite karegi.

    2. j = i — i se shuru, i - gap se nahi. Ye insertion sort se thoda alag likha hai: yahan j "khali jagah ka index" hai, aur hum arr[j - gap] se compare karte hain. Insertion sort mein humne j = i - 1 liya tha aur arr[j] se compare kiya tha. Dono styles sahi hain; ye wala shell sort mein zyada readable hai kyunki gap ka arithmetic ek hi jagah (j - gap) par dikhta hai.

    3. while j >= gap and arr[j - gap] > key — do conditions:

    4. j >= gap pehle — taaki arr[j - gap] ka index kabhi negative na ho. j = gap - 1 par arr[-1] = last element, silent corruption. Wahi Python negative-index trap jo insertion sort mein tha. Yahan j >= 0 galat hoga — j = 1, gap = 4 par arr[-3] uth jayega. Bound gap hai, 0 nahi.

    5. arr[j - gap] > key — strict greater-than. Yahan bhi equal par ruk jaate hain. Par dhyaan do: isse shell sort stable nahi ban jata — kyunki alag alag sublists ke beech elements jump karte hain, aur do equal elements alag sublists mein ho sakte hain. Neeche counterexample hai.

    6. arr[j] = arr[j - gap] — gap ki doori par shift. Ek shift = gap inversions tak hat sakti hain. Yahi shell sort ka poora fayda hai.

    7. j -= gap — gap ke steps mein peeche, 1 ke nahi. Agar aap galti se j -= 1 likh dete, to loop sublist chhod kar padosi elements dekhne lagta — algorithm galat ho jata (par output kabhi kabhi sahi aa jata, jo debug karna aur mushkil bana deta hai).

    8. arr[j] = key — key ko uski jagah. Yahan j, j + gap nahi — kyunki humne j ko "khali jagah" ki tarah define kiya tha (line 8 mein j = i), aur har shift ke baad khali jagah j - gap par chali gayi (line 11). Loop rukne par j hi sahi jagah hai.

    9. gap //= 3 — Knuth sequence ulta chalate hue. 3*gap+1 ka inverse (gap-1)//3 hota, par gap // 3 practically wahi sequence deta hai aur simple hai: 40 → 13 → 4 → 1 → 0. Integer division (//) zaroori hai — / float deta aur range(gap, n) TypeError phenkta. Aur gap kabhi 1 se 0 ho kar loop khatam kar dega — isliye line 5 ki condition >= 1 hai, na ki > 0 (dono same hain integers ke liye, par >= 1 intent zyada clear karta hai).

    10. Return.

    Simple version (Shell's original sequence) — samajhne ke liye:

    def shell_sort_simple(arr):
    n = len(arr)                                   # 1
    gap = n // 2                                   # 2
    while gap > 0:                                 # 3
        for i in range(gap, n):                    # 4
            key = arr[i]                           # 5
            j = i                                  # 6
            while j >= gap and arr[j - gap] > key: # 7
                arr[j] = arr[j - gap]              # 8
                j -= gap                           # 9
            arr[j] = key                           # 10
        gap //= 2                                  # 11
    return arr                                     # 12
    1. Length.
    2. gap = n // 2 — aadhi array se shuru. Ye Shell ki original choice thi.
    3. gap > 0 — jab tak gap positive hai. Aakhri iteration gap = 1 par hoti hai (kyunki 1 // 2 = 0 loop tod deta hai). Correctness gap-1 pass se aati hai.
    4. gap se n-1 tak — har element jo apne sublist ka pehla nahi hai.
    5. Key bachai.
    6. Khali jagah tracker.
    7. Bounds check pehle (j >= gap), phir comparison.
    8. Gap-shift.
    9. Gap-step peeche.
    10. Key place.
    11. gap //= 2 — halving. Iska worst case O(n²) hai kyunki saare gaps 2 ke powers hain, to jab tak gap = 1 nahi aata, odd-index aur even-index elements kabhi milte hi nahi. Classic counterexample: array jisme chhote elements sab odd positions par aur bade sab even positions par — sab gap passes kuchh nahi karte, aur poora kaam gap-1 pass par aa jata hai = plain insertion sort = O(n²).
    12. Return.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Shell sort ki complexity poori tarah solve nahi hui hai — ye ek open problem hai. Par jo pata hai wo derive kar sakte hain.

    Ek gap pass ki cost:

    gap = h par, array h sublists mein banta hai, har sublist ka size ~n/h

Har sublist par insertion sort:  O((n/h)²) worst case
h sublists:                      h * O((n/h)²) = O(n²/h)

Yaani bada gap = sasta pass. Chhota gap = mehnga pass... PAR chhote gap tak
array already nearly-sorted ho chuka hota hai, isliye actual cost bahut kam.

    Yahi tension hai: bade gaps sasta kaam karte hain par kam sort karte hain; chhote gaps zyada sort karte hain par mehnge hote hain — agar array pehle se nearly-sorted na ho to. Achhi gap sequence dono ko balance karti hai.

    Shell's original (n/2, n/4, ..., 1) — worst case O(n²) ka proof sketch:

    n = 16 ka array banao:
  chhote elements (1..8) sirf ODD indices par
  bade elements (9..16) sirf EVEN indices par

  [9, 1, 10, 2, 11, 3, 12, 4, 13, 5, 14, 6, 15, 7, 16, 8]

gap = 8: sublists (0,8), (1,9), (2,10)... har sublist ka pehla EVEN index se hai
         aur doosra bhi EVEN index se -> dono bade -> already sorted -> kuchh nahi hota
gap = 4: wahi kahani -- sab gaps even hain, to sublist ke andar sab elements
         same parity ke indices se aate hain -> chhote aur bade kabhi mile hi nahi
gap = 2: wahi
gap = 1: ab pehli baar chhote aur bade milte hain -> poora kaam yahin ->
         plain insertion sort par worst-case input -> O(n²)

    Isi wajah se gaps coprime hone chahiye. Knuth ka 3h+1 ye ensure karta hai.

    Knuth sequence — O(n^1.5):

    Proof poora nahi likhenge (wo research-level hai), par intuition:

    Gaps: 1, 4, 13, 40, 121, ... ~ (3^k)/2
Number of gaps: O(log_3 n)

Pratt ke theorem se: agar array h1-sorted aur h2-sorted hai (h1, h2 coprime),
to koi element apni jagah se zyada door nahi ho sakta.

Knuth ke gaps ke saath, gap = h ke pass mein har element zyada se zyada O(h)
positions move karta hai (kyunki wo pehle hi 3h-sorted aur 9h+1-sorted hai).

Cost per pass:  O(n * h) / h = O(n) ... nahi, actual bound O(n^1.5) nikalta hai
summation se: sum over gaps of (n * gap) is dominated by sqrt(n) terms.

    Practical numbers (measured comparisons):

    n Insertion sort Shell (Shell's gaps) Shell (Knuth) Merge sort
    100 ~2,500 ~1,000 ~700 ~670
    1,000 ~250,000 ~25,000 ~15,000 ~10,000
    10,000 ~25,000,000 ~800,000 ~400,000 ~130,000
    100,000 ~2.5 billion ~30,000,000 ~12,000,000 ~1,700,000

    Dekho: shell sort insertion se hazaar guna tez ho jata hai bade n par, par merge sort se peeche reh jata hai. Iski jagah wo hai jahan aapko O(n log n)-ish speed bina extra memory aur bina recursion ke chahiye.

    Space: key, i, j, gap, n — O(1). Koi recursion, koi extra array. Ye shell sort ka sabse bada practical selling point hai.

    Case Time Note
    Best O(n log n) Already sorted — har pass ek comparison per element
    Average Gap sequence par depend (~O(n^1.25) Sedgewick ke saath) Theoretically fully solved nahi
    Worst (Shell gaps) O(n²) Coprimality na hone ki wajah se
    Worst (Knuth gaps) O(n^1.5) Proven
    Worst (Sedgewick gaps) O(n^1.33) Proven
    Space O(1) Hamesha

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Nahi Door ke swaps equal elements ko ek doosre ke aar paar phenk dete hain
    In-place Haan O(1) extra — ye iski sabse badi khoobi hai
    Adaptive Haan, kaafi Sorted input par O(n log n), aur har gap pass insertion sort hai jo nearly-sorted par tez

    Instability ka counterexample:

    Input: [ 5a, 3, 5b, 1 ],  gap sequence: 2, 1

gap = 2:
  sublist (0, 2): 5a, 5b   ->  5a > 5b ? nahi (equal) -> koi swap nahi
  sublist (1, 3): 3, 1     ->  3 > 1 ? haan -> swap
  Array: [5a, 1, 5b, 3]

gap = 1 (normal insertion sort):
  i=1, key=1:  5a > 1 -> shift  -> [5a, 5a, 5b, 3] -> arr[0]=1 -> [1, 5a, 5b, 3]
  i=2, key=5b: 5a > 5b ? nahi (equal) -> ruko -> [1, 5a, 5b, 3]
  i=3, key=3:  5b > 3 -> shift; 5a > 3 -> shift; 1 > 3 ? nahi -> ruko
               [1, 3, 5a, 5b]

Is example mein order bach gaya. Ek aisa example jahan toot ta hai:

Input: [ 2a, 2b, 1 ],  gap = 2 se shuru (n=3, n//2 = 1... to gap=1 hi hoga)

Better example, n = 4:  [ 2a, 3, 2b, 1 ],  gaps: 2, 1
gap = 2:
  sublist (0,2): 2a, 2b  ->  equal, no swap
  sublist (1,3): 3, 1    ->  swap  ->  [2a, 1, 2b, 3]
gap = 1:
  i=1, key=1: 2a>1 shift -> [1, 2a, 2b, 3]
  i=2, key=2b: 2a > 2b? nahi -> ruko
  i=3, key=3: 2b > 3? nahi
  Result: [1, 2a, 2b, 3]  -- stable is baar bhi

Asli break: [ 3, 2a, 1, 2b ],  n=4, gaps 2, 1
gap = 2:
  sublist (0,2): 3, 1  ->  3 > 1 -> swap  ->  [1, 2a, 3, 2b]
  sublist (1,3): 2a, 2b -> equal, no swap
gap = 1:
  i=1, key=2a: 1 > 2a? nahi -> ruko
  i=2, key=3:  2a > 3? nahi -> ruko
  i=3, key=2b: 3 > 2b -> shift; 2a > 2b? nahi -> ruko  -> [1, 2a, 2b, 3]

    Ye chhote examples par pakadna mushkil hai. Practical rule: shell sort ko unstable maano kyunki gap-swaps ki wajah se koi guarantee nahi di ja sakti. Ek clean 5-element counterexample: [5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 1] gap 2 ke saath — 1 sublist (0,2,4) mein hai aur wo 5a aur 5c ke aar paar jump karta hai, jisse 5a apni jagah se hilta hai jabki 5b nahi hilta.

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Embedded / memory-constrained systems. O(1) space, no recursion — stack overflow ka darr nahi. Kernel code, bootloaders, microcontrollers mein shell sort real mein use hota hai (uClibc ka qsort shell sort hai). - Medium-sized arrays (1,000 - 50,000) jahan O(n log n) chahiye par merge sort ka O(n) buffer afford nahi kar sakte. - Aapko simple, dependable, worst-case-bounded code chahiye — quicksort ke O(n²) surprise ke bina.

    Mat use karo jab: - Stability chahiye — shell sort de hi nahi sakta. - Bada data aur memory available hai — merge sort ya Timsort behtar hai. - Guaranteed O(n log n) chahiye — shell sort ki best proven bound O(n^1.33) hai, log-linear nahi.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Knuth gaps (3h+1) instead of n/2 Worst case O(n²) → O(n^1.5) Kuchh nahi, 2 extra lines
    2 Sedgewick gaps O(n^1.33) worst case, practically fastest proven Sequence hard-code karni padti hai
    3 Ciura gaps (1,4,10,23,57,132,301,701) Empirically fastest for n < 4000 Koi proof nahi, aur bade n ke liye extend karna padta hai (×2.25 se)
    4 Aakhri gap-1 pass ko optimised insertion sort banao (sentinel ke saath) ~5-10% Ek extra pre-pass
    5 Chhote gaps ke liye alag inner loop Cache locality behtar Code duplication
    6 Shell sort ko chhod kar merge/quick use karo Guaranteed O(n log n) Space ya worst-case risk

    Ciura sequence ka code (practically best):

    CIURA = [701, 301, 132, 57, 23, 10, 4, 1]         # 1

def shell_sort_ciura(arr):
    n = len(arr)                                   # 2
    gaps = [g for g in CIURA if g < n]             # 3
    g = 701                                        # 4
    extra = []                                     # 5
    while g * 2.25 < n:                            # 6
        g = int(g * 2.25)                          # 7
        extra.append(g)                            # 8
    gaps = sorted(extra, reverse=True) + gaps      # 9
    for gap in gaps:                               # 10
        for i in range(gap, n):                    # 11
            key = arr[i]                           # 12
            j = i                                  # 13
            while j >= gap and arr[j - gap] > key: # 14
                arr[j] = arr[j - gap]              # 15
                j -= gap                           # 16
            arr[j] = key                           # 17
    return arr                                     # 18
    1. Ciura ki empirically-derived sequence, bade se chhote order mein. Ye numbers experiments se nikale gaye the, kisi formula se nahi.
    2. Length.
    3. Sirf wo gaps rakho jo n se chhote hain — bade gaps ka pass khali chalega.
    4. g = 701 — Ciura sequence ka sabse bada element. Isse aage extend karna hai.
    5. extra — bade gaps jo hum khud generate karenge.
    6. while g * 2.25 < n — Ciura ne khud aage ki values nahi di; standard practice hai ×2.25 se extend karna. < n isliye ki gap n se bada ho to pass khali.
    7. int(g * 2.25) — float ko int banaya, kyunki range() ko int chahiye.
    8. List mein add.
    9. sorted(extra, reverse=True) + gaps — bade extra gaps pehle, phir Ciura ke chhote. Poora sequence descending order mein hona chahiye taaki hum bade se chhote gaps par chalen. Agar order ulta hota to algorithm galat ho jata — chhote gap ke baad bada gap chalane ka koi matlab nahi, aur last gap 1 na hone se array unsorted reh jata.
    10. Har gap par ek pass. 11-17. Wahi gapped insertion sort jo pehle explain kiya.
    11. Return. Note: last gap hamesha 1 hoga kyunki CIURA list 1 par khatam hoti hai — correctness guaranteed.

    Interview answer: Shell sort is insertion sort generalised over a gap. Instead of only comparing adjacent elements, it first sorts elements that are h positions apart for some large h, then repeats with progressively smaller h, ending with h = 1. The final h = 1 pass is a plain insertion sort, which is what guarantees correctness — everything before it is preparation.

    The reason it works is that insertion sort's cost is proportional to the number of inversions, and a single gapped swap can remove up to h inversions at once instead of one. So the big gaps cheaply get the array roughly ordered, and by the time we reach h = 1 the array is nearly sorted, where insertion sort runs close to linear.

    The gap sequence determines the complexity, and choosing it badly matters. Shell's original n/2, n/4, ..., 1 is O(n²) in the worst case, because all the gaps are powers of two, so elements at odd and even indices never get compared until the final pass. Knuth's 3h+1 sequence gives O(n^1.5) and Sedgewick's gives about O(n^1.33), because consecutive gaps are coprime and every pass touches genuinely new pairs.

    It's in-place with O(1) space and uses no recursion, which is why it shows up in embedded and kernel code — uClibc's qsort is a shell sort. It's not stable, because gapped moves jump equal elements past each other.

    Cross-question: "Why does the gap sequence have to end at 1?"

    Because gap-h sorting only guarantees that elements h apart are ordered relative to each other. Nothing about the array is globally sorted until you do a gap-1 pass, which is a full insertion sort and therefore correct by itself. All the earlier passes are an optimisation that makes the gap-1 pass cheap; they contribute nothing to correctness.

    Cross-question: "You said a k-sorted array stays k-sorted after a j-sort. Why does that matter?"

    Because it means no pass undoes the work of a previous pass. If gap-13 sorting could destroy the gap-40 ordering, the whole layered strategy would be pointless. The theorem guarantees the array only gets closer to sorted, which is exactly why the final gap-1 pass finds a nearly sorted array.

    Cross-question: "Shell sort is around O(n^1.3). Merge sort is O(n log n), which is better. Why would anyone use shell sort?"

    Memory and predictability. Merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space, which can be prohibitive for large arrays or embedded targets. Quicksort is in-place but recursive and has an O(n²) worst case. Shell sort is in-place, iterative — no stack depth risk — has a proven sub-quadratic worst case, and its code is about fifteen lines. In constrained environments that combination is genuinely hard to beat.

    Merge Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Merge sort array ko beech se do halves mein todta hai, dono halves ko recursively sort karta hai, aur phir do sorted halves ko ek sorted array mein merge kar deta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Do log answer-sheets check kar rahe hain. Aap 100 sheets ko do dher mein baant dete ho, ek dher A ko, doosra B ko. A apni 50 sheets ko roll number se laga leta hai, B apni 50 laga leta hai. Ab dono apne dher ko mez par rakhte hain aur dono dhero ke top se dekh kar — jiska roll number chhota, wo pehle — ek final dher banate hain. Ye aakhri kadam merge hai, aur wahi merge sort ka asli dimaag hai. Todna to aasan hai; jodna smart hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Ab tak jitne algorithms dekhe — bubble, selection, insertion, shell — sabka worst case O(n²) ya usse thoda behtar tha. Insertion sort adaptive tha par reverse-sorted par mar jata tha. Shell sort behtar tha par uski complexity proven O(n log n) nahi hai.

    Merge sort ne pehli baar guaranteed O(n log n) diya — best, average, worst, teenon mein. Ye kaise? Ek fundamentally alag idea se:

    Purana idea:  ek element ko uski sahi jagah tak le jao (insertion/selection/bubble)
              -> ek element ko n positions tak chalna pad sakta hai -> O(n) per element
              -> n elements -> O(n²)

Naya idea:    do PEHLE SE SORTED lists ko merge karna sirf O(n + m) leta hai
              -> agar hum recursively sorted halves bana len, to poora sort
              -> merging ka cost sirf linear

    Merge itna sasta kyun hai? Kyunki dono lists sorted hain, to aapko sirf dono ke pehle elements dekhne hain. Jo chhota hai wo pakka overall minimum hai — us list mein uske peeche sab bade hain, doosri list mein pehla hi usse bada hai. Ye ek O(1) decision hai, aur har decision ek element place kar deti hai. n + m elements → n + m decisions → O(n + m).

    Yahi wo insight hai jo divide-and-conquer ki poori family ko unlock karta hai. Iske baad quicksort, binary search, closest pair, FFT — sab isi soch ke variations hain.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Do phases:

    DIVIDE (neeche jaate hue):

                [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
                 /                        \
        [38, 27, 43]                    [3, 9, 82, 10]
         /        \                      /            \
     [38]     [27, 43]              [3, 9]          [82, 10]
               /     \               /   \           /     \
            [27]    [43]          [3]   [9]       [82]    [10]

CONQUER / MERGE (upar aate hue):

            [27]    [43]          [3]   [9]       [82]    [10]
               \     /               \   /           \     /
            [27, 43]                 [3, 9]         [10, 82]
         /        \                      \            /
    [38]      [27, 43]                 [3, 9, 10, 82]
         \       /                              |
        [27, 38, 43]                            |
                 \                             /
                [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]

    Merge step ko dhyaan se samjho — yahi asli algorithm hai:

    Left  = [27, 38, 43]      i -> pointer left mein
Right = [3, 9, 10, 82]    j -> pointer right mein
Out   = []                k -> pointer output mein

i=0, j=0:  L[0]=27 vs R[0]=3   ->  3 chhota  ->  Out=[3],           j=1
i=0, j=1:  L[0]=27 vs R[1]=9   ->  9 chhota  ->  Out=[3,9],         j=2
i=0, j=2:  L[0]=27 vs R[2]=10  ->  10 chhota ->  Out=[3,9,10],      j=3
i=0, j=3:  L[0]=27 vs R[3]=82  ->  27 chhota ->  Out=[3,9,10,27],   i=1
i=1, j=3:  L[1]=38 vs R[3]=82  ->  38 chhota ->  Out=[...,38],      i=2
i=2, j=3:  L[2]=43 vs R[3]=82  ->  43 chhota ->  Out=[...,43],      i=3
i=3 -> Left khatam. Right ka bacha hua (82) seedha copy kar do.
Out = [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]

    Har step mein exactly ek comparison hui aur exactly ek element place hua. Isliye merge exactly n + m - 1 se kam comparisons aur n + m writes karta hai. Linear.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10], n = 7.

    Recursion tree — call by call (depth-first order, jaise Python actually chalega):

    # Call Kya karta hai Result
    1 ms([38,27,43,3,9,82,10]) mid = 3, split → [38,27,43] aur [3,9,82,10] pending
    2 ms([38,27,43]) mid = 1, split → [38] aur [27,43] pending
    3 ms([38]) len == 1 → base case [38]
    4 ms([27,43]) mid = 1, split → [27] aur [43] pending
    5 ms([27]) base case [27]
    6 ms([43]) base case [43]
    7 merge [27] + [43] 27 < 43 [27,43]
    8 merge [38] + [27,43] detail neeche [27,38,43]
    9 ms([3,9,82,10]) mid = 2, split → [3,9] aur [82,10] pending
    10 ms([3,9]) mid = 1 → [3], [9] pending
    11 ms([3]), ms([9]) base cases [3], [9]
    12 merge [3] + [9] 3 < 9 [3,9]
    13 ms([82,10]) mid = 1 → [82], [10] pending
    14 ms([82]), ms([10]) base cases [82], [10]
    15 merge [82] + [10] 10 < 82 [10,82]
    16 merge [3,9] + [10,82] detail neeche [3,9,10,82]
    17 merge [27,38,43] + [3,9,10,82] detail neeche [3,9,10,27,38,43,82]

    Step 8 ka detailed merge — [38] + [27,43]:

    Step i (L) j (R) L[i] R[j] Chhota Out Pointer badla
    1 0 0 38 27 R (27) [27] j → 1
    2 0 1 38 43 L (38) [27,38] i → 1
    3 1 1 — 43 L khatam [27,38,43] R ka bacha hua copy

    Step 16 ka detailed merge — [3,9] + [10,82]:

    Step i j L[i] R[j] Chhota Out Pointer
    1 0 0 3 10 L (3) [3] i → 1
    2 1 0 9 10 L (9) [3,9] i → 2
    3 2 0 — 10 L khatam [3,9,10,82] R ka bacha hua copy

    Step 17 ka detailed merge — [27,38,43] + [3,9,10,82]:

    Step i j L[i] R[j] Comparison Chhota Out
    1 0 0 27 3 27 <= 3? No R [3]
    2 0 1 27 9 27 <= 9? No R [3,9]
    3 0 2 27 10 27 <= 10? No R [3,9,10]
    4 0 3 27 82 27 <= 82? Yes L [3,9,10,27]
    5 1 3 38 82 38 <= 82? Yes L [3,9,10,27,38]
    6 2 3 43 82 43 <= 82? Yes L [3,9,10,27,38,43]
    7 3 3 — 82 L khatam copy rest [3,9,10,27,38,43,82]

    Total comparisons pure poore run mein: step 7 (1) + step 8 (2) + step 12 (1) + step 15 (1) + step 16 (2) + step 17 (6) = 13 comparisons.

    Compare karo: bubble sort n=7 par 21 comparisons karta, insertion sort average ~12 par worst case 21. Aur n = 1,000,000 par? Merge sort ~20 million, insertion sort ~250 billion.

    Level-wise view (ye complexity samajhne ke liye zaroori hai):

    Level 0:  [38,27,43,3,9,82,10]                            7 elements  <- 1 merge of size 7
Level 1:  [38,27,43]  [3,9,82,10]                         3 + 4 = 7   <- 2 merges, total 7
Level 2:  [38] [27,43]  [3,9] [82,10]                     1+2+2+2 = 7 <- merges, total 7
Level 3:  [38] [27] [43] [3] [9] [82] [10]                7 singles

Har level par TOTAL kaam = O(n).
Levels ki sankhya = log2(n) = log2(7) ~ 3.
Total = O(n) * O(log n) = O(n log n)

    Code¶

    Version 1 — top-down recursive (samajhne ke liye sabse clear):

    def merge_sort(arr):
    """Naya sorted list return karta hai. Original ko nahi badalta."""
    if len(arr) <= 1:                             # 1
        return arr                                # 2
    mid = len(arr) // 2                           # 3
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])                  # 4
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])                 # 5
    return merge(left, right)                     # 6


def merge(left, right):
    """Do sorted lists ko ek sorted list mein jodta hai. Stable."""
    result = []                                   # 7
    i = j = 0                                     # 8
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):       # 9
        if left[i] <= right[j]:                   # 10
            result.append(left[i])                # 11
            i += 1                                # 12
        else:                                     # 13
            result.append(right[j])               # 14
            j += 1                                # 15
    result.extend(left[i:])                       # 16
    result.extend(right[j:])                      # 17
    return result                                 # 18

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. if len(arr) <= 1 — base case. Ek element ya khali list already sorted hai. <= 1 kyun, == 1 kyun nahi? Kyunki khali list bhi aa sakti hai (agar koi merge_sort([]) call kare). == 1 likhte to khali list par recursion chalti: mid = 0, arr[:0] = [], arr[0:] = [] — dono halves khali, dono par recursion, infinite recursion → RecursionError. Ye ek line ka bug hai jo poora program crash karta hai. <= 1 dono cases cover karta hai.

    2. return arr — base case ka result. Note: ye wahi list object return kar raha hai, copy nahi. Yahan safe hai kyunki line 4/5 mein arr[:mid] pehle hi nayi list bana chuka hai.

    3. mid = len(arr) // 2 — integer division (//), / nahi. / float deta hai aur arr[:3.5] TypeError phenkta hai. Ye Python 3 ki common galti hai (Python 2 mein / integers par integer deta tha). // 2 se split kitna even hota hai? n = 7 par mid = 3 → [0:3] (3 elements) aur [3:7] (4 elements). Farak 1 ka. Ye best possible balance hai, aur balanced split hi log n depth deta hai. Agar aap mid = 1 likh dete (yaani hamesha ek element alag karo), to recursion depth n ho jati aur algorithm insertion sort ban jata, O(n²).

    4. left = merge_sort(arr[:mid]) — pehla half recursively sort. arr[:mid] ek nayi list banata hai (Python slicing hamesha copy karta hai) jisme indices 0 se mid-1 tak. Ye O(mid) time aur O(mid) space leta hai — yahi wajah hai ki ye version O(n log n) space use karta hai, O(n) nahi. Neeche in-place version mein ye theek karenge.

    5. right = merge_sort(arr[mid:]) — doosra half. arr[mid:] mein indices mid se end tak. Dhyaan do: arr[:mid] aur arr[mid:] mil kar poora array cover karte hain, bina overlap ke. Python slicing ka [start:end) convention (end exclusive) is baat ko automatic bana deta hai. Agar aap arr[mid+1:] likh dete, to arr[mid] gum ho jata — ek element hamesha missing rehta. Agar arr[:mid+1] likhte to arr[mid] do baar aata — duplicate.

    6. return merge(left, right) — dono sorted halves ko jodo. Ye line hi poora "conquer" hai.

    7. result = [] — output list. Ye naya array hai — isi wajah se merge sort in-place nahi hai. Ek alternative hai left mein hi likhna, par wo tab hi kaam karta hai jab left mein jagah ho.

    8. i = j = 0 — dono input lists ke pointers. Chained assignment se dono ek saath 0. Note: ye integers ke liye safe hai (immutable). Agar aap a = b = [] likhte to dono same list object ko point karte aur ek mein append karne se doosri bhi badalti — classic Python trap. Yahan integers hain to koi problem nahi.

    9. while i < len(left) and j < len(right) — dono lists mein elements bache hon tabhi compare karna hai. and hai, or nahi. Agar or likh dete to ek list khatam hone par bhi loop chalta aur left[i] par IndexError aata.

    10. if left[i] <= right[j] — <= hai, < nahi. Ye ek character stability decide karta hai. Socho left[i] == right[j]:

      • <= ke saath: left wala pehle jayega. Left original array mein pehle tha (kyunki hum arr[:mid] ko left bolte hain). To original order bacha → stable. ✓
      • < ke saath: condition False hogi, else branch chalega, right wala pehle jayega. Right original mein baad mein tha. Order ulta → unstable. ✗ Ye merge sort ki stability ka poora raaz hai, aur interview mein exactly yahi poochha jata hai.

    11. result.append(left[i]) — chhota element output mein. append amortised O(1) hai Python mein.

    12. i += 1 — left pointer aage. Sirf left ka pointer badha — right wala wahin hai kyunki uske current element ko abhi place nahi kiya. Agar aap dono badha dete to elements skip ho jate.

    13. else — yaani left[i] > right[j].

    14-15. Right wala element aur uska pointer.

    1. result.extend(left[i:]) — jab while loop khatam hua, ek list zaroor khatam ho chuki hai, par doosri mein elements bache ho sakte hain. left[i:] mein wo saare bache hue elements hain (agar left khatam ho chuki hai to left[i:] khali list hai — extend([]) kuchh nahi karta, koi error nahi). Ye do lines (16, 17) kyun zaroori hain? Bina inke, bache hue elements gum ho jaate. Aur ye "drain" step comparison-free hai — bache hue elements pehle se sorted hain aur doosri list ke saare elements unse chhote hain, to unhe compare karne ki zaroorat hi nahi.

    2. result.extend(right[j:]) — same right ke liye. Dono lines chahiye kyunki hume nahi pata konsi list pehle khatam hui. Ek if/else bhi likh sakte the, par dono extend call karna simpler hai aur khali slice ka cost zero hai.

    3. return result — poori sorted list.

    Version 2 — in-place-ish (indices ke saath, ek hi buffer):

    Ye version production-quality hai — bar bar naye slices nahi banata.

    def merge_sort_inplace(arr):
    """arr ko in-place sort karta hai, ek hi O(n) buffer use karke."""
    buffer = [0] * len(arr)                       # 1
    _ms(arr, buffer, 0, len(arr) - 1)             # 2
    return arr                                    # 3


def _ms(arr, buffer, low, high):
    if low >= high:                               # 4
        return                                    # 5
    mid = low + (high - low) // 2                 # 6
    _ms(arr, buffer, low, mid)                    # 7
    _ms(arr, buffer, mid + 1, high)               # 8
    if arr[mid] <= arr[mid + 1]:                  # 9
        return                                    # 10
    _merge(arr, buffer, low, mid, high)           # 11


def _merge(arr, buffer, low, mid, high):
    for x in range(low, high + 1):                # 12
        buffer[x] = arr[x]                        # 13
    i, j, k = low, mid + 1, low                   # 14
    while i <= mid and j <= high:                 # 15
        if buffer[i] <= buffer[j]:                # 16
            arr[k] = buffer[i]                    # 17
            i += 1                                # 18
        else:                                     # 19
            arr[k] = buffer[j]                    # 20
            j += 1                                # 21
        k += 1                                    # 22
    while i <= mid:                               # 23
        arr[k] = buffer[i]                        # 24
        i += 1                                    # 25
        k += 1                                    # 26

    Line-by-line:

    1. buffer = [0] * len(arr) — ek hi baar, poore algorithm ke liye, ek scratch array. Top-down version har recursive call par nayi lists banata tha — total O(n log n) allocations. Yahan sirf ek O(n) allocation hai, aur wahi buffer har merge dobara use karta hai. Ye memory allocator par pressure hataata hai aur practically 2-3x tez hai.

    2. Helper ko call — indices 0 se len-1 (inclusive high, ye is code ka convention hai).

    3. Original array return — ab ye in-place modified hai.

    4. if low >= high — base case. low == high matlab ek element. low > high matlab khali range (aisa tab hota hai jab original array khali ho: low=0, high=-1). Dono par turant return. >= zaroori hai, == nahi — khali array par == infinite recursion deta.

    5. Return, kuchh nahi karna.

    6. mid = low + (high - low) // 2 — (low + high) // 2 kyun nahi likha? Python mein integers unbounded hain, to dono same hain. Par C/C++/Java mein low + high integer overflow kar sakta hai agar dono bade hon (jaise 2 billion + 2 billion > INT_MAX). low + (high - low) // 2 mein high - low hamesha chhota rehta hai, to overflow nahi hota. Ye ek famous bug tha — Java ki binary search mein 9 saal tak zinda raha. Python mein zaroorat nahi par interview mein ye likhna aur wajah batana bahut acha impression banata hai, aur agar aap kabhi doosri language mein likhein to habit kaam aayegi.

    7. Left half [low, mid] sort.

    8. Right half [mid+1, high] sort. mid+1 zaroori hai — mid left half mein already include hai. Agar mid likh dete to mid do baar process hota aur low = mid, high = high wali call kabhi chhoti nahi hoti (agar high = mid + 1 ho) → infinite recursion.

    9. if arr[mid] <= arr[mid + 1] — ye optimisation hai, correctness nahi. Agar left half ka sabse bada element (jo arr[mid] hai, kyunki left sorted ho chuka hai) right half ke sabse chhote element (arr[mid+1]) se chhota ya barabar hai, to poora range already sorted hai — merge ki zaroorat hi nahi. Ye check nearly-sorted data par bahut bada fayda deta hai: already-sorted array par har level par ye check pass ho jayega aur zero merges honge → O(n log n) comparisons ki jagah sirf O(n) merges + O(n log n) recursion. Actually recursion abhi bhi O(n) calls karti hai, par merging ka O(n log n) kaam bach jata hai. Ye Timsort ki soch ki taraf pehla kadam hai. <= hai < nahi — equal case mein bhi merge ki zaroorat nahi.

    10. Skip merge.

    11. Merge call.

    12. for x in range(low, high + 1) — poora range buffer mein copy. high + 1 kyunki high inclusive hai is code ke convention mein aur range exclusive end leta hai.

    13. Copy.

    14. i, j, k = low, mid + 1, low — teen pointers: i = left half mein (buffer ke andar), j = right half mein (buffer ke andar), k = jahan likhna hai (arr ke andar). Dhyaan do ki i aur j buffer padhte hain aur k arr likhta hai. Agar dono ek hi array par hote to hum abhi tak na padhe hue elements ko overwrite kar dete.

    15. while i <= mid and j <= high — dono halves mein elements bache hon. <= kyunki dono bounds inclusive hain.

    16. if buffer[i] <= buffer[j] — wahi stability wala <=.

    17-18. Left ka element arr[k] par, i aage.

    19-21. Warna right ka element, j aage.

    1. k += 1 — dono branches ke baad, ek hi baar. Isliye if/else ke bahar likha hai. Agar dono branches mein alag alag likhte to code duplicate hota; galat nahi, bas gandaa.

    2. while i <= mid — left half ke bache hue elements copy karo.

    24-26. Copy aur pointers.

    Right half ke bache hue elements ke liye loop kyun nahi likha? Ye ek sundar trick hai. Agar left half khatam ho gaya aur right mein elements bache hain, to wo bache hue elements buffer mein j se high tak hain — aur unhe arr[k] se arr[high] tak jaana hai. Par kyunki har step mein j aur k dono ek saath badhe hain, aur shuruaat mein k = low, j = mid+1... jab left khatam hua to k aur j ka farak exactly wahi hai jitne left ke elements copy hue. Actually k == j ho jata hai us waqt! Aur buffer[j..high] hi arr[j..high] hai (line 12-13 ne copy kiya tha aur unhe abhi tak overwrite nahi kiya). To wo elements pehle se sahi jagah par hain. Isliye kuchh karne ki zaroorat nahi.

    Ye subtle hai — interview mein agar aap ye samjha do to bahut strong lagta hai. Agar aap sure nahi ho, to safety ke liye doosra drain loop bhi likh do; galat nahi hoga, bas fizool copies.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Recurrence relation likho:

    T(n) = 2 * T(n/2)  +  O(n)
       ^^^^^^^^^^     ^^^^
       do halves      merge (linear)
       recursively

T(1) = O(1)

    Recursion tree se solve karo — ye sabse intuitive tareeka hai:

    Level 0:   1 problem of size n         ->  merge cost = n
              |
Level 1:   2 problems of size n/2      ->  merge cost = 2 * (n/2) = n
              |
Level 2:   4 problems of size n/4      ->  merge cost = 4 * (n/4) = n
              |
Level 3:   8 problems of size n/8      ->  merge cost = 8 * (n/8) = n
              |
             ...
              |
Level k:   2^k problems of size n/2^k  ->  merge cost = 2^k * (n/2^k) = n
              |
Last level: problems of size 1  ->  n/2^k = 1  ->  2^k = n  ->  k = log2(n)

TOTAL = (cost per level) * (number of levels)
      = n * (log2(n) + 1)
      = O(n log n)

    Har level par cost exactly n kyun hai? Kyunki har level par saare subproblems mil kar poore array ko exactly ek baar cover karte hain. Level 2 par 4 subarrays hain, har ek n/4 size ka — total n. Merging linear hai, to us level ka total merging cost n.

    Levels exactly log2(n) kyun hain? Kyunki har level par size aadha hota hai:

    n -> n/2 -> n/4 -> n/8 -> ... -> 1

Kitni baar aadha karna pada?  n / 2^k = 1  =>  2^k = n  =>  k = log2(n)

n = 8:    8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1     3 halvings  = log2(8) = 3  ✓
n = 1024: 1024 -> ... -> 1     10 halvings = log2(1024) = 10  ✓
n = 10^6: ~20 halvings         log2(10^6) ~ 20  ✓

    Ye number kitna chhota hai — feel karo: n = 10 lakh par log2(n) ~ 20. Yaani merge sort ~2 crore operations karega. Insertion sort ~5 kharab (5 × 10^11). 25,000 guna farak.

    Best, average, worst — sab same kyun?

    Merge sort ka split hamesha exactly beech se hota hai, chahe data kaisa bhi ho. Wo data dekh kar decide nahi karta (jaisa quicksort pivot par karta hai). Isliye recursion tree hamesha exactly wahi shape ki hoti hai:

    Best case  (sorted):        T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)
Average    (random):        T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)
Worst      (reverse):       T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)

    Ye guarantee merge sort ki sabse badi taakat hai. Quicksort average mein tez hai par worst case O(n²). Merge sort kabhi surprise nahi deta.

    Comparisons exactly kitne? Merge of size n mein at most n-1 comparisons (best case mein sirf min(len(L), len(R)) — jab ek list poori pehle khatam ho jaye).

    Worst case total comparisons ~ n*log2(n) - n + 1
n = 1000:  ~9,000 comparisons
n = 10^6:  ~19,000,000 comparisons

    Space derive karo — ye interview mein galat bola jata hai:

    Top-down slicing version: 

    Har recursive call arr[:mid] aur arr[mid:] se DO NAYI lists banata hai.
Ek waqt mein (call stack ki depth par) kitni lists zinda hain?

Level 0: n elements ka input
Level 1: n elements (do halves)
Level 2: n elements (chaar quarters)
...
Har level par n elements zinda hain, aur log n levels hain.

Peak memory: O(n log n)   <- ye Python ke naive slicing version ki sacchai hai

    Hmm — par actually Python mein depth-first execution hoti hai, to ek waqt mein poore log n levels ke saare slices zinda nahi hote. Jo zinda hote hain: current path par har level ka left result + abhi ban rahi slices. Wo n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + ... = n hai, plus result list n — to peak ~O(n), par allocations total O(n log n) hote hain. Practically ye version buffer version se ~2-3x dheema hai isi allocation churn ki wajah se.

    Buffer version (line 1 wala): 

    buffer:           O(n)   <- ek hi baar allocate
recursion stack:  O(log n)  <- depth log n, har frame O(1)

Total auxiliary space: O(n)

    Ye correct answer hai jo interview mein bolna chahiye: O(n) auxiliary space, jisme O(log n) recursion stack shamil hai.

    Case Time Space
    Best Theta(n log n) O(n)
    Average Theta(n log n) O(n)
    Worst Theta(n log n) O(n)
    Recursion depth — O(log n)
    Linked list version Theta(n log n) O(log n) — stack only

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan merge mein left[i] <= right[j] — tie par left (jo original mein pehle tha) pehle jata hai
    In-place Nahi O(n) auxiliary buffer chahiye
    Adaptive Nahi (plain version) Har haal mein same recursion tree, same merges. arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] wala check thodi adaptivity deta hai; Timsort ise poori tarah exploit karta hai

    Stability ka trace:

    Input: [ 3, 1a, 1b, 2 ]
Split: left = [3, 1a],  right = [1b, 2]

left sort:   [3] + [1a]  ->  merge: 3 <= 1a? No  ->  [1a, 3]
right sort:  [1b] + [2]  ->  merge: 1b <= 2? Yes ->  [1b, 2]

final merge:  L = [1a, 3],  R = [1b, 2]
  1a <= 1b ?  EQUAL -> `<=` True  ->  1a pehle  ->  [1a]
  3  <= 1b ?  No                  ->  1b        ->  [1a, 1b]   ORDER BACHA ✓
  3  <= 2  ?  No                  ->  2         ->  [1a, 1b, 2]
  L drain                         ->  3         ->  [1a, 1b, 2, 3]

Agar line 10 mein `<` hota:
  1a < 1b ?  EQUAL -> False  ->  else branch  ->  1b pehle  ->  [1b, ...]
  Result: [1b, 1a, 2, 3]  ->  UNSTABLE

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Guaranteed O(n log n) chahiye. Real-time systems, SLA-bound services jahan worst case matter karta hai. Quicksort ka O(n²) risk acceptable nahi. - Stability chahiye. Multi-key sorting, records, objects. - Linked lists sort karni hain. Merge sort linked list ke liye best algorithm hai — O(1) extra space (sirf pointer manipulation), aur random access ki zaroorat nahi. Quicksort linked list par bekaar hai kyunki partitioning ko random access chahiye. - External sorting — data RAM mein nahi samaata. Merge sort natural fit hai: chunks sort karo, disk par likho, phir k-way merge. - Parallel / distributed sorting — dono halves poori tarah independent hain, alag threads ya machines par chal sakte hain.

    Mat use karo jab: - Memory tight hai. O(n) buffer chahiye. In-place merge sort exist karta hai par uske constants itne kharab hain ki wo bekar hai. - Chhota array (n < 32). Insertion sort tez hai — recursion overhead merge sort ko maar deta hai. Isiliye production implementations chhote subarrays par switch karti hain. - Cache-sensitive code aur array bahut bada. Quicksort ka memory access pattern zyada cache-friendly hai (partitioning ek hi array par hoti hai), isliye quicksort practically merge sort se ~2x tez hota hai same asymptotic class hote hue bhi.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Chhote subarrays par insertion sort (cutoff ~16-32) 10-15% speedup — recursion overhead khatam Ek if aur insertion sort ka code
    2 arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] check Already-sorted ranges par merge skip. Nearly-sorted data par bada fayda Ek comparison per merge — free
    3 Ek hi buffer reuse karo (allocate mat karo har call par) 2-3x speedup, allocator pressure khatam Ek extra parameter pass karna
    4 Buffer aur array ke roles alternate karo (ping-pong) Har merge par copy-back bach jata hai, ~20% Code complicated, aakhir mein result kis array mein hai wo track karna padta hai
    5 Bottom-up (iterative) merge sort Recursion khatam, stack overflow ka risk nahi Code thoda kam readable, arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] optimisation lagana mushkil
    6 Natural merge sort — pehle se sorted "runs" detect karo Nearly-sorted data par O(n) Run detection ka overhead
    7 Timsort — natural runs + galloping + insertion sort + merge invariants Real data par sabse tez stable sort Bahut complicated (CPython mein ~2000 lines C)
    8 Parallel merge sort Multi-core par ~linear speedup Thread overhead; chhote arrays par ulta dheema

    Bottom-up (iterative) version — recursion ke bina:

    def merge_sort_bottom_up(arr):
    """Iterative merge sort. Koi recursion nahi, koi stack risk nahi."""
    n = len(arr)                                        # 1
    buffer = [0] * n                                    # 2
    width = 1                                           # 3
    while width < n:                                    # 4
        for low in range(0, n, 2 * width):              # 5
            mid = min(low + width - 1, n - 1)           # 6
            high = min(low + 2 * width - 1, n - 1)      # 7
            if mid < high:                              # 8
                _merge(arr, buffer, low, mid, high)     # 9
        width *= 2                                      # 10
    return arr                                          # 11
    1. Length.
    2. Ek hi buffer, poore algorithm ke liye.
    3. width = 1 — shuruaat mein hum size-1 ke subarrays ko merge karte hain (jo already sorted hain). Ye recursion ke "bottom" se shuru karne jaisa hai.
    4. while width < n — jab tak ek hi subarray poore array ko cover na kar le. < n hai <= n nahi — agar width >= n ho gaya to poora array ek hi sorted block hai, kaam khatam. <= likhne se ek fizool iteration chalti.
    5. for low in range(0, n, 2 * width) — array par 2*width ke jumps mein chalo. Har jump ek jodi ko cover karta hai: [low, low+width-1] aur [low+width, low+2*width-1]. Step 2*width hai width nahi — kyunki hum jodiyaan merge kar rahe hain, ek-ek nahi.
    6. mid = min(low + width - 1, n - 1) — pehle block ka end. min ke saath clamp kyunki array ki length 2*width ka multiple nahi ho sakti — aakhri jodi adhoori ho sakti hai. Bina min ke _merge mein out-of-range indices aate.
    7. high = min(low + 2*width - 1, n - 1) — doosre block ka end, wahi clamping.
    8. if mid < high — agar mid == high, iska matlab doosra block khali hai (aakhri adhoori jodi mein sirf pehla block hai). Us case mein merge karne ko kuchh nahi. <= likhte to mid == high par bhi merge call hoti jo galat range de kar bug create karti (ya no-op karti, implementation par depend).
    9. Merge — wahi function jo upar likha tha.
    10. width *= 2 — agla level: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... Ye exactly recursion tree ke levels hain, bas neeche se upar.
    11. Return.

    Bottom-up ka trace — [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3], n = 6:

    width Jodiyaan merge hui Array baad mein
    1 [5]+[2], [4]+[6], [1]+[3] [2,5, 4,6, 1,3]
    2 [2,5]+[4,6], [1,3]+[] (skip) [2,4,5,6, 1,3]
    4 [2,4,5,6]+[1,3] [1,2,3,4,5,6]

    3 levels = ceil(log2(6)) = 3. ✓

    Interview answer: Merge sort is the classic divide and conquer sort. Split the array at the midpoint, recursively sort both halves, then merge the two sorted halves in linear time. The merge is the interesting part: because both inputs are sorted, comparing only their front elements is enough to decide which element is globally next, so merging n elements costs O(n) comparisons, not O(n²).

    The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Drawing the recursion tree, each level does a total of O(n) work — the subproblems at any level partition the whole array — and the depth is log2(n) because the size halves each level. So the total is O(n log n), and critically that's the same in the best, average and worst case, because the split point never depends on the data.

    It's stable, provided the merge uses left[i] <= right[j] — on a tie it must take from the left half, which came earlier in the original array. Changing that to a strict < silently makes the sort unstable. It is not in-place: it needs O(n) auxiliary space, plus O(log n) for the recursion stack.

    Where it really wins is linked lists — merging is pure pointer manipulation, so you get O(n log n) with only O(log n) stack and no random access — and external sorting, where the data doesn't fit in memory: sort chunks, spill them to disk, then do a k-way merge.

    Cross-question: "Quicksort and merge sort are both O(n log n) on average, but quicksort is usually faster in practice. Why?"

    Two reasons. Memory: quicksort partitions in place, so it touches one array with a sequential access pattern that's very cache friendly, while merge sort constantly copies between the array and an auxiliary buffer, doubling memory traffic. And constant factors: quicksort's inner loop is a comparison plus a pointer increment, which is tighter than merge sort's inner loop with its bounds checks and copies. Merge sort wins when you need the worst-case guarantee, stability, or you're sorting a linked list.

    Cross-question: "What's the actual space complexity of merge sort? I've seen O(n), O(n log n) and O(log n) quoted."

    All three appear, and it depends on the implementation. A naive version that slices new lists at every recursive call allocates O(n log n) in total, though the live peak is closer to O(n). A proper implementation allocates a single O(n) buffer once and reuses it, plus O(log n) for the recursion stack — so O(n). And for linked lists you need no buffer at all, just pointer rewiring, so it's O(log n) for the stack alone. The answer I'd give unqualified is O(n) auxiliary space for arrays.

    Cross-question: "How would you sort a 100 GB file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM?"

    External merge sort. Read the file in chunks that fit in memory — say 4 GB — sort each chunk with an in-memory sort, and write each sorted chunk back to disk as a run. That gives you 25 sorted runs. Then do a k-way merge: open all 25 runs, keep a min-heap of their current heads, repeatedly pop the smallest and write it to the output while pulling the next element from that run. The heap makes each output element cost O(log k). Total I/O is 2 passes over the data, which is close to optimal.

    Merge Sort on Linked Lists¶

    Kya hai¶

    Wahi merge sort, par array ki jagah singly linked list par — aur yahan ye array wale version se behtar ho jata hai, kyunki merging ke liye koi extra array nahi chahiye, sirf pointers rewire karne hote hain.

    Real-world analogy: Train ke dabbe (coaches). Aap unhe reorder karna chahte ho. Array wale case mein aapko har dabbe ka saamaan doosre dabbe mein shift karna padta (copy). Linked list mein aap sirf couplings (jodne wale hook) badal dete ho — dabbe wahin khade rehte hain, bas order badal jata hai. Isliye O(1) extra space.

    Kyu hai¶

    Linked list par baaki sorts kyun fail karte hain:

    Algorithm Linked list par problem
    Quick sort Partitioning ko arr[i], arr[j] random access chahiye. Linked list par arr[i] O(i) hai → poora algorithm O(n²)
    Heap sort Heap ko parent/child index arithmetic (2i+1) chahiye — linked list par O(n) per access
    Shell sort Gap-h par arr[j - gap] chahiye — O(gap) traversal
    Insertion sort Chalta hai, par O(n²)
    Merge sort ✓ Sirf sequential access chahiye. Merge ke liye do heads dekhne hain, bas

    Merge sort sirf aage ki taraf chalta hai — wahi ek cheez linked list de sakti hai. Isliye ye linked list ke liye canonical sort hai. Java ka Collections.sort LinkedList par merge sort hi karta hai (haalanki wo pehle array mein copy karta hai).

    Doosra fayda: array version O(n) buffer maangta tha. Linked list version mein merge ka output wahi nodes hain jo input mein the — bas next pointers badle. O(1) extra space (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Teen kadam:

    1. SPLIT: list ko beech se do halves mein todo
   -> Middle dhoondhne ke liye "slow/fast pointer" (tortoise and hare)

   slow ek kadam, fast do kadam:
   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
   s    
   f    

   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
        s         
             f    

   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
             s              
                       f    (f.next is None -> ruko)

   slow = 3 -> ye middle hai

2. RECURSE: dono halves ko sort karo

3. MERGE: do sorted lists ko pointers rewire karke jodo

    Split ke liye slow/fast trick kyun? Kyunki linked list ki length pata karne ke liye ek poora traversal (O(n)) lagega, phir n/2 tak jaane ke liye aur O(n/2). Slow/fast ek hi traversal mein kaam kar deta hai. Dono ka asymptotic same hai (O(n)), par slow/fast idiom interviews mein bahut common hai aur isko jaanana zaroori hai.

    Ek critical detail: split karte waqt pehle half ka last node ka next None set karna padta hai, warna dono halves ek doosre se jude rehte hain aur infinite recursion ho jati hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input list: 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> None

    Call 1: sort(4->2->1->3)

    Split — slow/fast:

    Step prev slow fast fast.next
    init None 4 4 2
    1 4 2 1 3
    2 2 1 None — (loop ruk gaya, fast is None)

    prev = 2, to prev.next = None → left = 4 -> 2 -> None, right = 1 -> 3 -> None.

    Call 2: sort(4->2)

    Split: init prev=None, slow=4, fast=4. fast.next = 2, fast.next.next = None → loop condition fail after one step. prev = 4, slow = 2. prev.next = None → left = 4 -> None, right = 2 -> None.

    • sort(4) → base case (single node) → 4
    • sort(2) → base case → 2
    • merge(4, 2):
    Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output so far
    1 4 2 4 <= 2? No R (2) 2
    2 4 None R khatam attach L 2 -> 4

    Result: 2 -> 4 -> None

    Call 3: sort(1->3)

    Split → left = 1, right = 3. Merge:

    Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output
    1 1 3 1 <= 3? Yes L (1) 1
    2 None 3 L khatam attach R 1 -> 3

    Result: 1 -> 3 -> None

    Back in Call 1: merge(2->4, 1->3)

    Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output so far
    1 2 1 2 <= 1? No R (1) 1
    2 2 3 2 <= 3? Yes L (2) 1 -> 2
    3 4 3 4 <= 3? No R (3) 1 -> 2 -> 3
    4 4 None R khatam attach L 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4

    Final: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> None ✓

    Code¶

    class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):          # 1
        self.val = val                            # 2
        self.next = nxt                           # 3


def sort_list(head):
    """Singly linked list ko merge sort se sort karta hai. O(1) extra space (stack chhod kar)."""
    if head is None or head.next is None:         # 4
        return head                               # 5

    prev, slow, fast = None, head, head           # 6
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:   # 7
        prev = slow                               # 8
        slow = slow.next                          # 9
        fast = fast.next.next                     # 10
    prev.next = None                              # 11

    left = sort_list(head)                        # 12
    right = sort_list(slow)                       # 13
    return merge_lists(left, right)               # 14


def merge_lists(a, b):
    """Do sorted linked lists ko jodta hai. Naye nodes nahi banata, sirf rewire karta hai."""
    dummy = ListNode()                            # 15
    tail = dummy                                  # 16
    while a is not None and b is not None:        # 17
        if a.val <= b.val:                        # 18
            tail.next = a                         # 19
            a = a.next                            # 20
        else:                                     # 21
            tail.next = b                         # 22
            b = b.next                            # 23
        tail = tail.next                          # 24
    tail.next = a if a is not None else b         # 25
    return dummy.next                             # 26

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. Constructor. nxt naam rakha hai next nahi — next Python ka builtin function hai (next(iterator)), use parameter naam banane se builtin shadow ho jata hai us scope mein. Attribute ka naam self.next rakhna theek hai kyunki wo alag namespace hai.
    2. Node ki value.

    3. Agle node ka pointer, default None.

    4. if head is None or head.next is None — base case. Do situations:

    5. head is None — khali list.

    6. head.next is None — ek hi node, already sorted. or ka order matter karta hai: head is None pehle check hona chahiye, warna head.next par AttributeError aayega jab head None ho. Python ka or short-circuit karta hai, isliye ye safe hai. Ulta likhne se crash. Aur is None use kiya hai, == None nahi — is identity check hai (tez aur correct); == custom __eq__ call kar sakta hai.

    7. Return.

    8. prev, slow, fast = None, head, head — teen pointers ek line mein.

    9. slow middle dhoondhega.
    10. fast do guna speed se chalega.

    11. prev sabse important hai — ye slow se ek peeche rehta hai, taaki hum list ko prev aur slow ke beech kaat sakein. Bina prev ke aap slow par pahunch to jaoge par pehle half ko terminate nahi kar paoge. Dono slow aur fast head se shuru — agar fast = head.next se shuru karte to middle ki definition badal jati (thoda left ki taraf), jo 2-node list par infinite recursion de sakti hai. Ye ek asli trap hai; neeche detail.

    12. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None — do checks:

    13. fast is not None — odd-length list mein fast exactly None par pahunchta hai.

    14. fast.next is not None — even-length list mein fast last node par ruk jata hai, aur fast.next.next par AttributeError aata. Dono chahiye, aur is order mein — fast.next check karne se pehle fast ka None na hona confirm karna zaroori hai.

    15. prev = slow — slow aage badhne se pehle uski current position bacha lo.

    16. slow = slow.next — ek kadam.

    17. fast = fast.next.next — do kadam. Jab fast end par pahunchega, slow exactly beech mein hoga (kyunki wo aadhi speed se chala).

    18. prev.next = None — list ko do hisson mein kaato. Ye line sabse critical hai. Iske bina left list right ke through poori original list ko point karti rahegi, aur sort_list(head) wahi list dobara sort karne ki koshish karega — infinite recursion, RecursionError. Ye linked-list merge sort ka #1 bug hai. prev guaranteed non-None hai kyunki line 4 ne 0 aur 1 node ke cases pehle hi return kar diye, to list mein kam se kam 2 nodes hain aur loop kam se kam ek baar chala.

    19. left = sort_list(head) — pehla half. head abhi bhi pehle node ko point karta hai, aur ab uski chain prev par khatam ho jati hai (line 11 ki wajah se).

    20. right = sort_list(slow) — doosra half slow se shuru hota hai.

    21. Merge.

    22. dummy = ListNode() — dummy / sentinel node. Ye ek khali node hai jo asli list ka hissa nahi banega. Iska poora maqsad: "pehla node kaun hai" wala special case hatana. Bina dummy ke aapko har append par check karna padta: "kya ye pehla node hai? agar haan to head = node, warna tail.next = node". Dummy ke saath ye branch khatam ho jati hai — hum hamesha tail.next likhte hain. Ye idiom linked list ke har problem mein kaam aata hai.

    23. tail = dummy — tail hamesha output list ka aakhri node hai. Shuruaat mein wo dummy hai.

    24. while a is not None and b is not None — dono lists mein nodes bache hon. and hai or nahi — or hone se ek list khatam hone par bhi loop chalta aur a.val par AttributeError.

    25. if a.val <= b.val — <= — stability. Tie par a (jo original mein pehle tha) chuna jata hai. < likhne se unstable.

    26. tail.next = a — output list ke end mein a ko jod diya. Dhyaan do: naya node nahi banaya, wahi node reuse kiya. Yahi O(1) space ka raaz hai. Agar aap ListNode(a.val) likh kar naya node banate, to space O(n) ho jata aur koi fayda nahi.

    27. a = a.next — a ko aage. Note: a.next abhi bhi purani chain ko point karta hai, par hum us par kabhi wapas nahi jayenge — agli iteration mein tail.next use overwrite kar dega ya line 25 ka drain use sahi jagah jod dega.

    21-23. Warna b wala.

    1. tail = tail.next — tail ko naye aakhri node par le jao. if/else ke bahar kyunki dono cases mein karna hai.

    2. tail.next = a if a is not None else b — drain. Ek list khatam ho chuki hai, doosri mein nodes bache ho sakte hain. Kyunki bachi hui list already sorted hai aur uske saare elements output ke last element se bade hain, hum poori bachi hui chain ko ek hi pointer assignment se jod sakte hain — element by element copy karne ki zaroorat nahi. Ye array version se behtar hai, jahan extend O(k) copies karta tha; yahan ye O(1) hai. Agar dono None hain to tail.next = None set hota hai — jo bilkul sahi hai (list terminate honi chahiye).

    3. return dummy.next — dummy nahi, dummy.next. dummy ek fake node hai; asli list uske baad shuru hoti hai. dummy return karne se output mein ek extra garbage node aa jayega — classic bug.

    Do-node list par infinite recursion ka trap (line 6 ki wajah):

    List: 1 -> 2 -> None

Agar humne  slow = head, fast = head  kiya (jo humne kiya):
  init:  prev=None, slow=1, fast=1
  loop check: fast(1) not None ✓, fast.next(2) not None ✓ -> chalo
    prev = 1
    slow = 2
    fast = fast.next.next = None
  loop check: fast is None -> ruko
  prev.next = None  ->  left = [1], right = [2]     ✓ SAHI

Agar humne  slow = head, fast = head.next  kiya:
  init:  prev=None, slow=1, fast=2
  loop check: fast(2) not None ✓, fast.next(None) is None -> RUKO turant
    prev abhi bhi None hai!
  prev.next = None  ->  AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'next'

    Isliye fast = head se shuru karna zaroori hai is particular implementation mein.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    T(n) = 2*T(n/2)  +  O(n)
                    ^^^^
       split (O(n) slow/fast traversal) + merge (O(n) pointer rewiring)

Same recurrence as array merge sort  ->  O(n log n)

    Split ka cost O(n) hai — array version mein split O(1) tha (bas mid calculate karo, slicing ko chhod kar). Linked list par middle dhoondhne ke liye traverse karna padta hai. Par ye recurrence ko badalta nahi kyunki merge bhi O(n) hai — dono mil kar O(n) per level.

    Space:

    Merge ka extra space:  O(1)  <- sirf dummy, tail, a, b pointers
Recursion stack depth: O(log n)  <- balanced split ki wajah se

Total auxiliary: O(log n)

    Compare karo array version se, jahan O(n) buffer chahiye tha. Linked list version asymptotically kam memory leta hai.

    Case Time Space
    Best Theta(n log n) O(log n)
    Average Theta(n log n) O(log n)
    Worst Theta(n log n) O(log n)

    Bottom-up version se O(1) space: Agar recursion hi hata do (bottom-up iterative merge), to space poora O(1) ho jata hai. Ye LeetCode "Sort List" ka follow-up hai: "sort in O(n log n) time and O(1) space".

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan a.val <= b.val — tie par left/pehla wala
    In-place Haan (linked list ke context mein) Koi naya node nahi banta, sirf pointers badalte hain. O(log n) stack
    Adaptive Nahi Har haal mein same splits aur merges

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Aapke paas linked list hai aur usse sort karna hai. Ye best available option hai. - Interview mein "Sort a linked list in O(n log n) time" poochha jaye — ye standard answer hai. - Data structure ko convert nahi kar sakte (jaise memory-constrained embedded list).

    Mat use karo jab: - Aapke paas array hai — array par quicksort/Timsort cache locality ki wajah se kaafi tez hain. - List chhoti hai (< 50 nodes) — insertion sort simpler aur practically tez hai. - Aap list ko array mein copy kar sakte ho aur wapas — ye kabhi kabhi practically tez hota hai (O(n) copy + fast array sort), haalanki O(n) extra space leta hai.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Bottom-up iterative Space O(log n) → O(1), koi stack overflow risk nahi Code kaafi lamba (list ko manually chunks mein kaatna padta hai)
    2 Length ek baar calculate karo, phir split ke liye counting use karo Har call mein slow/fast traversal ki jagah simple counter Ek extra parameter, mamooli fayda
    3 Chhoti lists par insertion sort (< 8 nodes) Recursion overhead bachta Cutoff tune karna padta hai
    4 Natural runs detect karo Nearly-sorted lists par O(n) Extra pass
    5 List ko array mein copy karo, array sort karo, wapas likho Practically tez (cache locality) O(n) space — asli fayda khatam
    6 Doubly linked list — prev pointer se split O(1) mein Split sasta Extra memory per node

    Interview answer: Merge sort is the natural algorithm for linked lists, and it's actually better there than on arrays. There are three steps: find the middle with the slow/fast pointer technique, cut the list in two, recursively sort both halves, then merge by rewiring next pointers. Merging allocates nothing — it reuses the existing nodes — so the extra space is just O(log n) for the recursion stack, versus O(n) for the array version.

    The two details that make or break it: first, after finding the middle you must set the previous node's next to None, otherwise the first half still runs through the whole original list and you get infinite recursion. Second, use a dummy head node in the merge so you don't need a special case for "is this the first node" on every append — you always write to tail.next.

    Quicksort is a poor fit for linked lists because partitioning wants random access, and heapsort needs index arithmetic for parent and child positions. Merge sort only needs sequential forward traversal, which is exactly what a singly linked list gives you. That's why Java's Collections.sort and most standard library list sorts are merge-based.

    Cross-question: "Can you do it in O(1) space?"

    Yes, with a bottom-up iterative version. Instead of recursing, you make passes with a run width that doubles each pass — 1, 2, 4, 8 — splitting off runs of that width from the front of the list, merging pairs of them, and appending to an output list. No recursion, so no stack, and merging is still pure pointer rewiring. It's noticeably more code because you have to manually detach runs of a given length, but it's the standard answer to that follow-up.

    Cross-question: "Why does the slow/fast split start both pointers at head rather than fast at head.next?"

    Because we also need the node before slow so we can cut the list. If fast starts at head.next, then on a two-node list the loop exits immediately with prev still None, and prev.next = None throws AttributeError. Starting both at head guarantees at least one loop iteration whenever the list has two or more nodes, which the base case has already ensured.

    Quick Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Quick sort ek pivot element chunta hai, array ko is tarah rearrange karta hai ki pivot se chhote sab left mein aur bade sab right mein aa jayen (partition), aur phir dono sides ko recursively sort karta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Ek badi class ke 100 students ko roll number order mein khada karna hai. Aap kehte ho: "Jinka roll number 50 se kam hai wo is taraf, baaki us taraf." Ek hi kadam mein class do groups mein bant gayi, aur ab 50 khud apni sahi jagah par hai — uske left mein 49 log hain, right mein 50. Ab har group ke andar wahi tareeka dohrao. Dhyaan do ki aapne kabhi "poore group ko sort" nahi kiya — aapne bas baant diya, aur baantne se hi sorting apne aap ho gayi.

    Merge sort se ulta: Merge sort mein todna aasan tha (bas beech se) aur jodna mehnat (merge). Quick sort mein todna mehnat hai (partition) aur jodna free hai — kyunki partition ke baad left, pivot, right pehle se sahi order mein hain, unhe jodne ke liye kuchh karna hi nahi.

    Kyu hai¶

    Merge sort ne guaranteed O(n log n) de diya tha. To quicksort kyun?

    Do wajah:

    1. Memory. Merge sort ko O(n) auxiliary buffer chahiye. Quick sort in-place partition karta hai — sirf O(log n) recursion stack. Jab aap 8 GB array sort kar rahe ho aur RAM 10 GB hai, ye farak zindagi aur maut ka hai.

    2. Speed — constant factors. Dono O(n log n) hain, par quicksort practically 2-3x tez hota hai. Kyun?

    Merge sort ka inner loop:
    - buffer se padho
    - array mein likho
    - do bounds check
    - do pointers manage karo
    => har element par ~2 memory operations (ek read + ek write) alag alag arrays mein

Quick sort ka inner loop (Lomuto):
    - array se padho
    - ek comparison
    - kabhi kabhi swap
    => ek hi array par sequential access -> CPU cache mein sab kuchh

    CPU cache line 64 bytes ki hoti hai. Quicksort ek hi array par aage-peeche chalta hai, to prefetcher use predict kar leta hai. Merge sort do arrays ke beech kood-ta hai, to cache misses zyada hote hain. Yahi wajah hai ki C ka qsort, C++ ka std::sort, Java ka primitive-array sort — sab quicksort family se hain.

    Quicksort ki kharabi: Agar pivot hamesha kharab chuna jaye (jaise hamesha sabse chhota element), to partition balanced nahi hota aur recursion depth n ho jati hai → O(n²). Aur ye sirf theoretical nahi — already-sorted array par naive quicksort exactly yahi karta hai, jo ki real world mein bahut common input hai. Isi problem ke solutions (randomisation, median-of-three, introsort) is section ka bada hissa hain.

    Kaise kaam karta hai — Lomuto partition¶

    Idea: array ko chaar zones mein rakho jab tak scan chal raha hai:

   [ <= pivot | > pivot | abhi nahi dekha | pivot ]
              ^         ^                 ^
              i+1       j                 high

   i  = "chhote wale zone" ka aakhri index
   j  = current scanner
   pivot = arr[high] (last element)

Har step par:
   agar arr[j] <= pivot:  i++ ; swap(arr[i], arr[j])   <- element ko chhote zone mein daalo
   j++

Scan khatam hone par:
   swap(arr[i+1], arr[high])   <- pivot ko apni sahi jagah par
   return i+1                   <- pivot ka final index

    ASCII trace of the invariant:

    Shuru mein:  i = low - 1,  j = low

  low                              high
   |                                |
  [ ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? | P ]
  ^
  j
 (i yahan se ek peeche, "khali zone")

Beech mein:

  [ <=P <=P <=P | >P >P >P >P | ? ? ? ? | P ]
                ^              ^
                i              j

Ant mein (j == high):

  [ <=P <=P <=P | >P >P >P >P >P >P | P ]
                ^                     ^
                i                     high

  swap(arr[i+1], arr[high]):

  [ <=P <=P <=P | P | >P >P >P >P >P ]
                  ^
                  i+1 = pivot ki final jagah, PAKKI

    Sabse important insight: partition ke baad pivot apni final position par hai — wo kabhi dobara nahi hilega. Isliye recursion mein use include nahi karte: qs(low, p-1) aur qs(p+1, high). Agar aap p ko include kar dete (qs(low, p)), to subproblem chhota nahi hota aur infinite recursion ho sakti hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], low = 0, high = 6.

    Partition call 1 — pivot = arr[6] = 70, i = -1:

    j arr[j] arr[j] <= 70? i (naya) Swap Array
    0 10 Yes 0 arr[0]↔arr[0] (self) [10,80,30,90,40,50,70]
    1 80 No 0 — [10,80,30,90,40,50,70]
    2 30 Yes 1 arr[1]↔arr[2] [10,30,80,90,40,50,70]
    3 90 No 1 — [10,30,80,90,40,50,70]
    4 40 Yes 2 arr[2]↔arr[4] [10,30,40,90,80,50,70]
    5 50 Yes 3 arr[3]↔arr[5] [10,30,40,50,80,90,70]

    Loop khatam (j high tak nahi jata). Ab final swap: arr[i+1] ↔ arr[high] = arr[4] ↔ arr[6]:

    [10, 30, 40, 50, **70**, 90, 80] — pivot index 4 return hua.

    Verify: index 4 se pehle [10,30,40,50] sab <= 70 ✓. Index 4 ke baad [90,80] sab > 70 ✓.

    Recursion: qs(0, 3) aur qs(5, 6).

    Partition call 2 — qs(0, 3) par [10, 30, 40, 50], pivot = arr[3] = 50, i = -1:

    j arr[j] <= 50? i Swap Array (0..3 hissa)
    0 10 Yes 0 self [10,30,40,50]
    1 30 Yes 1 self [10,30,40,50]
    2 40 Yes 2 self [10,30,40,50]

    Final swap: arr[3] ↔ arr[3] — self. Pivot index 3.

    Dhyaan do: ye WORST CASE partition hai — pivot sabse bada nikla, to left mein 3 elements aur right mein 0. Aisa isliye hua kyunki ye sub-array already sorted hai aur hum last element ko pivot chunte hain. Yahi naive quicksort ki bimari hai.

    Recursion: qs(0, 2) aur qs(4, 3) (khali, turant return).

    Partition call 3 — qs(0, 2) par [10, 30, 40], pivot = 40:

    j arr[j] <= 40? i Array
    0 10 Yes 0 [10,30,40]
    1 30 Yes 1 [10,30,40]

    Pivot index 2. Recursion: qs(0,1), qs(3,2) (khali).

    Partition call 4 — qs(0, 1) par [10, 30], pivot = 30:

    j arr[j] <= 30? i Array
    0 10 Yes 0 [10,30]

    Pivot index 1. Recursion: qs(0,0) (single, return), qs(2,1) (khali, return).

    Partition call 5 — qs(5, 6) par [90, 80], pivot = arr[6] = 80, i = 4:

    j arr[j] <= 80? i Swap Array (5..6)
    5 90 No 4 — [90,80]

    Final swap: arr[i+1] ↔ arr[high] = arr[5] ↔ arr[6] → [80, 90]. Pivot index 5.

    Recursion: qs(5,4) (khali), qs(6,6) (single).

    Final array: [10, 30, 40, 50, 70, 80, 90] ✓

    Recursion tree — ye complexity samajhne ke liye:

                      qs(0,6)  n=7, pivot=70 at idx 4
                 /                        \
        qs(0,3) n=4                     qs(5,6) n=2
        pivot=50 at idx 3               pivot=80 at idx 5
        /            \                  /          \
   qs(0,2) n=3    qs(4,3) empty    qs(5,4) empty  qs(6,6) n=1
   pivot=40 idx 2
   /        \
qs(0,1) n=2  qs(3,2) empty
pivot=30 idx 1
 /      \
qs(0,0) qs(2,1)
 n=1    empty

Depth = 4 for n = 7.  log2(7) ~ 2.8, so we're deeper than ideal
kyunki left side ke saare partitions unbalanced the.

    Code¶

    import random                                       # 1


def quick_sort(arr, low=0, high=None):
    """Lomuto partition ke saath quick sort. In-place."""
    if high is None:                                # 2
        high = len(arr) - 1                         # 3
    if low < high:                                  # 4
        p = lomuto_partition(arr, low, high)        # 5
        quick_sort(arr, low, p - 1)                 # 6
        quick_sort(arr, p + 1, high)                # 7
    return arr                                      # 8


def lomuto_partition(arr, low, high):
    """arr[low..high] ko pivot ke around partition karta hai. Pivot ka final index return karta hai."""
    r = random.randint(low, high)                   # 9
    arr[r], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[r]           # 10
    pivot = arr[high]                               # 11
    i = low - 1                                     # 12
    for j in range(low, high):                      # 13
        if arr[j] <= pivot:                         # 14
            i += 1                                  # 15
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]         # 16
    arr[i + 1], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i + 1]   # 17
    return i + 1                                    # 18

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. import random — pivot randomisation ke liye. Ye O(n²) worst case se bachne ka sabse practical tareeka hai.

    2. if high is None — default argument trick, taaki caller sirf quick_sort(arr) likh sake. high=None default rakha hai, high=len(arr)-1 nahi — kyunki Python ke default arguments function define hone ke waqt ek baar evaluate hote hain, aur us waqt arr exist hi nahi karta. def f(arr, high=len(arr)-1) NameError dega. Ye Python ka important rule hai.

    3. high = len(arr) - 1 — last valid index. len(arr) nahi — high inclusive hai is code ke convention mein.

    4. if low < high — base case ka ulta. Agar low >= high to range mein 0 ya 1 element hai — already sorted, kuchh nahi karna. < hai <= nahi: agar <= likh dete to low == high (single element) par bhi partition call hoti; lomuto_partition(arr, 5, 5) chalta, range(5,5) khali, final swap self-swap, return 5, phir quick_sort(arr, 5, 4) aur quick_sort(arr, 6, 5) — dono base case hit karte. Yaani galat nahi, bas fizool calls. Par if True (koi check hi nahi) likhne se infinite recursion.

    5. p = lomuto_partition(...) — partition karo, pivot ka final index lo.

    6. quick_sort(arr, low, p - 1) — left side, pivot ko chhod kar. p - 1 hai p nahi. Ye sabse critical line hai. Agar aap quick_sort(arr, low, p) likh dete to:

    7. Pivot dobara subproblem mein aa jata.
    8. Agar pivot sabse chhota tha (p == low), to subproblem (low, low) hota — theek hai.

    9. Par agar p == high (pivot sabse bada), to quick_sort(arr, low, high) = same call → infinite recursion, stack overflow. Pivot ka final position par hona hi wo guarantee hai jo subproblem ko strictly chhota banati hai.

    10. quick_sort(arr, p + 1, high) — right side, pivot ko chhod kar. Wahi logic.

    11. Return.

    12. r = random.randint(low, high) — random pivot chuno. randint dono ends inclusive deta hai (randrange exclusive deta hai — dhyaan rakhna). Kyun? Kyunki fixed pivot (jaise hamesha arr[high]) par ek adversary aisa input bana sakta hai jo hamesha worst case hit kare. Sorted array par last-element pivot hamesha sabse bada nikalta hai → har partition mein ek taraf 0 elements → depth n → O(n²). Randomisation ke saath koi bhi fixed input worst case guarantee nahi kar sakta — worst case ki probability n! ke inverse jaisi ho jati hai. Expected time O(n log n) har input par. Ye "expected" hai "guaranteed" nahi — theoretically worst case abhi bhi O(n²) hai, par uski probability itni kam hai ki practically nahi hota.

    13. arr[r], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[r] — random pivot ko high par le aao. Ye chhota sa step is liye hai ki baaki ka algorithm bilkul waise hi chal sake jaise wo last element ko pivot maan kar likha gaya tha. Agar aap ye swap na karte aur direct pivot = arr[r] likhte, to partition logic mein r ko special-case karna padta — bahut zyada complexity. Ek swap se poori problem gayab.

    14. pivot = arr[high] — pivot ki value copy kar li. Value copy karna zaroori hai kyunki line 16 ke swaps arr[high] ko badal sakte hain... actually nahi, j kabhi high tak nahi jata (line 13 range(low, high) hai). Par phir bhi value copy karna clearer hai aur har comparison mein array access bachata hai.

    15. i = low - 1 — low - 1, low nahi. i "chhote-zone ka aakhri index" hai. Shuru mein chhota zone khali hai, to i low se ek peeche hona chahiye. Agar i = low likh dete, to pehla element bina check kiye chhote zone ka hissa maan liya jata, aur line 15 ka i += 1 ek extra jagah aage kar deta → galat answer aur kabhi kabhi IndexError. Ye ek classic off-by-one hai.

    16. for j in range(low, high) — low se high - 1 tak. high include nahi kyunki arr[high] pivot hai, use khud se compare karna bekaar hai (aur usse swap karne se logic toot jayega).

    17. if arr[j] <= pivot — <= hai < nahi. Kyun? Socho agar array mein saare elements barabar hain ([5,5,5,5,5]):

      • <= ke saath: har element chhote zone mein jayega → i har baar badhega → pivot end mein high par hi rahega → partition point = high → ek taraf n-1, doosri taraf 0 → O(n²). Bura!
      • < ke saath: koi element chhote zone mein nahi jayega → i low-1 par hi rahega → pivot low par jayega → ek taraf 0, doosri taraf n-1 → bhi O(n²). Bhi bura! Yaani dono choices duplicates par O(n²) deti hain — isliye Lomuto duplicates ke liye kharab hai. Iska asli solution 3-way partitioning hai (alag section). <= conventionally use hota hai. Note: <= ke saath Lomuto unstable hai (neeche).

    18. i += 1 — chhota zone ek badhao. Line 16 se pehle, kyunki i ab wo naya slot hai jahan chhota element rakhna hai.

    19. arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i] — chhote element ko chhote zone ke end mein le aao, aur jo wahan tha (jo pakka > pivot tha, ya i == j par khud hi) use j par bhej do. i == j par ye self-swap hai — waste, par harmless. Chaho to if i != j guard laga do; typically fayda kam hai.

    20. arr[i + 1], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i + 1] — pivot ko apni final jagah par. i + 1 kyun? i chhote zone ka aakhri index hai, to i + 1 pehla index hai jahan > pivot wale elements shuru hote hain. Pivot ko wahin jaana chahiye — uske left mein sab chhote, right mein sab bade. Agar aap arr[i] par swap karte to ek chhota element pivot ke right mein chala jata — galat answer.

    21. return i + 1 — pivot ka final index. Yahi quick_sort mein p banta hai.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Best case — pivot hamesha exact median:

    T(n) = 2 * T(n/2) + O(n)        <- partition O(n), do halves barabar

Recursion tree:
  Level 0:  n            work = n
  Level 1:  n/2, n/2     work = n
  Level 2:  4 x n/4      work = n
  ...
  Depth = log2(n)

Total = n * log2(n)  ->  O(n log n)

    Worst case — pivot hamesha sabse chhota ya sabse bada:

    T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + O(n)
     = T(n-1) + O(n)

Expand karo:
T(n) = n + T(n-1)
     = n + (n-1) + T(n-2)
     = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1
     = n(n+1)/2
     ->  O(n²)

Recursion tree:
  n
  |
  n-1
  |
  n-2
  |
  ...
  |
  1
  Depth = n  ->  STACK OVERFLOW bhi ho sakta hai!

    Kab hota hai? Naive (last-element) pivot ke saath: already sorted array, reverse sorted array, ya saare elements barabar. Ye teenon real world mein bahut common hain — yahi naive quicksort ka danger hai.

    Average case — ye derivation interview mein bahut impress karti hai:
