    Code¶

    def heap_sort(arr):
    """In-place heap sort. Guaranteed O(n log n), O(1) extra space."""
    n = len(arr)                                    # 1
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):             # 2
        sift_down(arr, i, n)                        # 3
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):                 # 4
        arr[0], arr[end] = arr[end], arr[0]         # 5
        sift_down(arr, 0, end)                      # 6
    return arr                                      # 7


def sift_down(arr, i, heap_size):
    """Node i ko neeche sarkao jab tak max-heap property bahal na ho jaye."""
    while True:                                     # 8
        largest = i                                 # 9
        left = 2 * i + 1                            # 10
        right = 2 * i + 2                           # 11
        if left < heap_size and arr[left] > arr[largest]:    # 12
            largest = left                          # 13
        if right < heap_size and arr[right] > arr[largest]:  # 14
            largest = right                         # 15
        if largest == i:                            # 16
            return                                  # 17
        arr[i], arr[largest] = arr[largest], arr[i] # 18
        i = largest                                 # 19

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. n = len(arr) — length.

    2. for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1) — build heap phase. Teen cheezein samajhni hain:

    3. Shuruaat n // 2 - 1 se kyun? Ye aakhri non-leaf node ka index hai. Last element ka index n-1 hai, uska parent (n-1-1)//2 = (n-2)//2 = n//2 - 1 (integer arithmetic). Us index se aage saare nodes leaves hain, aur ek leaf apne aap ek valid heap hai (uske koi children hi nahi). To unhe sift karne ki zaroorat nahi. Isse aadha kaam bach jata hai.
    4. -1 end (exclusive) kyun? Taaki i = 0 bhi include ho. range(x, 0, -1) 1 par rukta hai; range(x, -1, -1) 0 par rukta hai. Agar -1 ki jagah 0 likh dete to root kabhi sift nahi hota aur heap invalid rehta.

    5. Ulta (-1 step) kyun chalte hain? Kyunki sift_down ka assumption hai ki node ke dono subtrees pehle se valid heaps hain. Neeche se upar chalne se ye guarantee milti hai. Agar aap upar se neeche chalte (range(0, n)), to root ko sift karte waqt uske subtrees valid heaps nahi hote aur result galat aata.

    6. sift_down(arr, i, n) — heap size poora n hai is phase mein.

    7. for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1) — sort phase. end wo index hai jahan current max rakha jayega.

    8. n - 1 se shuru — last position.

    9. 0 par rukta hai (exclusive) — yaani end 1 tak jata hai. -1 nahi likha kyunki jab sirf ek element bacha ho (end = 0), wo apne aap sorted hai — arr[0] ↔ arr[0] ek fizool self-swap hoti.

    10. arr[0], arr[end] = arr[end], arr[0] — root (max) ko end par bhejo. Ye element ab apni final position par hai aur dobara nahi hilega. Aur jo end par tha (jo heap ka koi bhi element ho sakta hai) wo ab root par aa gaya — jo galat hai, isliye line 6.

    11. sift_down(arr, 0, end) — end, end + 1 nahi. Heap ka naya size end hai kyunki arr[end] ab sorted region ka hissa hai aur use heap se bahar rakhna hai. Agar aap end + 1 ya n pass kar dete, to sift_down us max element ko dobara heap mein le aata aur wo kabhi settle nahi hota → infinite behaviour / wrong answer. Ye sabse critical parameter hai.

    12. Return.

    13. while True — iterative sift down. Recursive bhi likh sakte the, par:

    14. Recursion depth O(log n) hoti, jo har call par stack frames banati.

    15. Iterative version tez hai (function call overhead nahi) aur Python ke recursion limit ka risk nahi. Loop se bahar nikalne ka ek hi raasta hai — line 17.

    16. largest = i — assumption: current node hi sabse bada hai. Index store kar rahe hain, value nahi — kyunki line 18 mein swap ke liye index chahiye.

    17. left = 2 * i + 1 — left child ka index. Ye formula complete binary tree ke level-order numbering se aata hai.

    18. right = 2 * i + 2 — right child. = left + 1 bhi likh sakte the, same hai.

    19. if left < heap_size and arr[left] > arr[largest] — do checks:

      • left < heap_size pehle — bounds check. Agar node leaf hai to left >= heap_size hoga aur hume arr[left] access nahi karna. Python mein arr[bahut bada index] IndexError dega (jo crash hai) — par agar heap_size < len(arr) ho (jo sort phase mein hota hai!) to arr[left] valid index hoga par wo sorted region ka element hoga — silently galat comparison. Isliye heap_size use karna hai, len(arr) nahi. Ye sabse subtle bug hai heap sort mein.
      • arr[left] > arr[largest] — max-heap ke liye >. Min-heap chahiye to < kar do.

    20. largest = left — index update.

    14-15. Same right child ke liye. Note: arr[largest] se compare kar rahe hain, arr[i] se nahi — kyunki line 13 ne largest update kar diya ho sakta hai. Isse teenon (parent, left, right) mein se sabse bada mil jata hai. Agar aap arr[i] se compare karte to left aur right ke beech ka comparison chhoot jata aur heap property toot jati.

    1. if largest == i — koi child parent se bada nahi hai → heap property yahan valid hai → aur neeche jaane ki zaroorat nahi (kyunki subtrees pehle se valid heaps hain).

    2. return — kaam khatam.

    3. arr[i], arr[largest] = arr[largest], arr[i] — parent aur sabse bade child ki adla badli.

    4. i = largest — neeche wale node par jaao aur dobara check karo. Kyunki jo element abhi neeche gaya wo apne naye children se bhi chhota ho sakta hai. Ye "sinking" hai. Agar ye line na hoti to loop infinite ho jata (i wahi rehta, wahi swap dobara).

    heapq module ka use (production Python):

    import heapq                                        # 1

def heap_sort_stdlib(arr):
    h = list(arr)                                   # 2
    heapq.heapify(h)                                # 3
    return [heapq.heappop(h) for _ in range(len(h))]   # 4
    1. heapq — CPython ka built-in binary heap, C mein implemented.
    2. Copy — heapify in-place kaam karta hai, original ko bachana hai to copy zaroori.
    3. heapify(h) — O(n) mein list ko min-heap banata hai. Dhyaan do: Python ka heapq sirf min-heap deta hai. Max-heap chahiye to values ko negate karo (-x) ya ek wrapper class banao __lt__ reverse karke.
    4. Baar baar heappop — har pop O(log n), n pops → O(n log n). Result ascending order mein. Ye O(n) extra space leta hai (naya list) — in-place nahi hai.

    Production mein agar sort chahiye to seedha sorted() use karo (Timsort, tez aur stable). heapq ki asli jagah priority queue hai, sort nahi.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Phase 1 — build heap. Ye O(n) hai, O(n log n) NAHI. Ye derivation interview mein bahut impress karti hai:

    Naive soch: n/2 nodes par sift_down, har sift_down O(log n) → O(n log n). Ye upper bound hai par tight nahi.

    Asli baat: sift_down ka cost node ki height par depend karta hai, tree ki height par nahi. Aur zyadatar nodes neeche hain, jahan height chhoti hai.

    Ek complete binary tree mein n nodes ke saath:

  Height 0 (leaves):     ~n/2 nodes,   sift cost 0
  Height 1:              ~n/4 nodes,   sift cost 1
  Height 2:              ~n/8 nodes,   sift cost 2
  Height 3:              ~n/16 nodes,  sift cost 3
  ...
  Height h:              ~n/2^(h+1) nodes, sift cost h

Total cost = sum over h from 0 to log(n) of  [ (n / 2^(h+1)) * h ]

           = (n/2) * sum over h of ( h / 2^h )

Ab wo summation solve karo:
  S = 0/1 + 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + ...

  Ye ek standard series hai. Trick:
  S     = 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + ...
  S/2   =       1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + ...
  ------------------------------------- ghatao
  S/2   = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + ...
  S/2   = 1                            (geometric series, ratio 1/2, sum = 1)
  S     = 2

Total cost = (n/2) * 2 = n  ->  O(n)  ✓

    Yaani build-heap O(n) hai, O(n log n) nahi. Ye counter-intuitive hai aur isi wajah se interview mein poochha jata hai. Intuition: aadhe nodes leaves hain (cost 0), quarter nodes height 1 par (cost 1), etc. — kaam exponentially ghatta hai jaise upar jaate hain.

    Phase 2 — sort:

    n-1 iterations, har iteration mein:
   1 swap                     -> O(1)
   1 sift_down from root      -> O(log(current heap size))

Total = sum over i from n-1 down to 1 of  log(i)
      = log((n-1)!)
      ~ n log n - n           (Stirling)
      ->  O(n log n)

    Total: O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).

    Best, average, worst — sab O(n log n) kyun?

    Heap sort ka structure input par depend nahi karta. Chahe array sorted ho ya random, wo har baar poora heap banata hai aur n extractions karta hai. Sift_down ki depth bhi lagbhag hamesha poori hoti hai (kyunki jo element root par aata hai wo heap ka last element hai, yaani sabse chhote elements mein se ek — wo lagbhag poore neeche tak sink karega).

    Interesting: already-sorted array par heap sort thoda dheema hota hai! Kyunki ascending sorted array already ek min-heap hai, aur use max-heap banane mein maximum kaam lagta hai.

    Comparisons ka exact count: ~2n log2(n) worst case. Merge sort n log2(n) karta hai, quicksort 1.39 n log2(n). Heap sort sabse zyada comparisons karta hai — yeh uske dheema hone ki ek wajah hai.

    Space: 

    Auxiliary data:  O(1)   <- sirf i, largest, left, right
Recursion:       O(1)   <- iterative sift_down (recursive hota to O(log n))

Total: O(1)  ->  TRUE in-place

    Case Time Space Kyun
    Best Theta(n log n) O(1) Structure input-independent
    Average Theta(n log n) O(1)
    Worst Theta(n log n) O(1) Koi input isse tod nahi sakta
    Build heap alone Theta(n) O(1) Summation derivation upar

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Nahi Root ko end par bhejne wala swap door ke elements ko jump karwata hai
    In-place Haan, poori tarah O(1) — merge sort ke O(n) aur quicksort ke O(log n) stack se bhi behtar
    Adaptive Nahi Sorted input par bhi poora kaam. Ulta, ascending-sorted input thoda mehnga hai

    Instability ka counterexample:

    Input: [ 2a, 2b, 1 ]

Build heap: n//2 - 1 = 0, so sift_down(0) with heap_size 3
  node 0 (2a), left = 1 (2b), right = 2 (1)
  arr[1]=2b > arr[0]=2a ?  strictly greater? NO (equal)  ->  largest stays 0
  arr[2]=1 > arr[0]=2a ?   No
  largest == i  ->  return
  Heap: [2a, 2b, 1]

Sort phase, end = 2:
  swap arr[0] <-> arr[2]  ->  [1, 2b, 2a]
  sift_down(0, heap_size=2): node 1, left = 1 (2b), right = 2 (out of heap)
     2b > 1 ? Yes -> largest = 1 -> swap -> [2b, 1, 2a]
  Sorted region: [2a]

Sort phase, end = 1:
  swap arr[0] <-> arr[1]  ->  [1, 2b, 2a]
  sift_down(0, heap_size=1): no children
  Sorted region: [2b, 2a]

Final: [1, 2b, 2a]   <- 2b, 2a se PEHLE. Original mein 2a pehle tha. UNSTABLE ✗

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Guaranteed O(n log n) + O(1) space dono chahiye. Ye combination sirf heap sort deta hai. Merge sort O(n) space leta hai, quicksort O(n²) worst case. - Introsort ka fallback — jab quicksort ki recursion depth 2·log2(n) paar kar jaye, to heap sort par switch karo. C++ std::sort yahi karta hai. - Priority queue chahiye — task scheduler, Dijkstra, A, event simulation, top-k. Yahan heap ka asli ghar hai. Python mein heapq. - Memory bilkul nahi hai — embedded systems. - Security-sensitive* — attacker crafted input se algorithmic complexity attack nahi ho sakta.

    Mat use karo jab: - General purpose sorting — Timsort/quicksort practically 2-3x tez hain cache ki wajah se. - Stability chahiye. - Data nearly sorted hai — heap sort ko koi fayda nahi milta, jabki Timsort O(n) mein nikal jayega.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Iterative sift_down (upar wala code) Recursion overhead khatam, stack risk khatam Kuchh nahi
    2 Bottom-up heapsort (Wegener) — pehle neeche tak jao "special path" par, phir upar aakar sahi jagah dhoondho Comparisons 2n log n → n log n, ~20-30% tez Code kaafi complicated
    3 d-ary heap (har node ke d children, jaise 4) Tree shallow hoti hai (log_4 n), cache behaviour behtar — practically 20-40% tez Har sift par d comparisons, aur code mein index arithmetic badalti
    4 heapify ko O(n) rakho (neeche se upar), O(n log n) wala insert-one-by-one mat karo Build phase n log n → n Kuchh nahi, bas sahi direction
    5 Introsort — quicksort + heapsort fallback Best of both Depth counter
    6 heapq.nlargest(k, ...) / partial heapsort Top-k O(n log k) mein, poora sort nahi Sirf top-k milta hai
    7 Smoothsort (Dijkstra) Adaptive — nearly-sorted par O(n) Bahut complicated (Leonardo heaps), practically kabhi use nahi hota

    Top-k with heap — QA mein sabse useful pattern:

    import heapq                                        # 1

def slowest_k_tests(results, k):
    """results = [(duration, test_name), ...]. k sabse dheeme tests do."""
    return heapq.nlargest(k, results)               # 2


def slowest_k_streaming(result_stream, k):
    """Memory-efficient: sirf k elements memory mein, chahe stream kitni bhi badi ho."""
    heap = []                                       # 3
    for duration, name in result_stream:            # 4
        if len(heap) < k:                           # 5
            heapq.heappush(heap, (duration, name))  # 6
        elif duration > heap[0][0]:                 # 7
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, (duration, name))   # 8
    return sorted(heap, reverse=True)               # 9
    1. heapq import.
    2. nlargest(k, iterable) — internally ek size-k min-heap maintain karta hai. O(n log k), memory O(k). Poora sort O(n log n) hota aur O(n) memory. Chhote k ke liye ye bahut behtar.
    3. heap = [] — khali list, hum ise min-heap ki tarah use karenge.
    4. Stream par iterate — poora data memory mein nahi aata.
    5. if len(heap) < k — pehle k elements bina soche daal do.
    6. heappush — O(log k).
    7. elif duration > heap[0][0] — heap[0] min-heap ka sabse chhota element hai, yaani ab tak ke top-k mein sabse kamzor candidate. Agar naya element usse bada hai, tabhi wo top-k mein ghusne ka haqdar hai. Ye check hi poore algorithm ki efficiency hai — agar ye na hota to har element par push+pop hota.
    8. heapreplace(heap, x) — ek hi operation mein pop + push. heappop + heappush se tez hai kyunki sirf ek sift_down chalti hai, do nahi.
    9. Result ko descending order mein. heap khud sorted nahi hai (heap property ≠ sorted).

    Interview answer: Heap sort has two phases. First it builds a max-heap in place over the whole array, then it repeatedly swaps the root — which is the maximum — with the last element of the heap, shrinks the heap by one, and sifts the new root down to restore the heap property. After n-1 iterations the array is sorted ascending.

    The heap is stored implicitly in the array: for index i, the children are at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent is at (i-1)//2. That works because a heap is a complete binary tree, so level-order numbering gives you the structure for free with no pointers.

    The interesting complexity result is that building the heap is O(n), not O(n log n). The naive bound multiplies n/2 nodes by log n height, but that's loose: sift-down cost depends on the node's height, and half the nodes are leaves with cost zero, a quarter are at height one, and so on. Summing n/2^(h+1) times h over all heights gives n times the series sum of h/2^h, which converges to 2, so the total is O(n). The sort phase is n extractions at O(log n) each, so overall it's O(n log n).

    Its unique selling point is that it's the only mainstream sort with both a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case and O(1) auxiliary space. Merge sort gives the guarantee but needs O(n) space; quicksort is in-place but has an O(n²) worst case. The reason it isn't the default is cache behaviour: the access pattern jumps by powers of two, so it misses cache constantly and runs two to three times slower than quicksort in practice. Its real homes are introsort's fallback and priority queues.

    Cross-question: "Why do you build the heap from n//2 - 1 downwards instead of from 0 upwards?"

    Because sift_down assumes both subtrees of the node are already valid heaps. Going bottom-up guarantees that: by the time you sift node i, everything below it has been fixed. Going top-down breaks the precondition and produces an invalid heap. And starting at n//2 - 1 skips the leaves, which are trivially valid heaps on their own — that's half the nodes for free.

    Cross-question: "Why do you pass end rather than n as the heap size in the sort phase?"

    Because the elements from index end onwards are already in final sorted position and must be outside the heap. If you passed n, sift_down would compare against and potentially pull back elements from the sorted region, and the maximum you just placed would be dragged into the heap again — the sort would never terminate correctly. The heap must shrink by exactly one each iteration.

    Cross-question: "You have a stream of a billion events and need the 100 largest. How?"

    A size-100 min-heap. Push the first 100 elements, then for every subsequent element compare it against the heap's root — the smallest of the current top 100. If it's larger, replace the root and sift down; otherwise discard it. That's O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, so 100 slots regardless of stream length. In Python that's heapq.nlargest(100, stream), or the explicit loop with heapq.heapreplace if you want to control memory precisely.

    Counting Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Counting sort elements ko compare karta hi nahi. Wo bas ginn leta hai ki har value kitni baar aayi hai, phir un counts se seedha sorted output likh deta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Ek school mein 500 bachchon ki age (5 se 18 saal) sort karni hai. Aap ek-ek bachche ko doosre se compare nahi karoge. Aap 14 dabbe rakh doge — "5 saal", "6 saal", ... "18 saal" — aur har bachche ko uske dabbe mein daal doge. Phir dabbon ko order mein khaali kar doge. Ek bhi comparison nahi hui, aur kaam ho gaya.

    Kyu hai¶

    Humne pehle derive kiya tha ki koi bhi comparison-based sort O(n log n) se tez nahi ho sakta (decision tree argument). To kya n log n hi limit hai?

    Nahi — agar aap comparisons chhod dein. Counting sort element ki value ko directly array ka index bana deta hai. Value 7 ka matlab "count[7] badhao". Ye ek O(1) operation hai jo kisi comparison ke bina element ki poori position information nikaal leti hai.

    Comparison sort:  har comparison 1 bit information deti hai (yes/no)
                  n! orderings ko distinguish karne ke liye log2(n!) bits chahiye
                  -> Omega(n log n)

Counting sort:    har element ki value SEEDHI position bata deti hai
                  -> koi decision tree hi nahi
                  -> O(n + k) jahan k = value range

    Cost: Aapko value range k ka O(k) memory chahiye. Agar values 0 se 100 tak hain aur n = 10 lakh — perfect. Agar values 0 se 10^9 tak hain aur n = 100 — disaster, 10^9 ka array banana padega.

    Rule of thumb: counting sort tab use karo jab k = O(n). Warna O(n + k) mein k dominate kar jayega.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Teen phases:

    PHASE 1 — COUNT:  har value kitni baar aayi
  input: [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1]
  count: index:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
         value:  0  1  2  2  1  0  0  0  1

PHASE 2 — PREFIX SUM:  har value ka "cumulative count" nikaalo
  ye batata hai ki har value ke elements output mein KAHAN TAK jayenge
  count: index:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
         cumul:  0  1  3  5  6  6  6  6  7
                     ^  ^
                     |  +- value 2 wale elements output ke index 1,2 par (0-based)
                     +---- value 1 wala element output ke index 0 par

PHASE 3 — PLACE:  input ko ULTA (right se left) scan karke output mein rakho
  har element x ke liye:  count[x] -= 1;  output[count[x]] = x

    Phase 3 ulta kyun chalta hai? Stability ke liye. Agar aap seedha (left se right) chalte, to same value ke elements ulte order mein output mein jaate. Ulta chalne se jo input mein aakhri tha wo output mein bhi apne group ka aakhri banta hai. Neeche detail mein trace hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Input: [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1], n = 7. Max value = 8, to k = 9 (0 se 8).

    Phase 1 — Count:

    Element process kiya count array (index 0..8)
    start [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]
    4 [0,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,0]
    2 [0,0,1,0,1,0,0,0,0]
    2 [0,0,2,0,1,0,0,0,0]
    8 [0,0,2,0,1,0,0,0,1]
    3 [0,0,2,1,1,0,0,0,1]
    3 [0,0,2,2,1,0,0,0,1]
    1 [0,1,2,2,1,0,0,0,1]

    Phase 2 — Prefix sum (cumulative):

    i count[i] pehle count[i-1] (cumulative) count[i] = count[i] + count[i-1]
    0 0 — 0
    1 1 0 1
    2 2 1 3
    3 2 3 5
    4 1 5 6
    5 0 6 6
    6 0 6 6
    7 0 6 6
    8 1 6 7

    Cumulative count: [0, 1, 3, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7]

    Iska matlab kya hai? count[v] = "kitne elements <= v hain". Yaani value v ke elements output mein index count[v-1] se count[v]-1 tak jayenge.

    Phase 3 — Place (input ko ULTA scan karte hue):

    Output array size 7, sab khali. Input ulta: 1, 3, 3, 8, 2, 2, 4.

    Step Element count[x] pehle count[x] -= 1 → naya output[naya] = x Output array
    1 1 count[1] = 1 0 output[0] = 1 [1,_,_,_,_,_,_]
    2 3 count[3] = 5 4 output[4] = 3 [1,_,_,_,3,_,_]
    3 3 count[3] = 4 3 output[3] = 3 [1,_,_,3,3,_,_]
    4 8 count[8] = 7 6 output[6] = 8 [1,_,_,3,3,_,8]
    5 2 count[2] = 3 2 output[2] = 2 [1,_,2,3,3,_,8]
    6 2 count[2] = 2 1 output[1] = 2 [1,2,2,3,3,_,8]
    7 4 count[4] = 6 5 output[5] = 4 [1,2,2,3,3,4,8]

    Final: [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8] ✓ — zero comparisons.

    Stability ka proof — ulta scan kyun:

    Maan lo input hai [ 2a, 2b ] (dono value 2, 2a pehle).
count[2] cumulative = 2 (yaani do elements <= 2 hain, indices 0 aur 1)

ULTA scan (right se left) — sahi tareeka:
  2b process:  count[2] = 2 -> 1  ->  output[1] = 2b
  2a process:  count[2] = 1 -> 0  ->  output[0] = 2a
  Output: [2a, 2b]   ORDER BACHA ✓

SEEDHA scan (left se right) — galat:
  2a process:  count[2] = 2 -> 1  ->  output[1] = 2a
  2b process:  count[2] = 1 -> 0  ->  output[0] = 2b
  Output: [2b, 2a]   ORDER TOOTA ✗

    Ye stability radix sort ke liye ABSOLUTELY zaroori hai — radix sort counting sort ko digit-by-digit call karta hai, aur agar counting sort unstable ho to pichhle digits ka kaam har naye pass mein barbaad ho jayega.

    Code¶

    def counting_sort(arr):
    """Non-negative integers ke liye stable counting sort. O(n + k)."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return arr                                  # 2
    max_val = max(arr)                              # 3
    min_val = min(arr)                              # 4
    k = max_val - min_val + 1                       # 5
    count = [0] * k                                 # 6
    for x in arr:                                   # 7
        count[x - min_val] += 1                     # 8
    for i in range(1, k):                           # 9
        count[i] += count[i - 1]                    # 10
    output = [0] * len(arr)                         # 11
    for x in reversed(arr):                         # 12
        count[x - min_val] -= 1                     # 13
        output[count[x - min_val]] = x              # 14
    return output                                   # 15

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. if not arr — khali list guard. Line 3 ka max([]) ValueError phenkta hai. Bina is check ke function khali input par crash karta.

    2. Khali list return.

    3. max_val = max(arr) — sabse badi value. Ye O(n) pass hai. Agar aapko range pehle se pata ho (jaise "values 0 se 100 tak hain") to ye pass skip kar sakte ho aur constant use kar sakte ho — thoda tez.

    4. min_val = min(arr) — sabse chhoti value. Ye offset ke liye hai. Agar aap sirf max lete aur min ignore karte, to [1000, 1001, 1002] sort karne ke liye 1003 size ka array banana padta — 1000 slots waste. min ke saath sirf 3 slots. Aur negative numbers bhi handle ho jaate hain ([-5, -3, -1] par offset -5 lagane se indices 0, 2, 4 ban jate hain). Bina min ke negative numbers par count[-5] Python mein silently galat element access karta (negative indexing) — bahut khatarnak bug.

    5. k = max_val - min_val + 1 — kitne distinct slots chahiye. +1 zaroori hai kyunki dono ends inclusive hain: [3, 5] mein 3 values hain (3, 4, 5) = 5 - 3 + 1. Bina +1 ke max value par IndexError.

    6. count = [0] * k — counts array, sab zero se shuru. [0] * k Python mein ek hi baar mein list banata hai — O(k). Note: [[]] * k aisa karna galat hota (saare sublists same object hote), par integers immutable hain to [0] * k safe hai.

    7. for x in arr — pehla pass, counting.

    8. count[x - min_val] += 1 — offset lagakar index. x - min_val hamesha 0 se k-1 ke beech hoga. Ye offset hi negative numbers aur bade offsets ko handle karta hai.

    9. for i in range(1, k) — prefix sum. 1 se shuru kyunki count[0] ka koi previous nahi hai. 0 se shuru karte to count[-1] access hota — Python mein wo last element hai, silently galat.

    10. count[i] += count[i - 1] — cumulative. Ab count[i] = "kitne elements value i+min_val se chhote ya barabar hain".

    11. output = [0] * len(arr) — output array, input jitna hi bada. In-place nahi kar sakte kyunki hume input ko poora scan karna hai jab tak output likh rahe hain.

    12. for x in reversed(arr) — ULTA scan — stability ka raaz. reversed() ek iterator deta hai, naya list nahi banata — memory efficient. Agar aap arr[::-1] likhte to poori copy banti (O(n) extra memory). Seedha (for x in arr) likhne se algorithm sahi output deta hai par UNSTABLE ho jata hai — aur radix sort tootjata hai.

    13. count[x - min_val] -= 1 — pehle ghatao. Kyunki count[v] cumulative hai — wo "kitne <= v" batata hai, yaani last valid index count[v] - 1 hai (0-based). Pehle ghatane se hume exact index milta hai. Agar aap pehle place karte phir ghatate (output[count[x]] = x; count[x] -= 1), to pehle element ke liye index count[v] hota jo out of bounds ho sakta hai (max value ke liye count[max] = n, aur output[n] IndexError).

    14. output[count[x - min_val]] = x — element ko uski jagah par.

    15. Return naya array. Ye function in-place nahi hai.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Line 3-4 (max, min):        O(n)
Line 6 (count allocate):    O(k)
Line 7-8 (counting):        O(n)
Line 9-10 (prefix sum):     O(k)
Line 11 (output allocate):  O(n)
Line 12-14 (placing):       O(n)

Total time:  O(n) + O(k) + O(n) + O(k) + O(n) + O(n)  =  O(n + k)
Total space: count array O(k) + output array O(n)     =  O(n + k)

    Best = average = worst = Theta(n + k). Input ka order koi farak nahi daalta.

    Kab ye O(n) hai? Jab k = O(n). Examples: - Ages (0-120), n = 10 lakh → k = 121, effectively O(n). ✓ - Exam marks (0-100), n = 50,000 → O(n). ✓ - HTTP status codes (100-599), n = 10^7 → O(n). ✓ - Sorting bytes (0-255) → O(n). ✓

    Kab ye disaster hai? - 32-bit integers, n = 100 → k = 4 billion → 16 GB ka count array. ✗ - Floats → range infinite. ✗ - Strings → koi natural integer index nahi (par hash/rank de sakte ho). ✗

    Metric Value
    Time (all cases) Theta(n + k)
    Space Theta(n + k)
    Comparisons Zero
    Stable Haan (ulta scan ke saath)

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan — agar ulta scan karo Ulta placing se equal elements apne original order mein bharte hain
    In-place Nahi O(n) output array + O(k) count array
    Adaptive Nahi Input order se koi farak nahi

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Values integers hain aur range chhoti hai (k = O(n)). - Stability chahiye aur values integer hain. - Radix sort ka building block — wahan counting sort ki stability zaroori hai. - Bucket/histogram calculations — count array khud hi ek useful output hai (frequency distribution).

    Mat use karo jab: - Range badi hai — memory phat jayegi. - Floats ya strings — direct nahi lag sakta. - Memory constrained — O(n + k) space chahiye. - General-purpose — sorted() almost hamesha behtar practical choice hai.

    QA context: Test results ko status ke hisaab se group karna (pass=0, fail=1, skip=2, error=3) — counting sort perfect hai, k=4. Ya response times ko 10ms buckets mein — pehle t // 10 karke integer banao, phir counting sort.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 min offset use karo (upar wala code) Range [1000, 1005] par 6 slots, 1006 nahi. Negatives bhi handle Ek extra O(n) pass
    2 Range pehle se pata ho to max/min pass skip karo Do O(n) passes bachte Caller ko range pata honi chahiye
    3 Sirf values chahiye, objects nahi to prefix sum skip karo — seedha counts se output likho Prefix-sum aur output array dono bachte, in-place likh sakte ho Stability chali jati hai (kyunki objects ki identity kho jati hai). Sirf plain integers ke liye
    4 dict use karo list ki jagah jab values scattered hon Space O(distinct values), O(k) nahi Hashing overhead, aur output banane ke liye keys sort karni padti hain
    5 Parallel counting — har thread apna local count, phir merge Multi-core speedup Merge overhead
    6 Radix sort par switch jab k bada ho O(n + k) → O(d·(n + b)) Multiple passes

    Optimisation #3 — simplified version jab sirf integers sort karne hain:

    def counting_sort_values_only(arr):
    """Sirf integer VALUES sort karta hai (objects nahi). Unstable par simpler aur tez."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return arr                                  # 2
    lo, hi = min(arr), max(arr)                     # 3
    count = [0] * (hi - lo + 1)                     # 4
    for x in arr:                                   # 5
        count[x - lo] += 1                          # 6
    idx = 0                                         # 7
    for value_offset, c in enumerate(count):        # 8
        for _ in range(c):                          # 9
            arr[idx] = value_offset + lo            # 10
            idx += 1                                # 11
    return arr                                      # 12

    1-2. Khali guard. 3. Range. 4. Count array. 5-6. Counting. 7. idx — output mein kahan likhna hai. Ab hum arr mein hi likh rahe hain — output array ki zaroorat nahi, kyunki hum values ko dobara construct kar rahe hain, move nahi kar rahe. 8. enumerate(count) — har (offset, count) jodi. 9. for _ in range(c) — us value ko c baar likho. 10. arr[idx] = value_offset + lo — value ko reconstruct kar rahe hain offset se. Yahi wajah hai ki ye unstable hai — agar arr mein objects hote (jaise (marks, name) tuples) to unhe reconstruct nahi kar sakte, sirf raw integers ko kar sakte hain. Objects ke liye upar wala stable version chahiye. 11. Aage. 12. In-place modified arr.

    Ye version O(1) extra space beyond the count array leta hai — output array nahi banata. Par sirf plain integers ke liye.

    Interview answer: Counting sort doesn't compare elements at all — it uses the values themselves as array indices. Three passes: count how many times each value occurs, convert those counts to a prefix sum so count[v] tells you how many elements are less than or equal to v, then walk the input backwards, decrementing the count for each element and writing it to that position in the output.

    Because it never compares, the Omega(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts doesn't apply. It runs in O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space, where k is the size of the value range. That's linear when k is O(n) — ages, exam scores, HTTP status codes, bytes — and catastrophic when k is huge, like sorting a hundred 32-bit integers, where you'd allocate a four-billion-entry array.

    The subtle and important detail is that the final pass walks the input in reverse. That's what makes it stable: the last occurrence of a value gets the last slot in its group. Walking forwards produces a correct sort but reverses the order of equal elements. That matters enormously because radix sort calls counting sort once per digit and relies on each pass preserving the ordering established by the previous ones — an unstable counting sort makes radix sort produce garbage.

    Cross-question: "Counting sort is O(n). Why isn't it always used?"

    Because the constant hidden in "linear" is the value range. It's O(n + k), and k can dwarf n. Sorting a hundred integers spread across the full 32-bit range would need a 4-billion-slot counting array. It also only works on values that map to small integers — no floats, no arbitrary strings — and it needs O(n) extra space for the output. Comparison sorts have none of those restrictions, which is why they're the general-purpose default.

    Cross-question: "Why the prefix sum? Couldn't you just write out each value count[v] times?"

    You could, if you're only sorting bare integers — the values are fully reconstructible from the index. But if the elements are records — a tuple of score and name, say — you can't rebuild the record from its key, so you have to move the actual objects. The prefix sum tells you exactly which output slots each key's records occupy, which is what lets you place the real objects and keep the sort stable.

    Radix Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Radix sort numbers ko digit by digit sort karta hai — pehle sabse chhote digit (ones place) se, phir tens, phir hundreds — aur har digit par ek stable sort (usually counting sort) chalata hai.

    Real-world analogy: Purane zamane ke punch-card sorting machines. Card par 10 columns hote the aur machine 10 dabbe (0-9) mein cards daal deti thi. Operator pehle aakhri column par sort karta, cards uthata, phir doosre aakhri column par sort karta, phir teesre... 10 passes ke baad poore 10-digit numbers sorted ho jaate. Machine ne kabhi do numbers compare nahi kiye — bas digit dekh kar dabba chuna. Radix sort literally isi machine se aaya hai (Herman Hollerith, 1887 US census).

    Kyu hai¶

    Counting sort ki problem: range k bada ho to memory phat jati hai. 6-digit numbers (0 se 999999) sort karne ke liye 10 lakh ka count array chahiye.

    Radix sort ne kaha: "Poori number ko ek unit maan kar sort mat karo. Use digits mein todo. Har digit ki range sirf 0-9 hai!"

    Counting sort par 6-digit numbers:
   k = 10^6  ->  10 lakh ka array  ->  memory kharab

Radix sort:
   6 passes, har pass mein k = 10  ->  10 ka array
   Total time: 6 * O(n + 10) = O(6n) = O(n)
   Total space: O(n + 10) = O(n)

    Aur ye "kam se kam significant digit se shuru karo" (LSD) kyun? Ye counter-intuitive hai — insaan hamesha bade digit se sochta hai. Par LSD hi kaam karta hai, aur wajah stability hai:

    Numbers: 170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66

MSD se (hundreds pehle) — galat approach without recursion:
   0xx: 45, 75, 90, 24, 2, 66     8xx: 802     1xx: 170
   Ab har group ko alag alag recursively sort karna padega -> complicated

LSD se (ones pehle) — sahi approach:
   Ones par sort:   170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66
   Tens par sort:   802, 2, 24, 45, 66, 170, 75, 90
                    ^ dhyaan do: 802 aur 2 dono ka tens digit 0 hai,
                      aur unka aapsi order ones-pass se aaya hai (802 pehle tha).
                      STABILITY ne wo order bacha liya.
   Hundreds par:    2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802
                    SORTED ✓

    LSD ka poora argument: Jab hum digit d par sort karte hain, to jo numbers ka digit d same hai, unka order pichhle passes se aaya hai — aur pichhle passes ne unhe lower digits par sort kiya tha. Stability us order ko bachati hai. Isliye har pass ke baad, "last d digits par sorted" invariant maintain rehta hai.

    Ye poori tarah stability par depend karta hai. Agar aap unstable sort use karte har digit par, radix sort poori tarah galat ho jata.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    d = sabse bade number mein kitne digits hain

for exp in [1, 10, 100, 1000, ...] up to d digits:
    counting_sort(arr, key = (x // exp) % 10)

Digit nikalne ka formula:
   (x // exp) % 10

   x = 4567, exp = 1:    (4567 // 1)   % 10 = 4567 % 10 = 7   (ones)
   x = 4567, exp = 10:   (4567 // 10)  % 10 = 456  % 10 = 6   (tens)
   x = 4567, exp = 100:  (4567 // 100) % 10 = 45   % 10 = 5   (hundreds)
   x = 4567, exp = 1000: (4567 // 1000)% 10 = 4    % 10 = 4   (thousands)

    Diagram:

    Input:    170  45  75  90  802  24  2  66

exp = 1 (ones digit):
  bucket 0: 170, 90        bucket 2: 802, 2
  bucket 4: 24             bucket 5: 45, 75
  bucket 6: 66
  Output:  170  90  802  2  24  45  75  66

exp = 10 (tens digit):

  bucket 4: 45             bucket 6: 66

  Output:  802  2  24  45  66  170  75  90

exp = 100 (hundreds digit):
  bucket 0: 2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90
  bucket 1: 170
  bucket 8: 802

    66 6 5 4 [_,_,_,_,66,_,_,_]

    Yahan stability ka jaadu dekho: 802 aur 2 dono ka tens digit 0 hai. Pass 1 ke baad 802 index 2 par tha aur 2 index 3 par — yaani 802 pehle. Pass 2 ke baad bhi 802 pehle hai. Aur 802 (ones digit 2) aur 2 (ones digit 2) — dono ka ones bhi same! Par unka relative order pass 1 se aaya tha aur bacha rahaa. Sahi bhi hai kyunki last do digits 02 dono ke same hain.

    Aur 170 (tens 7) aur 75 (tens 7): pass 1 ke baad 170 index 0 par tha, 75 index 6 par. Pass 2 mein 170 pehle aaya ✓ — sahi, kyunki last do digits 70 vs 75, aur 70 < 75.

    90 0 6 5 [_,_,_,_,_,90,_,_]

    Code¶

    def radix_sort(arr):
    """LSD radix sort, base 10, non-negative integers ke liye."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return arr                                  # 2
    max_val = max(arr)                              # 3
    exp = 1                                         # 4
    while max_val // exp > 0:                       # 5
        arr = counting_sort_by_digit(arr, exp)      # 6
        exp *= 10                                   # 7
    return arr                                      # 8


def counting_sort_by_digit(arr, exp):
    """arr ko us digit par stable sort karta hai jo `exp` position par hai."""
    n = len(arr)                                    # 9
    output = [0] * n                                # 10
    count = [0] * 10                                # 11
    for x in arr:                                   # 12
        digit = (x // exp) % 10                     # 13
        count[digit] += 1                           # 14
    for i in range(1, 10):                          # 15
        count[i] += count[i - 1]                    # 16
    for x in reversed(arr):                         # 17
        digit = (x // exp) % 10                     # 18
        count[digit] -= 1                           # 19
        output[count[digit]] = x                    # 20
    return output                                   # 21

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1-2. Khali list guard — max([]) ValueError deta hai.

    1. max_val = max(arr) — sabse bada number. Isse pata chalega kitne digits process karne hain.

    2. exp = 1 — ones place se shuru. LSD approach.

    3. while max_val // exp > 0 — jab tak max number mein is position par koi digit hai.

    4. max_val = 802: 802//1 = 802 > 0 ✓, 802//10 = 80 > 0 ✓, 802//100 = 8 > 0 ✓, 802//1000 = 0 ✗ → 3 passes.
    5. > 0 hai >= 0 nahi — >= 0 hamesha true rahega (integer division kabhi negative nahi hoti non-negative inputs par) → infinite loop.

    6. Alternative likh sakte the for _ in range(len(str(max_val))) — same cheez, par string conversion dheema hai.

    7. arr = counting_sort_by_digit(arr, exp) — reassignment, kyunki counting_sort_by_digit naya list return karta hai. Agar function in-place hota to arr ko reassign na karte. Ye arr local variable ko rebind karta hai — caller ki original list modify nahi hoti. Agar caller in-place chahta hai to arr[:] = radix_sort(arr) likhna padega.

    8. exp *= 10 — agli digit position. Base 10 use kiya hai kyunki insaan ko samajhna aasan hai. Practically base 256 (bytes) ya base 2^16 zyada tez hote hain — kam passes lagte hain.

    9. Return.

    10. Length.

    11. output = [0] * n — result array. Har pass mein naya banta hai. Optimisation: ek hi buffer allocate karke reuse kar sakte ho — allocations bachte hain.

    12. count = [0] * 10 — exactly 10 slots, kyunki base 10 mein digit sirf 0-9 ho sakta hai. Ye counting sort par bada fayda hai — wahan k value range jitna bada tha, yahan hamesha 10.

    12-14. Counting pass. digit = (x // exp) % 10 do steps mein: - x // exp — us position ke aage ke digits hata do. 4567 // 100 = 45. - % 10 — sirf aakhri digit rakho. 45 % 10 = 5. Agar aap % bhool jaate to count[45] par IndexError (count sirf 10 lamba hai). Agar // bhool jaate to hamesha ones digit hi milta — saare passes same kaam karte, result galat.

    15-16. Prefix sum. range(1, 10) — 10 tak (exclusive), kyunki 10 slots hain.

    1. for x in reversed(arr) — ULTA. Stability ke liye ZAROORI. Radix sort mein ye counting sort se bhi zyada critical hai. Counting sort mein ulta na karna sirf stability todta tha (output phir bhi sorted hota). Radix sort mein stability tootne se poora algorithm galat output deta hai, kyunki har pass pichhle passes ke order par depend karta hai.

    18-20. Digit nikaalo, count ghatao, place karo.

    1. Naya sorted-by-this-digit array return.

    Negative numbers handle karna:

    def radix_sort_with_negatives(arr):
    """Negative numbers ke saath radix sort."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return arr                                  # 2
    negatives = [-x for x in arr if x < 0]          # 3
    positives = [x for x in arr if x >= 0]          # 4
    if negatives:                                   # 5
        negatives = radix_sort(negatives)           # 6
        negatives = [-x for x in reversed(negatives)]   # 7
    if positives:                                   # 8
        positives = radix_sort(positives)           # 9
    return negatives + positives                    # 10

    1-2. Khali guard. 3. negatives = [-x for x in arr if x < 0] — negatives ko positive bana kar alag list mein. -(-5) = 5. Radix sort digits par kaam karta hai aur negative numbers ka (x // exp) % 10 Python mein weird results deta hai (Python ka // floor division hai, -7 // 10 = -1). Isliye sign ko alag handle karna hi saaf tareeka hai. 4. Positives (aur zero) alag. 5. Agar negatives hain. 6. Unhe (positive banaye hue) sort karo. 7. Wapas negative banao aur ULTA karo. Kyunki [1, 3, 5] (jo -1, -3, -5 the) ka sahi sorted order -5, -3, -1 hai — yaani magnitude descending. reversed + negation dono chahiye. Agar sirf negation karte to [-1, -3, -5] milta — galat. 8-9. Positives sort. 10. Negatives pehle (kyunki sab positives se chhote hain), phir positives.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    d = digits ki sankhya sabse bade number mein
b = base (radix), yahan 10
n = elements

Har pass:  counting sort with k = b  ->  O(n + b)
Passes:    d

Total time:  O( d * (n + b) )

Base 10 ke saath, b = 10 (constant):
   O(d * n)

Agar max value M hai, to d = log_b(M) = log_10(M)
   O(n * log_10(M))

Agar M polynomial in n hai (jaise M = n^c), to log(M) = c*log(n) — constant multiple
   O(n * c) = O(n)   <- LINEAR!

    Ye claim carefully samjho. "Radix sort O(n) hai" tabhi sach hai jab d constant maana jaye. Agar numbers arbitrary bade ho sakte hain, to d = log(M) hai aur radix sort O(n log M) hai. Aur agar sab numbers distinct hain to M >= n, yaani log M >= log n — to radix sort O(n log n) se behtar nahi in that sense.

    Par practically: 64-bit integers sort kar rahe ho? d = 8 passes with base 256. n = 10 lakh par: 8 × (10^6 + 256) ≈ 80 lakh operations. Quicksort: 1.39 × 10^6 × 20 ≈ 2.8 crore. Radix ~3.5x tez. Ye asli measured farak hai.

    Base ka choice — trade-off:

    Base b Passes for 32-bit int Count array size Total ops (n = 10^6)
    2 32 2 32 × 10^6
    10 10 10 10 × 10^6
    16 8 16 8 × 10^6
    256 4 256 4 × 10^6
    65536 2 65536 2 × 10^6 + 131072
    2^32 1 4 billion Memory disaster

    Optimal base ~ n (theoretically): passes = log_n(M), aur count array n size ka. Practically base 256 ya 2^16 use hoti hai kyunki wo byte/word boundaries par align hoti hai aur bit-shifting se digit extraction bahut tez hoti hai ((x >> 8) & 0xFF).

    Space: 

    output array:  O(n)
count array:   O(b)
Total:         O(n + b)

    Metric Value
    Time Theta(d · (n + b)), practically O(n) for fixed-width integers
    Space O(n + b)
    Comparisons Zero
    Stable Haan (aur ye mandatory hai)

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Stable Haan — aur ye compulsory hai Counting sort ki ulta-scan stability. Iske bina algorithm galat
    In-place Nahi O(n) output buffer har pass
    Adaptive Nahi Har pass poora chalta hai chahe data kaisa bhi ho

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Fixed-width integers — IDs, timestamps, IP addresses, hashes, zip codes. - Fixed-length strings — car plates, product codes, dates in YYYYMMDD format. - n bahut bada hai aur data integer hai — radix quicksort ko practically beat karta hai. - Stability chahiye aur speed bhi. - GPU / parallel sorting — radix sort GPU par extremely well parallelise hota hai; CUDA ke sorting libraries mostly radix use karti hain.

    Mat use karo jab: - Floats — IEEE-754 ka bit layout radix ke liye tricky hai (sign bit, exponent bias). Ho sakta hai par transformation chahiye. - Variable-length strings — MSD radix chahiye, jo complicated hai. - Memory tight — O(n) extra buffer. - Chhota n — passes ka overhead comparison sort se zyada ho jata hai. n < ~1000 par quicksort behtar. - Custom comparator chahiye — radix sort keys ko digits mein todta hai, arbitrary comparison function support nahi karta.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Base 256 (bytes) use karo 32-bit int par 10 passes → 4 passes. Digit extraction bit-shift se O(1) 256-slot count array (trivial)
    2 Buffer reuse — har pass mein naya output list mat banao Allocations d → 1 Ek extra parameter
    3 Skip empty passes — agar kisi digit position par sab same hain to pass skip Real data par kaafi passes bach sakte hain Ek extra check per pass
    4 MSD radix + insertion sort fallback Chhote buckets par insertion sort; variable-length strings handle hote hain Recursion, zyada complicated
    5 In-place American Flag sort (MSD, counts se in-place permute) O(1) extra space (count array ke alawa) Cache-unfriendly, complicated
    6 Parallel / GPU radix Massive speedup Sync overhead
    7 Hybrid: pehle radix se motta sort, phir insertion Cache-friendly Tuning

    Base 256 version (production quality):

    def radix_sort_base256(arr):
    """32-bit non-negative integers, base 256 — sirf 4 passes."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return arr                                  # 2
    max_val = max(arr)                              # 3
    output = [0] * len(arr)                         # 4
    shift = 0                                       # 5
    while (max_val >> shift) > 0:                   # 6
        count = [0] * 256                           # 7
        for x in arr:                               # 8
            count[(x >> shift) & 0xFF] += 1         # 9
        for i in range(1, 256):                     # 10
            count[i] += count[i - 1]                # 11
        for x in reversed(arr):                     # 12
            d = (x >> shift) & 0xFF                 # 13
            count[d] -= 1                           # 14
            output[count[d]] = x                    # 15
        arr, output = output, arr                   # 16
        shift += 8                                  # 17
    return arr                                      # 18

    1-3. Guards aur max. 4. Ek hi output buffer, poore algorithm ke liye — har pass mein naya nahi banta. 5. shift = 0 — bit shift amount. Base 256 = 2^8, to har digit 8 bits ka hai. 6. while (max_val >> shift) > 0 — jab tak max value mein is byte position par kuchh hai. >> bitwise right shift — // (2**shift) ka tez version. 7. Count array, 256 slots. 8-9. (x >> shift) & 0xFF — shift bits right shift karke, aakhri 8 bits nikal lo. 0xFF = 255 = binary 11111111 — 8 ones. AND karne se sirf wo 8 bits bachte hain. Ye (x // exp) % 256 ka bahut tez equivalent hai — CPU mein ek hi instruction. 10-11. Prefix sum, 256 slots par. 12-15. Ulta placing (stability). 16. arr, output = output, arr — ping-pong / double buffering. Result output mein hai, to use arr bana do aur purana arr agle pass ka buffer ban jaye. Isse allocation bilkul nahi hoti — sirf do references swap. Ye ek elegant trick hai jo merge sort mein bhi use hoti hai. 17. shift += 8 — agla byte. 18. Return arr — jo aakhri pass ke baad result rakhta hai. Kyunki line 16 swap karti hai, arr hamesha latest result hota hai loop ke end par.

    Interview answer: Radix sort sorts numbers digit by digit, using a stable counting sort on each digit. The standard LSD variant starts at the least significant digit and works up. After processing d digits, the array is sorted on the last d digits.

    The whole thing rests on stability. When two numbers share the same digit at the current position, their relative order must be preserved, because that order encodes the result of the previous, lower-digit passes. If the per-digit sort were unstable, radix sort would produce garbage — this isn't a nice-to-have, it's load bearing.

    Complexity is O(d · (n + b)) where d is the number of digits and b is the base. With a fixed integer width — 32-bit values in base 256, so four passes — that's effectively O(n), and in practice radix sort beats quicksort by a factor of two to four on large integer arrays. The caveat is that "O(n)" hides d: for arbitrarily large keys d is log(M), so it's really O(n log M).

    Its restrictions are real: it needs keys decomposable into small fixed-width digits, so integers and fixed-length strings are fine but floats need bit-level transformation and arbitrary comparators aren't supported at all. And it needs O(n) auxiliary space. Where it shines is large integer datasets, and GPU sorting, since it parallelises very cleanly.

    Cross-question: "Why least significant digit first? Sorting by the most significant digit feels more natural."

    Because LSD lets you do d flat passes over the whole array with no recursion. MSD-first requires you to partition into buckets by the top digit and then recursively sort each bucket independently, since numbers in different top-digit buckets never interact again. That's more complex and more memory-hungry, though MSD does have advantages — it can terminate early on distinguishing prefixes, which makes it the right choice for variable-length strings.

    Cross-question: "Radix sort is O(n). Does that break the Omega(n log n) lower bound?"

    No, because that bound only applies to comparison-based sorts. Radix never compares two elements; it uses digit values as array indices, which is outside the decision-tree model the bound is proved in. And the O(n) claim assumes the key width d is a constant. If you require all n keys to be distinct, the keys need at least log(n) bits, so d is Omega(log n) and the total is Omega(n log n) again — the bound reasserts itself through the back door.

    Bucket Sort¶

    Kya hai¶

    Bucket sort elements ko unki value ke hisaab se kai buckets mein baant deta hai, har bucket ko alag alag sort karta hai (usually insertion sort se), aur phir buckets ko order mein jod deta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Post office mein hazaaron chitthiyaan aati hain aur unhe pincode ke hisaab se lagana hai. Aap ek-ek chitthi doosri se compare nahi karte. Aap 100 dabbe rakhte ho — "110001-110010", "110011-110020", etc. — aur har chitthi apne dabbe mein daal dete ho. Phir har dabbe ke andar ki chitthiyon ko haath se sort kar dete ho (har dabbe mein sirf 20-30 chitthiyaan hain, aasan hai). Phir dabbon ko order mein khaali karo — poora sorted.

    Kyu hai¶

    Counting sort ki problem: values integers honi chahiye aur range chhoti honi chahiye. Radix sort ki problem: keys ko digits mein todna padta hai; floats mushkil.

    Bucket sort in dono se aage jata hai: wo floats aur arbitrary distributions handle kar sakta hai, bas ek assumption ke saath — data uniformly distributed ho.

    n elements, uniformly distributed 0 se 1 ke beech.
n buckets banao, bucket i mein wo elements jinki value [i/n, (i+1)/n) mein hai.

Expected elements per bucket = n / n = 1

Har bucket ko sort karna:  O(1) average (kyunki bucket mein ~1 element hai)
n buckets:                 O(n)
Buckets ko jodna:          O(n)

Total: O(n)  average

    Ye "average case O(n)" hai, "worst case" nahi. Agar data uniform nahi hai — sab elements ek hi bucket mein — to us bucket ka sort O(n²) ho jata hai (insertion sort ke saath).

    Ye trade-off honest hona chahiye interview mein: bucket sort ka O(n) data distribution par ek assumption hai, algorithm ki guarantee nahi.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Input: [0.42, 0.32, 0.33, 0.52, 0.37, 0.47, 0.51]   (n = 7, values in [0,1))

Step 1 — n buckets banao:
   bucket index = int(n * value)

   0.42 -> int(7 * 0.42) = int(2.94) = 2
   0.32 -> int(7 * 0.32) = int(2.24) = 2
   0.33 -> int(7 * 0.33) = int(2.31) = 2
   0.52 -> int(7 * 0.52) = int(3.64) = 3
   0.37 -> int(7 * 0.37) = int(2.59) = 2
   0.47 -> int(7 * 0.47) = int(3.29) = 3
   0.51 -> int(7 * 0.51) = int(3.57) = 3

Step 2 — buckets:
   [0]: []
   [1]: []
   [2]: [0.42, 0.32, 0.33, 0.37]
   [3]: [0.52, 0.47, 0.51]
   [4]: []
   [5]: []
   [6]: []

Step 3 — har bucket ko sort karo (insertion sort):
   [2]: [0.32, 0.33, 0.37, 0.42]
   [3]: [0.47, 0.51, 0.52]

Step 4 — jodo:
   [0.32, 0.33, 0.37, 0.42, 0.47, 0.51, 0.52]   ✓

    Dhyaan do: is example mein data uniform nahi tha (sab 0.32-0.52 ke beech), isliye buckets 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 khali reh gaye aur buckets 2, 3 mein bhaari load. Ye bucket sort ki weakness dikhata hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Step 4 — Concatenate in bucket order:

    bucket 0: (empty)
bucket 1: 0.12, 0.17
bucket 2: 0.21, 0.23, 0.26

bucket 4: (empty)
