    Code¶

    Recursive DFS:

    def dfs_recursive(graph, start, visited=None, order=None):
    """Recursive DFS. Visit order return karta hai."""
    if visited is None:                             # 1
        visited = set()                             # 2
    if order is None:                               # 3
        order = []                                  # 4
    visited.add(start)                              # 5
    order.append(start)                             # 6
    for nb in graph[start]:                         # 7
        if nb not in visited:                       # 8
            dfs_recursive(graph, nb, visited, order)    # 9
    return order                                    # 10

    Line-by-line:

    1-4. None sentinels, mutable defaults NAHI. visited=set() likhne se saare calls ek hi set share karte — pehle call ke baad har call "sab already visited" dekhta. Silent catastrophic bug. 5. Visit mark PEHLE, recursion se pehle. Warna cycles mein infinite recursion. 6. Record. 7. Neighbours. 8. Unvisited check. 9. Recurse, visited aur order pass karte hue. Pass na karne se har call apna naya set banata — infinite recursion cycles mein. 10. Return.

    Iterative DFS (stack overflow se bachne ke liye):

    def dfs_iterative(graph, start):
    """Iterative DFS. Koi recursion limit nahi."""
    visited = set()                                 # 1
    stack = [start]                                 # 2
    order = []                                      # 3
    while stack:                                    # 4
        node = stack.pop()                          # 5
        if node in visited:                         # 6
            continue                                # 7
        visited.add(node)                           # 8
        order.append(node)                          # 9
        for nb in reversed(graph[node]):            # 10
            if nb not in visited:                   # 11
                stack.append(nb)                    # 12
    return order                                    # 13

    1-3. Setup. stack ek plain list hai — append/pop dono O(1) hain (end se). BFS mein deque chahiye tha kyunki front se pop karna tha; DFS mein back se pop karte hain, jo list par O(1) hai. 4. Loop. 5. stack.pop() — END se (LIFO). BFS ka popleft() (FIFO) yahan pop() ban gaya. Ek method ka farak, do bilkul alag algorithms. 6-7. Visited check POP KE BAAD — ye BFS se important farak hai. Kyun zaroori hai? Kyunki DFS mein ek node stack par kai baar aa sakti hai (line 12 push karta hai bina ye guarantee ke ki wo abhi tak visit nahi hui). Jab hum use pop karein to check karna padega. Kya hum push par mark kar sakte hain (BFS jaisa)? Kar sakte hain, par tab traversal order recursive DFS se match nahi karega — kyunki push par mark karne se hum nodes ko "reserve" kar lete hain aur unka exploration order badal jata hai. Debugging ke liye recursive-matching order helpful hota hai. 8-9. Mark aur record. 10. reversed(graph[node]) — ULTA. Kyun? Stack LIFO hai. Agar neighbours [B, C, D] order mein push karein, to pop order D, C, B hoga — ulta. reversed() se push order D, C, B hota hai aur pop order B, C, D — recursive DFS jaisa. Agar order matter nahi karta to reversed chhod sakte ho. 11-12. Push. 13. Return.

    DFS with timestamps aur edge classification:

    WHITE, GREY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2                        # 1


def dfs_full(graph, vertices):
    """Poora DFS with colours, timestamps, aur edge classification."""
    colour = {v: WHITE for v in vertices}           # 2
    discovery = {}                                  # 3
    finish = {}                                     # 4
    parent = {}                                     # 5
    edges = {'tree': [], 'back': [], 'forward': [], 'cross': []}   # 6
    time = [0]                                      # 7

    def visit(u):                                   # 8
        colour[u] = GREY                            # 9
        time[0] += 1                                # 10
        discovery[u] = time[0]                      # 11
        for v in graph[u]:                          # 12
            if colour[v] == WHITE:                  # 13
                parent[v] = u                       # 14
                edges['tree'].append((u, v))        # 15
                visit(v)                            # 16
            elif colour[v] == GREY:                 # 17
                edges['back'].append((u, v))        # 18
            elif discovery[u] < discovery[v]:       # 19
                edges['forward'].append((u, v))     # 20
            else:                                   # 21
                edges['cross'].append((u, v))       # 22
        colour[u] = BLACK                           # 23
        time[0] += 1                                # 24
        finish[u] = time[0]                         # 25

    for v in vertices:                              # 26
        if colour[v] == WHITE:                      # 27
            visit(v)                                # 28

    return discovery, finish, parent, edges         # 29
    1. Teen colours. Ye CLRS ka standard model hai.
    2. Sab WHITE se shuru. 3-5. Timestamps aur parent tree.
    3. Edge categories.
    4. time = [0] — list mein, plain integer NAHI. Kyun? Kyunki nested function visit time ko modify karta hai. Python mein nested function outer scope ke immutable variables ko modify nahi kar sakta bina nonlocal ke. [0] ek mutable container hai, to time[0] += 1 kaam karta hai. Alternative: nonlocal time declare karo aur plain integer use karo. Dono theek hain; list wala trick purane Python (2.x) se aata hai jahan nonlocal nahi tha.
    5. Nested visit function.
    6. GREY — "abhi explore kar rahe hain". 10-11. Discovery timestamp.
    7. Neighbours. 13-16. WHITE neighbour → TREE EDGE, recurse. 17-18. GREY neighbour → BACK EDGE. Ye sabse important line hai. GREY ka matlab hai wo node abhi bhi call stack par hai, yaani wo u ka ancestor hai. u se uske ancestor tak ka edge = CYCLE. Directed graph mein cycle detection ka poora test yahi hai. 19-20. BLACK neighbour, aur u pehle discover hua → FORWARD EDGE (descendant tak shortcut). 21-22. Warna CROSS EDGE (alag subtree mein). 23-25. BLACK — poori tarah khatam. Finish timestamp. 26-28. Har vertex se try karo — graph disconnected ho sakta hai. Bina is loop ke sirf start se reachable component milega.
    8. Return.

    Ye function DFS ka "full power" version hai — isse cycle detection, topological sort, SCC — sab derive hote hain.

    Grid DFS (islands counting jaisa):

    def count_islands(grid):
    """Kitne connected '1' regions hain. Classic DFS problem."""
    if not grid or not grid[0]:                     # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])            # 3
    count = 0                                       # 4

    def sink(r, c):                                 # 5
        if not (0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols):   # 6
            return                                  # 7
        if grid[r][c] != '1':                       # 8
            return                                  # 9
        grid[r][c] = '0'                            # 10
        sink(r + 1, c)                              # 11
        sink(r - 1, c)                              # 12
        sink(r, c + 1)                              # 13
        sink(r, c - 1)                              # 14

    for r in range(rows):                           # 15
        for c in range(cols):                       # 16
            if grid[r][c] == '1':                   # 17
                count += 1                          # 18
                sink(r, c)                          # 19
    return count                                    # 20

    1-4. Guards aur setup. 5. sink — ek poore island ko "duba" deta hai (0 bana deta hai). 6-7. Bounds check pehle. 8-9. Already water ya visited → return. Ye base case hai. 10. grid[r][c] = '0' — GRID KO HI VISITED MARKER KI TARAH USE KAR RAHE HAIN. Ye ek elegant trick hai — alag visited set ki zaroorat nahi, O(m·n) memory bachti. Trade-off: input modify ho jata hai. Agar caller ko original chahiye to pehle copy banao, ya alag visited set use karo. 11-14. Chaar directions. Recursion se hi neighbours explore. 15-17. Har cell par. 18-19. Naya '1' mila → naya island → count badhao aur poore island ko sink karo. Sink ke baad wo poora island '0' ban chuka hai, to wo dobara count nahi hoga. 20. Return.

    Ye recursion m × n deep ja sakti hai ek poore grid par jo sab '1' hai. 1000 × 1000 grid par depth 10^6 → RecursionError. Us case mein iterative version chahiye.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Har vertex EXACTLY EK BAAR visit hoti hai (visited check)
   -> O(V)

Har edge EXACTLY EK BAAR examine hoti hai (directed) ya do baar (undirected)
   -> O(E)

TOTAL TIME: O(V + E)     -- BFS jaisa hi

    Space:

    visited set:      O(V)
Recursion stack:  O(depth)

   Best case (star graph):     depth = 2       -> O(1) stack
   Average (balanced tree):    depth = log V   -> O(log V)
   Worst case (path graph):    depth = V       -> O(V)

TOTAL SPACE: O(V)  worst case

    DFS vs BFS space — ye interview mein poochha jata hai:

    Graph shape DFS stack BFS queue
    Path (1→2→3→...→n) O(n) O(1)
    Star (center + n leaves) O(1) O(n)
    Complete binary tree O(log n) O(n)
    Grid (m × n) O(mn) worst O(min(m,n))

    Rule: DFS deep-narrow graphs par memory-heavy hai; BFS wide-shallow par. Balanced trees par DFS clearly jeetta hai (log n vs n).

    Metric DFS BFS
    Time O(V + E) O(V + E)
    Space O(depth) O(width)
    Shortest path (unweighted) Nahi Haan
    Cycle detection Aasan (back edge) Possible par awkward
    Topological sort Natural (finish times) Kahn's algorithm
    SCC Zaroori (Kosaraju/Tarjan) Nahi kar sakta
    Recursion friendly Haan Nahi

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Deterministic order Haan (agar adjacency order fixed)
    Shortest path Nahi Deep-first, level-first nahi
    Modifies graph Nahi (grid trick ko chhod kar)
    Works on disconnected graphs Sirf agar har vertex se try karo Ek DFS call sirf ek component cover karta hai

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Cycle detection — back edge test trivial hai. - Topological sort — finish times ka reverse order. - Strongly connected components — Kosaraju, Tarjan. - Bridges / articulation points — DFS tree zaroori hai. - Backtracking / exhaustive search — saare paths, permutations, N-Queens. - Tree traversals — preorder, inorder, postorder. - Memory tight aur graph deep-narrow nahi hai. - Connected components (BFS bhi chalega). - Maze solving jab koi bhi path chahiye (shortest nahi).

    Mat use karo jab: - Shortest path chahiye → BFS. - Graph bahut deep hai (> 1000) → recursion limit. Iterative version use karo. - Level-wise processing chahiye → BFS.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Iterative version Recursion limit khatam Order thoda alag, code lamba
    2 Grid ko visited marker banao O(mn) memory bachti Input modify hota hai
    3 Early exit — target milte hi return Average case aadha Return values propagate karne padte
    4 reversed() neighbours iterative mein Recursive order se match Ek function call
    5 Colours (WHITE/GREY/BLACK) Edge classification, cycle detection free Ek dict extra
    6 Iterative deepening (IDDFS) BFS ki shortest-path property + DFS ki memory Repeated work (par sirf ~2x)
    7 Tarjan's SCC (ek DFS pass) Kosaraju ke do passes ki jagah ek Complicated code

    Iterative Deepening DFS — dono ka best:

    def iddfs(graph, start, goal, max_depth=100):
    """DFS ki memory (O(d)) + BFS ki shortest path guarantee."""
    for depth in range(max_depth + 1):              # 1
        found = _dls(graph, start, goal, depth, set())   # 2
        if found:                                   # 3
            return depth                            # 4
    return -1                                       # 5


def _dls(graph, node, goal, depth, path):
    """Depth-limited search."""
    if node == goal:                                # 6
        return True                                 # 7
    if depth == 0:                                  # 8
        return False                                # 9
    path.add(node)                                  # 10
    for nb in graph[node]:                          # 11
        if nb not in path:                          # 12
            if _dls(graph, nb, goal, depth - 1, path):   # 13
                return True                         # 14
    path.discard(node)                              # 15
    return False                                    # 16
    1. Depth 0, 1, 2, 3... badhate jao.
    2. Har depth par ek depth-limited DFS. 3-4. Pehli baar mila = shortest distance (kyunki hum depth badhate hue aaye).
    3. Not found within limit.

    6-7. Goal. 8-9. Depth limit hit — is branch par aur nahi jaana. 10. Current path mein add (cycle prevention). 11-14. Neighbours, depth ek kam. 15. Backtrack — path se hatao. visited set nahi, path set hai — kyunki ek node alag paths se alag depths par reachable ho sakta hai. 16. Not found.

    Repeated work ka analysis — ye counter-intuitive hai:

    Depth d tak ki search mein, IDDFS depths 0, 1, 2, ..., d sab karta hai.
Lagta hai bahut waste hai. Par:

Branching factor b ke saath, depth k par nodes: b^k

Total nodes IDDFS visit karta hai:
   b^0 + b^1 + ... + b^d   (depth d ki search)
   + b^0 + ... + b^(d-1)   (depth d-1 ki search)
   + ...

Actually har node depth k par (d - k + 1) baar visit hota hai:
   Total = sum over k of (d - k + 1) * b^k

Dominant term (k = d):  1 * b^d
Next term (k = d-1):    2 * b^(d-1)

Total = b^d * (1 + 2/b + 3/b² + ...)
      = b^d * (b/(b-1))²

b = 10:  b^d * 1.23    -> sirf 23% extra kaam
b = 2:   b^d * 4       -> 4x, par abhi bhi exponential class same

MEMORY: O(d) instead of O(b^d)  <- BFS se HAZAARON guna kam

    Isliye IDDFS AI/game search mein use hota hai (chess engines, puzzle solvers) jahan BFS ki memory affordable nahi hai.

    Interview answer: DFS goes as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. It uses a stack, either explicitly or via the call stack in the recursive version, versus BFS's queue. Time is O(V + E), same as BFS, but space is O(depth) rather than O(width), so on a balanced tree DFS uses O(log n) while BFS uses O(n).

    The real reason DFS matters isn't traversal — it's structure discovery. Colouring nodes white, grey, and black gives you edge classification: an edge to a grey node is a back edge, and a back edge means a cycle. That's the basis for cycle detection in directed graphs. Finish times give you topological sort for free — reverse finishing order is a valid topological order. And strongly connected components, bridges, and articulation points all require the DFS tree; BFS simply can't produce them.

    Two implementation notes. In the iterative version I check visited after popping, not before pushing, because unlike BFS a node can legitimately be pushed several times, and I iterate neighbours in reverse so the pop order matches the recursive version. And in Python I watch the recursion limit — a DFS on a path-shaped graph with more than a thousand nodes will raise RecursionError, so for large graphs I use the iterative version.

    Cross-question: "When would you choose DFS over BFS for pathfinding?"

    When I don't need the shortest path and memory matters. On a wide, shallow graph — say a node with a million children — BFS's queue holds a million entries while DFS's stack holds two. Also when I need all paths rather than one, since that's backtracking, which is DFS with undo. If I need shortest paths but can't afford BFS's memory, iterative deepening DFS gives me BFS's optimality with DFS's O(depth) memory, at only about 25% extra work for a branching factor of ten.

    Dijkstra¶

    Kya hai¶

    Dijkstra's algorithm ek weighted graph mein ek source se saare nodes tak ka shortest path nikaalta hai — bashart ki saare edge weights non-negative hon.

    Real-world analogy: Aap Delhi se saare shehron tak ka sabse sasta route nikaalna chahte ho. Aap Delhi se shuru karte ho. Jo shehar sabse sasta reachable hai (say Gurgaon, 30 rupees), uska price FINAL hai — usse sasta koi raasta ho hi nahi sakta, kyunki har doosra raasta kisi aur shehar se hokar jayega jo Gurgaon se mehnga hai. Ab Gurgaon se aage ke shehron ki prices update karo. Phir agla sabse sasta shehar lock karo. "Sabse sasta wala pakka hai" — yahi Dijkstra ka poora dimaag hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    BFS unweighted graphs mein shortest path deta hai kyunki wo edge count minimise karta hai. Par weighted graphs mein:

        A --1--> B --1--> C
    |                 ^
    +-------5---------+

BFS from A:  C ki distance 1 (ek edge, direct)
ACTUAL shortest: A -> B -> C = 2

BFS FAIL ho gaya kyunki usne WEIGHTS ignore kiye.

    Naive fix — har edge ko uske weight ke barabar chhote edges mein todo:

    A --5--> C  ko  A -> x1 -> x2 -> x3 -> x4 -> C  bana do (5 unit edges)
Phir BFS chalao.

Kaam karta hai! PAR:
   - Weights 10^9 ho sakte hain -> 10^9 dummy nodes -> IMPOSSIBLE
   - Float weights par kaam hi nahi karta

    Dijkstra ka insight: BFS queue ki jagah priority queue (min-heap) use karo. BFS "kam edges wala pehle" karta hai; Dijkstra "kam total weight wala pehle" karta hai.

    BFS:       queue (FIFO)          -> nodes distance order mein aate hain (unweighted)
Dijkstra:  priority queue (heap) -> nodes WEIGHTED distance order mein aate hain

    Dijkstra ki limitation: negative weights par TOOT jata hai. Uske liye Bellman-Ford.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    1. dist[source] = 0, baaki sab = infinity
2. Ek min-heap mein (0, source) daalo
3. Jab tak heap khali na ho:
     a. Heap se SABSE CHHOTI distance wala node nikaalo -> u
     b. Agar u already finalised hai, skip
     c. u ko FINALISE karo (uski distance ab pakki hai)
     d. Har neighbour v ke liye:
          new_dist = dist[u] + weight(u, v)
          agar new_dist < dist[v]:
              dist[v] = new_dist          <- RELAXATION
              heap mein (new_dist, v) daalo

    "Relaxation" ka matlab: ek edge ko dekh kar poochna "kya is edge se hokar jaana sasta hai?" Agar haan, to distance update karo.

    Relaxation:

   dist[u] = 5
              |
              +--- weight 3 ---> v
                                 dist[v] = 10 currently

   new_dist = 5 + 3 = 8
   8 < 10  ->  RELAX!  dist[v] = 8

    Greedy choice ka proof — Dijkstra sahi kyun hai:

    CLAIM: Jab hum heap se sabse chhoti distance wala node u nikaalte hain,
       dist[u] uska FINAL shortest distance hai.

PROOF (contradiction se):
   Maan lo koi chhota path P source se u tak exist karta hai.
   P mein kam se kam ek edge (x, y) hoga jahan x finalised hai aur y nahi.
   (Kyunki source finalised hai aur u nahi, kahin transition hoga.)

   dist[y] <= dist[x] + weight(x,y)     (kyunki humne x ko relax kiya tha)
           <= length of P up to y
           <= length of P                (kyunki BAAKI edges NON-NEGATIVE hain)
           <  dist[u]                    (assumption)

   Par phir y heap mein u se PEHLE aata (kyunki dist[y] < dist[u]).
   CONTRADICTION -- humne u ko chuna tha kyunki wo sabse chhota tha.

   ->  Aisa chhota path exist nahi karta.  QED

DHYAAN DO: "BAAKI edges NON-NEGATIVE hain" -- yahi wo step hai jo
negative weights par TOOT jata hai.

    Poora dry run¶

    Graph:

             4
    A -------- B
    |  \       |
   2|   \1     |5
    |    \     |
    C ---- D --+
      3  /  |
        /   |1
      8/    |
      E ----+

Edges:
   A-B: 4    A-C: 2    A-D: 1
   B-D: 5
   C-D: 3    C-E: 8
   D-E: 1

    Adjacency list: 

    A: [(B,4), (C,2), (D,1)]
B: [(A,4), (D,5)]
C: [(A,2), (D,3), (E,8)]
D: [(A,1), (B,5), (C,3), (E,1)]
E: [(C,8), (D,1)]

    Dijkstra from A:

    Initial: dist = {A:0, B:inf, C:inf, D:inf, E:inf}, heap = [(0,A)]

    Step 1 — pop (0, A):

    Neighbour Current dist New dist Relax? Heap after
    B inf 0+4 = 4 Yes push (4,B)
    C inf 0+2 = 2 Yes push (2,C)
    D inf 0+1 = 1 Yes push (1,D)

    dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1, E:inf}, heap = [(1,D), (2,C), (4,B)], finalised = {A}

    Step 2 — pop (1, D):

    Neighbour Current dist New dist (1 + w) Relax? Action
    A 0 1+1 = 2 2 > 0, No —
    B 4 1+5 = 6 6 > 4, No —
    C 2 1+3 = 4 4 > 2, No —
    E inf 1+1 = 2 Yes push (2,E)

    dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1, E:2}, heap = [(2,C), (2,E), (4,B)], finalised = {A,D}

    Step 3 — pop (2, C) (ya (2,E) — tie, heap kisi ek ko dega):

    Neighbour Current dist New dist (2 + w) Relax? Action
    A 0 2+2 = 4 No —
    D 1 2+3 = 5 No —
    E 2 2+8 = 10 No —

    dist unchanged, heap = [(2,E), (4,B)], finalised = {A,D,C}

    Step 4 — pop (2, E):

    Neighbour Current dist New dist (2 + w) Relax?
    C 2 2+8 = 10 No
    D 1 2+1 = 3 No

    heap = [(4,B)], finalised = {A,D,C,E}

    Step 5 — pop (4, B):

    Neighbour Current dist New dist (4 + w) Relax?
    A 0 4+4 = 8 No
    D 1 4+5 = 9 No

    heap = [], finalised = {A,D,C,E,B} — DONE

    Final distances from A:

    Node Distance Path
    A 0 A
    B 4 A → B (direct, weight 4)
    C 2 A → C (direct, weight 2)
    D 1 A → D (direct, weight 1)
    E 2 A → D → E (1 + 1)

    Verify E: A→C→E = 2+8 = 10. A→D→E = 1+1 = 2 ✓ Shortest.

    Finalisation order: A(0), D(1), C(2), E(2), B(4) — increasing distance order ✓ Yahi Dijkstra ka invariant hai.

    Code¶

    import heapq                                        # 1


def dijkstra(graph, source):
    """Non-negative weighted graph mein single-source shortest paths.
    graph: {node: [(neighbour, weight), ...]}"""
    dist = {source: 0}                              # 2
    parent = {source: None}                         # 3
    heap = [(0, source)]                            # 4
    finalised = set()                               # 5
    while heap:                                     # 6
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)                  # 7
        if u in finalised:                          # 8
            continue                                # 9
        finalised.add(u)                            # 10
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 11
            nd = d + w                              # 12
            if v not in dist or nd < dist[v]:       # 13
                dist[v] = nd                        # 14
                parent[v] = u                       # 15
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))       # 16
    return dist, parent                             # 17

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. heapq — Python ka min-heap. heappop sabse chhota element deta hai.

    2. dist = {source: 0} — dict use kiya, array nahi. Fayda: unreachable nodes dict mein aate hi nahi (inf se compare karne ki zaroorat nahi), aur nodes ke naam kuchh bhi ho sakte hain (strings, tuples).

    3. parent — path reconstruction.

    4. heap = [(0, source)] — tuple (distance, node). Order critical hai: distance PEHLE. Python tuples ko lexicographically compare karta hai, to (distance, node) distance par sort karta hai. (node, distance) likhne se node par sort hota — poora algorithm galat. Aur ek gotcha: agar do entries ki distance same ho to Python node par compare karega. Agar nodes comparable nahi hain (jaise custom objects bina __lt__ ke) to TypeError. Fix: (distance, counter, node) use karo jahan counter ek unique increasing integer hai.

    5. finalised set — kaunse nodes ki distance pakki ho chuki hai.

    6. while heap — jab tak kuchh process karne ko hai.

    7. heapq.heappop(heap) — sabse chhoti distance wala. O(log n).

    8-9. if u in finalised: continue — LAZY DELETION. Ye sabse important line hai. Python ke heapq mein "decrease-key" operation nahi hai — aap heap ke andar kisi entry ki priority change nahi kar sakte. To hum kya karte hain? Har relaxation par ek NAYI entry push kar dete hain, aur purani stale entry heap mein padi rehti hai. Jab wo stale entry pop hoti hai, hum use skip kar dete hain (kyunki node already finalised hai). Bina is check ke: - Node kai baar process hoti. - Uske neighbours kai baar relax hote. - Complexity O(E log V) se badh kar bahut zyada. - Answer phir bhi sahi aata (kyunki relaxation idempotent hai) — silent performance bug.

    1. Finalise.

    2. graph.get(u, []) — .get with default. Agar u ka koi outgoing edge nahi hai (sink node) to graph[u] KeyError deta. .get khali list deti hai.

    3. nd = d + w — d use kiya, dist[u] nahi. Dono same hain yahan (kyunki u abhi finalise hua aur d uski final distance hai), par d use karna thoda tez hai (ek dict lookup kam).

    4. if v not in dist or nd < dist[v] — do conditions:

      • v not in dist — pehli baar dekha, koi bhi distance behtar hai infinity se.
      • nd < dist[v] — pehle se acchi distance mili. Order matter karta hai — v not in dist pehle, warna dist[v] par KeyError. Strict < hai, <= nahi. <= likhne se equal distances par bhi push hota — fizool heap entries, koi fayda nahi.

    14-15. Distance aur parent update.

    1. heappush(heap, (nd, v)) — nayi entry. Purani (agar hai) heap mein padi rahegi aur line 8 use skip kar degi.

    2. Return.

    Early exit version (agar sirf ek target chahiye):

    import heapq


def dijkstra_target(graph, source, target):
    """Sirf source se target tak ki shortest distance."""
    dist = {source: 0}                              # 1
    heap = [(0, source)]                            # 2
    finalised = set()                               # 3
    while heap:                                     # 4
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)                  # 5
        if u == target:                             # 6
            return d                                # 7
        if u in finalised:                          # 8
            continue                                # 9
        finalised.add(u)                            # 10
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 11
            nd = d + w                              # 12
            if v not in dist or nd < dist[v]:       # 13
                dist[v] = nd                        # 14
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))       # 15
    return float('inf')                             # 16

    1-5. Same. 6-7. u == target par turant return. Kyunki jab target heap se pop hota hai, uski distance final ho chuki hai (Dijkstra ka invariant). Aage chalane ka koi matlab nahi. Ye check finalised check se PEHLE hona chahiye — warna agar target pehle hi finalised ho (nahi ho sakta, par defensively) to hum miss kar dete. Average case mein ye aadha kaam bachata hai. 8-15. Same. 16. Unreachable.

    Path reconstruction:

    def dijkstra_with_path(graph, source, target):
    dist, parent = dijkstra(graph, source)          # 1
    if target not in dist:                          # 2
        return None, float('inf')                   # 3
    path = []                                       # 4
    node = target                                   # 5
    while node is not None:                         # 6
        path.append(node)                           # 7
        node = parent[node]                         # 8
    path.reverse()                                  # 9
    return path, dist[target]                       # 10
    1. Run Dijkstra. 2-3. Unreachable check. 4-9. Parent chain se backwards walk, phir reverse. BFS wala same pattern.
    2. Path aur distance.

    Grid Dijkstra (bahut common):

    import heapq


def min_cost_path(grid):
    """Grid ke top-left se bottom-right tak minimum cost path.
    Har cell ka cost = us cell ki value."""
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])            # 1
    dist = {(0, 0): grid[0][0]}                     # 2
    heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]                     # 3
    seen = set()                                    # 4
    directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)] # 5
    while heap:                                     # 6
        d, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)               # 7
        if (r, c) == (rows - 1, cols - 1):          # 8
            return d                                # 9
        if (r, c) in seen:                          # 10
            continue                                # 11
        seen.add((r, c))                            # 12
        for dr, dc in directions:                   # 13
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc                 # 14
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols):   # 15
                continue                            # 16
            nd = d + grid[nr][nc]                   # 17
            if (nr, nc) not in dist or nd < dist[(nr, nc)]:   # 18
                dist[(nr, nc)] = nd                 # 19
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, nr, nc))  # 20
    return -1                                       # 21
    1. Dimensions. 2-3. Start cell ka cost include kiya (grid[0][0]). Problem statement par depend — kuchh versions start cell ka cost nahi ginte. Heap entry (distance, row, col) — distance pehle.
    2. Seen set.
    3. Chaar directions. Note: yahan (0,-1) aur (-1,0) bhi hain — yaani wapas ja sakte ho. Agar problem sirf right/down allow karti hai to un dono ko hata do (aur tab ye DP se solve ho jayega, Dijkstra ki zaroorat nahi). 6-7. Pop. 8-9. Target par early exit. 10-12. Lazy deletion skip. 13-16. Neighbours with bounds check.
    4. New distance = current + naye cell ka cost. 18-20. Relaxation.
    5. Unreachable (grid mein possible nahi, par defensive).

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Binary heap ke saath (Python heapq):

    Har node ek baar finalise hoti hai:  V pops
Har edge ek relaxation attempt:      E pushes (worst case)

Heap operations:
   push: O(log(heap size))
   pop:  O(log(heap size))

Heap size zyada se zyada E ho sakta hai (har edge ek push)

Total = V * O(log E) + E * O(log E)
      = O((V + E) log E)

Kyunki E <= V², log E <= 2 log V
      = O((V + E) log V)

Connected graph mein E >= V-1, to E dominate karta hai:
      = O(E log V)

    Ye standard answer hai: O(E log V).

    Alag heap implementations:

    Priority queue Insert Extract-min Decrease-key Total Dijkstra
    Array (linear scan) O(1) O(V) O(1) O(V² + E) = O(V²)
    Binary heap O(log V) O(log V) O(log V) O((V+E) log V)
    Binary heap + lazy deletion O(log E) O(log E) — O(E log V)
    Fibonacci heap O(1) O(log V) amortised O(1) amortised O(E + V log V)
    d-ary heap (d = E/V) O(log_d V) O(d log_d V) O(log_d V) O(E log_{E/V} V)

    Kab kaunsa behtar hai:

    Dense graph (E ~ V²):
   Array:  O(V²)
   Binary: O(V² log V)      <- ARRAY BEHTAR!

Sparse graph (E ~ V):
   Array:  O(V²)
   Binary: O(V log V)       <- HEAP BEHTAR

Rule: agar E > V²/log V, to simple array behtar hai.

    Fibonacci heap theoretically best hai (O(E + V log V)) par uske constants itne bade hain ki practically binary heap se dheema hota hai zyadatar cases mein. Ye ek classic "theory vs practice" example hai.

    Space: 

    dist dict:  O(V)
parent:     O(V)
heap:       O(E) worst case (lazy deletion ki wajah se duplicates)
finalised:  O(V)

TOTAL: O(V + E)

    Case Time Space
    Best (target jaldi mil jaye) O(E log V) O(V + E)
    Average O(E log V) O(V + E)
    Worst O(E log V) O(V + E)
    Dense graph with array PQ O(V²) O(V)

    Negative weights par kyun fail hota hai¶

    Ye interview mein ZAROOR poochha jata hai. Concrete counterexample:

            A
      /   \
    2/     \5
    /       \
   B         C
    \       /
     \     /
     3\   /-10
       \ /
        D

Edges: A→B (2), A→C (5), B→D (3), C→D (-10)

DIJKSTRA:
   Step 1: pop A (dist 0). Relax:
      dist[B] = 2, dist[C] = 5
   Step 2: pop B (dist 2, sabse chhota). FINALISE B.  Relax:
      dist[D] = 2 + 3 = 5
   Step 3: pop C (dist 5) ya D (dist 5) -- tie
      Maan lo D pop hua. FINALISE D with dist 5.
   Step 4: pop C (dist 5). FINALISE C. Relax:
      dist[D] = 5 + (-10) = -5
      PAR D ALREADY FINALISED HAI!  Update ignore ho jayega.

   DIJKSTRA KA ANSWER:  dist[D] = 5
   ACTUAL SHORTEST:      A -> C -> D = 5 + (-10) = -5

   GALAT ANSWER.

    Root cause: Dijkstra ka poora proof is assumption par khada hai ki "path aage badhne se sirf lamba hi ho sakta hai" (kyunki weights non-negative hain). Negative edge is assumption ko tod deta hai — ek lamba raasta baad mein sasta ho sakta hai.

    Aur ek subtle point: log sochte hain "saare weights mein ek constant jod do taaki sab positive ho jayen". Ye galat hai:

    Har weight mein +10 jodo:
   A→B: 12,  A→C: 15,  B→D: 13,  C→D: 0

   A→B→D = 12 + 13 = 25   (2 edges)
   A→C→D = 15 + 0  = 15   (2 edges)

   Yahan same edge count hai to comparison bacha.
   PAR agar paths mein ALAG number of edges hon:

   Path P1: 5 edges, original total 10, shifted total 10 + 5*10 = 60
   Path P2: 2 edges, original total 20, shifted total 20 + 2*10 = 40

   Original: P1 (10) shorter
   Shifted:  P2 (40) shorter

   ORDER BADAL GAYA -> GALAT ANSWER

    Constant shift edge count par depend karta hai, isliye relative order bigad jata hai. Negative weights ka sahi solution: Bellman-Ford.

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Correctness precondition Non-negative weights Greedy proof ka core assumption
    Handles negative cycles Nahi (detect bhi nahi karta) Bellman-Ford karta hai
    Deterministic Ties par implementation-dependent Same total distance wale paths mein koi bhi
    Modifies graph Nahi Read-only

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Weighted graph, non-negative weights, shortest path chahiye. - Network routing — OSPF protocol Dijkstra use karta hai. - GPS navigation (A actually, jo Dijkstra ka extension hai). - Minimum cost path in grids. - Single source to all destinations.*

    Mat use karo jab: - Negative weights hain → Bellman-Ford. - Unweighted graph → BFS (O(V+E), Dijkstra se tez). - Saare pairs ke beech shortest path chahiye → Floyd-Warshall (O(V³), jo dense graphs par V baar Dijkstra chalane se behtar hai). - Target ka rough direction pata hai → A* (heuristic se bahut kam nodes explore). - Weights sirf 0 aur 1 hain → 0/1 BFS with deque, O(V+E).

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Lazy deletion (upar wala code) decrease-key ki zaroorat nahi, code simple Heap mein duplicates, O(E) space
    2 Early exit target par Average case aadha Sirf single-target ke liye
    3 Bidirectional Dijkstra O(E log V) → practically ~half nodes explore Dono ends pata hone chahiye
    4 A* (heuristic) Dramatic reduction — roads par 10-100x Admissible heuristic chahiye
    5 Fibonacci heap Theoretical O(E + V log V) Practically dheema (bade constants)
    6 d-ary heap (d = E/V) Dense graphs par ~20-30% tez Tuning
    7 Array PQ dense graphs par O(V²) — heap ke O(V² log V) se behtar Sparse par bahut dheema
    8 Contraction hierarchies Road networks par 1000x+ (preprocessing ke baad) Bahut heavy preprocessing
    9 Bucket queue (integer weights, bounded range) O(E + V·C) — heap se tez Weights integer aur bounded hone chahiye

    Bidirectional Dijkstra:

    import heapq


def bidirectional_dijkstra(graph, rev_graph, source, target):
    """Dono ends se Dijkstra. Practically ~2x tez."""
    if source == target:                            # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    df = {source: 0}                                # 3
    db = {target: 0}                                # 4
    hf = [(0, source)]                              # 5
    hb = [(0, target)]                              # 6
    seen_f, seen_b = set(), set()                   # 7
    best = float('inf')                             # 8
    while hf and hb:                                # 9
        if hf[0][0] + hb[0][0] >= best:             # 10
            break                                   # 11
        if hf[0][0] <= hb[0][0]:                    # 12
            best = _step(graph, hf, df, db, seen_f, best)     # 13
        else:                                       # 14
            best = _step(rev_graph, hb, db, df, seen_b, best) # 15
    return best if best < float('inf') else -1      # 16


def _step(g, heap, own, other, seen, best):
    d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)                      # 17
    if u in seen:                                   # 18
        return best                                 # 19
    seen.add(u)                                     # 20
    for v, w in g.get(u, []):                       # 21
        nd = d + w                                  # 22
        if v not in own or nd < own[v]:             # 23
            own[v] = nd                             # 24
            heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))           # 25
        if v in other:                              # 26
            best = min(best, nd + other[v])         # 27
    return best                                     # 28

    1-2. Trivial. 3-6. Do independent Dijkstra states. rev_graph = saare edges ulte (directed graphs ke liye zaroori; undirected mein graph hi kaafi hai). 7-8. Seen sets aur best-so-far. 9. Dono heaps mein kuchh hona chahiye. 10-11. TERMINATION CONDITION — ye sabse subtle hai. Agar dono frontiers ki minimum distances ka sum already best se zyada hai, to koi behtar path mil hi nahi sakta. Ye condition sahi hona zaroori hai — bidirectional Dijkstra mein "jab dono searches mile tab ruk jao" GALAT hai (BFS mein wo sahi tha). Kyunki weighted graphs mein meeting point optimal nahi hota necessarily. 12-15. Chhota frontier expand karo — balanced search. 16. Result.

    17-20. Standard pop + lazy deletion. 21-25. Relaxation. 26-27. v in other — doosri search ne v dekha hai → ek complete path mil gaya. Total = nd (source se v) + other[v] (v se target). Best update. Note: hum yahan break nahi karte — behtar path baad mein mil sakta hai. 28. Return best.

    Bidirectional Dijkstra ka speedup: Nodes explored V se ~2·sqrt(V) ya better (graph structure par depend). Road networks par typically 2-5x tez.

    Interview answer: Dijkstra finds single-source shortest paths in a weighted graph with non-negative edges. It's BFS with a priority queue instead of a plain queue: instead of visiting nodes in order of edge count, you visit them in order of accumulated weight. Pop the closest unfinalised node, mark it final, and relax all its outgoing edges — if going through this node gives a shorter distance to a neighbour, update it and push the new distance.

    The correctness argument is greedy: when you pop the minimum-distance node, its distance is final, because any alternative path would have to pass through some node still in the queue, which by definition has a larger distance, and since all remaining edges are non-negative the path can only get longer from there. That step is exactly where negative weights break it — a longer path can later become cheaper, so the finalised distance is wrong.

    Complexity with a binary heap is O(E log V). In Python, heapq has no decrease-key operation, so the standard trick is lazy deletion: push a new entry on each relaxation and skip stale entries when they pop by checking a finalised set. Without that check the answer is still correct but you reprocess nodes and the performance quietly degrades.

    One implementation detail: heap entries must be (distance, node), with distance first, since Python compares tuples lexicographically. And if two entries tie on distance, Python compares the nodes — which raises TypeError for objects without ordering, so I'd add a monotonic counter as a tiebreaker in that case.

    Cross-question: "Can you just add a large constant to all weights to make them non-negative and then use Dijkstra?"

    No. Adding a constant c to every edge adds c times the number of edges to each path, so paths with different edge counts are shifted by different amounts, and the relative ordering changes. A five-edge path of total weight 10 becomes 60 while a two-edge path of weight 20 becomes 40 — the shorter path is now the longer one. The correct tool for negative weights is Bellman-Ford.

    Cross-question: "Dijkstra with a binary heap is O(E log V). When would a simple array be better?"

    On dense graphs. With a linear-scan array as the priority queue, extract-min is O(V) but done V times, and relaxations are O(1), so total is O(V² + E), which is O(V²) when E is O(V²). A binary heap gives O(V² log V) there — worse. The crossover is roughly when E exceeds V²/log V. Fibonacci heaps give the best theoretical bound, O(E + V log V), but their constants are large enough that binary heaps usually win in practice — a classic case of theory and practice diverging.

    Bellman Ford¶

    Kya hai¶

    Bellman-Ford single-source shortest paths nikaalta hai negative edge weights ke saath bhi, aur negative cycles detect kar leta hai. Wo har edge ko V-1 baar relax karta hai.

    Real-world analogy: Currency exchange. Aap rupee se dollar, dollar se euro, euro se rupee convert karte ho. Kabhi kabhi aisa chain mil jata hai jisme aap shuru se zyada paise lekar wapas aa jaate ho — wo ek negative cycle hai (arbitrage). Dijkstra aisi cheez samajh hi nahi sakta; Bellman-Ford use dhoondh leta hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Dijkstra negative weights par galat answer deta hai (pichhle section ka counterexample). Kyunki uska greedy assumption — "finalised distance kabhi kam nahi hogi" — toot jata hai.

    Bellman-Ford ne greedy chhod diya aur brute-force-ish approach liya:

    Dijkstra:      "Sabse chhota node lo, use FINALISE karo"  <- greedy, ek pass
Bellman-Ford:  "Har edge ko baar baar relax karte raho jab tak kuchh na badle"
               <- koi finalisation nahi, V-1 passes

    Aur ye "V-1 passes" ka number kahan se aaya?

    Kisi bhi shortest path mein zyada se zyada V-1 edges ho sakti hain.
   (Kyunki V nodes hain, aur agar path mein V ya zyada edges hon to koi node
    do baar aayega -> cycle -> agar cycle ka weight >= 0 to use hata do,
    path chhota ho jayega)

Har pass mein, hum kam se kam EK aur edge ka contribution "propagate" kar dete hain.

Pass 1: 1-edge paths correct ho jate hain
Pass 2: 2-edge paths correct
Pass 3: 3-edge paths correct
...
Pass V-1: (V-1)-edge paths correct  ->  SAB correct

Agar pass V mein bhi kuchh badal raha hai -> koi path V ya zyada edges ka
"chhota" ho raha hai -> NEGATIVE CYCLE

    Ye "negative cycle detection" Bellman-Ford ka unique superpower hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    1. dist[source] = 0, baaki sab = infinity

2. V-1 baar dohrao:
      har edge (u, v, w) ke liye:
         agar dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + w        <- RELAX

3. Ek aur pass karo (V-th pass):
      agar koi edge abhi bhi relax ho sakti hai:
         -> NEGATIVE CYCLE exists

    Visualisation — information "wave" ki tarah failti hai:

    Graph:  A --1--> B --1--> C --1--> D

Pass 0 (initial):   A=0,  B=inf, C=inf, D=inf

Pass 1: edges ko kisi bhi order mein relax karo
   Agar order (A,B), (B,C), (C,D) ho:
      A=0, B=1, C=2, D=3   <- LUCKY, ek hi pass mein sab
   Agar order (C,D), (B,C), (A,B) ho:
      (C,D): dist[C]=inf, kuchh nahi
      (B,C): dist[B]=inf, kuchh nahi
      (A,B): dist[A]=0, dist[B] = 1
      Result: A=0, B=1, C=inf, D=inf   <- sirf EK edge propagate hui

Pass 2 (same bad order):
      (C,D): dist[C]=inf, kuchh nahi
      (B,C): dist[B]=1, dist[C] = 2
      (A,B): koi change nahi
      Result: A=0, B=1, C=2, D=inf

Pass 3:  D=3 ho jayega

WORST CASE MEIN har pass mein sirf EK edge ka info propagate hota hai
-> V-1 passes zaroori hain

    Isliye edge order matter karta hai speed ke liye, par correctness ke liye nahi.

    Poora dry run¶

    Graph (negative weights ke saath, no negative cycle):

            4
    A ------> B
    |         |
   5|        -3|
    v         v
    C ------> D
        4

Aur:  B --> C  weight -2

Edges:
   (A, B, 4)
   (A, C, 5)
   (B, C, -2)
   (B, D, -3)
   (C, D, 4)

    V = 4, to V-1 = 3 passes.

    Initial: dist = {A:0, B:inf, C:inf, D:inf}

    PASS 1 (edges order: A→B, A→C, B→C, B→D, C→D):

    Edge u v w dist[u] dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New dist[v]
    A→B A B 4 0 4 inf Yes 4
    A→C A C 5 0 5 inf Yes 5
    B→C B C -2 4 2 5 Yes 2
    B→D B D -3 4 1 inf Yes 1
    C→D C D 4 2 6 1 No 1

    After pass 1: dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1}

    PASS 2:

    Edge u v w dist[u] dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax?
    A→B A B 4 0 4 4 No
    A→C A C 5 0 5 2 No
    B→C B C -2 4 2 2 No
    B→D B D -3 4 1 1 No
    C→D C D 4 2 6 1 No

    Koi change nahi → EARLY EXIT possible!

    After pass 2: dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1} — converged.

    PASS 3 (negative cycle check): koi edge relax nahi hoti → no negative cycle ✓

    Final:

    Node Distance Path
    A 0 A
    B 4 A → B
    C 2 A → B → C (4 + (-2) = 2) ✓ better than A → C (5)
    D 1 A → B → D (4 + (-3) = 1) ✓

    Dijkstra is graph par kya karta?

    Dijkstra pop order: A(0)
   Relax: B=4, C=5
Pop C(5) -- sabse chhota... nahi, C=5 aur B=4, to B pop hoga
Pop B(4).  FINALISE B.  Relax: C = min(5, 4-2) = 2, D = 4-3 = 1
Pop D(1).  FINALISE D.  (C=2 se bada hai? nahi, 1 < 2, to D pehle)
   D ke koi outgoing edges nahi
Pop C(2).  FINALISE C.  Relax: D = 2+4 = 6, par D already finalised

Dijkstra ka answer: A=0, B=4, C=2, D=1  <- IS CASE MEIN SAHI!

    Interesting — Dijkstra yahan sahi nikla. Kyunki is graph mein negative edges ne kabhi kisi already-finalised node ko affect nahi kiya. Par ye luck hai, guarantee nahi.

    Ab negative CYCLE wala example:

        A --1--> B
             |
             |2
             v
    D <--(-4)-- C
    |
    |1
    +--> B  (D --1--> B)

Edges:
   (A, B, 1)
   (B, C, 2)
   (C, D, -4)
   (D, B, 1)

Cycle: B -> C -> D -> B  weight = 2 + (-4) + 1 = -1   <- NEGATIVE CYCLE

    V = 4, 3 passes.

    Initial: dist = {A:0, B:inf, C:inf, D:inf}

    PASS 1:

    Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New
    A→B (1) 0+1 = 1 inf Yes B = 1
    B→C (2) 1+2 = 3 inf Yes C = 3
    C→D (-4) 3-4 = -1 inf Yes D = -1
    D→B (1) -1+1 = 0 1 Yes B = 0

    dist = {A:0, B:0, C:3, D:-1}

    PASS 2:

    Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New
    A→B (1) 1 0 No —
    B→C (2) 0+2 = 2 3 Yes C = 2
    C→D (-4) 2-4 = -2 -1 Yes D = -2
    D→B (1) -2+1 = -1 0 Yes B = -1

    dist = {A:0, B:-1, C:2, D:-2} — distances GIR rahi hain, har pass mein -1

    PASS 3:

    Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New
    B→C (2) -1+2 = 1 2 Yes C = 1
    C→D (-4) 1-4 = -3 -2 Yes D = -3
    D→B (1) -3+1 = -2 -1 Yes B = -2

    dist = {A:0, B:-2, C:1, D:-3}

    PASS 4 (V-th pass, detection pass):

    Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax?
    B→C (2) -2+2 = 0 1 YES — abhi bhi relax ho raha hai!

    → NEGATIVE CYCLE DETECTED ✓

    Ye har pass mein distance -1 girti rehti — infinite loop mein -infinity tak jati. Isliye "shortest path" ka koi matlab hi nahi hai jab negative cycle ho.

    Code¶

    def bellman_ford(vertices, edges, source):
    """Single-source shortest paths with negative weights.
    edges: [(u, v, weight), ...]
    Returns: (dist, parent) ya (None, None) agar negative cycle ho."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    parent = {v: None for v in vertices}            # 3

    for i in range(len(vertices) - 1):              # 4
        changed = False                             # 5
        for u, v, w in edges:                       # 6
            if dist[u] == float('inf'):             # 7
                continue                            # 8
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 9
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 10
                parent[v] = u                       # 11
                changed = True                      # 12
        if not changed:                             # 13
            break                                   # 14

    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 15
        if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 16
            return None, None                       # 17

    return dist, parent                             # 18

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. Sab distances inf. Dict comprehension. float('inf') use kiya, koi bada number nahi (jaise 999999). Kyun? Kyunki negative weights ke saath 999999 + (-1000000) negative ho jata aur galat relaxation hoti. inf + anything = inf (except -inf), jo safe hai.

    2. Source ki distance 0.

    3. Parent tree.

    4. for i in range(len(vertices) - 1) — exactly V-1 passes. V-1 kyun, V kyun nahi? Kyunki koi bhi simple path mein zyada se zyada V-1 edges hoti hain, aur har pass kam se kam ek edge ka contribution propagate karta hai. V passes karna galat nahi hai, bas ek fizool pass. (Aur wo V-th pass hum line 15 par detection ke liye alag se karte hain.)

    5. changed = False — early exit optimisation ka flag.

    6. for u, v, w in edges — har edge par. Order matter nahi karta correctness ke liye (sirf convergence speed ke liye).

    7-8. if dist[u] == float('inf'): continue — u abhi tak reachable nahi hai. Ye check zaroori hai. Bina iske: inf + w = inf (agar w finite hai), aur inf < dist[v] False hoga to actually galat nahi hota... par agar w negative infinity ke paas ho ya numeric edge cases hon to problem. Aur ye ek O(1) skip hai jo fizool arithmetic bachata hai. Aur zyada important: ye unreachable nodes ko inf par rakhta hai, jo semantically sahi hai.

    1. if dist[u] + w < dist[v] — RELAXATION test. Strict <.

    10-11. Update.

    1. changed = True — kuchh badla.

    13-14. if not changed: break — EARLY EXIT. Agar ek poore pass mein koi distance nahi badli, to aage ke passes bhi kuchh nahi badlenge (kyunki input same hai). Converged. Ye practically bahut bada fayda deta hai — random graphs par typically 2-3 passes mein convergence ho jati hai, V-1 nahi. Sparse road networks par ye 100x speedup de sakta hai.

    15-17. NEGATIVE CYCLE DETECTION — V-th pass. V-1 passes ke baad, agar graph mein negative cycle nahi hai to saari distances final hain. Agar koi edge abhi bhi relax ho sakti hai, to iska matlab hai ki koi path V se zyada edges ka "chhota" ho raha hai — jo sirf negative cycle se possible hai. dist[u] != inf check zaroori hai — unreachable nodes ko ignore karna hai.

    1. Return.

    Negative cycle mein kaun se nodes hain — ye bhi nikaal sakte hain:

    def bellman_ford_find_cycle(vertices, edges, source):
    """Negative cycle mein shamil nodes bhi return karta hai."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    parent = {v: None for v in vertices}            # 3

    for _ in range(len(vertices) - 1):              # 4
        for u, v, w in edges:                       # 5
            if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 6
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 7
                parent[v] = u                       # 8

    affected = set()                                # 9
    x = None                                        # 10
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 11
        if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 12
            x = v                                   # 13
            break                                   # 14

    if x is None:                                   # 15
        return dist, None                           # 16

    for _ in range(len(vertices)):                  # 17
        x = parent[x]                               # 18

    cycle = []                                      # 19
    v = x                                           # 20
    while True:                                     # 21
        cycle.append(v)                             # 22
        if v == x and len(cycle) > 1:               # 23
            break                                   # 24
        v = parent[v]                               # 25
    cycle.reverse()                                 # 26
    return dist, cycle                              # 27

    1-8. Standard V-1 passes. 9-14. Koi node dhoondho jo V-th pass mein relax hoti hai. Wo node negative cycle se affected hai (par zaroori nahi ki cycle mein ho — wo cycle se reachable ho sakti hai). 15-16. Koi negative cycle nahi. 17-18. x ko V baar parent chain par peeche le jao. Ye trick kyun kaam karti hai? x cycle se reachable hai. Parent chain follow karne se hum eventually cycle mein pahunch jayenge (kyunki cycle mein infinite backwards chal sakte hain). V steps guarantee karte hain ki hum cycle ke andar aa gaye (kyunki cycle ki length <= V hai). 19-25. Cycle traverse karo parent chain par jab tak x par wapas na aa jayen. 23. v == x and len(cycle) > 1 — len > 1 zaroori hai warna pehli iteration mein hi break ho jata. 26-27. Reverse aur return.

    SPFA (Shortest Path Faster Algorithm) — practical optimisation:

    from collections import deque


def spfa(graph, vertices, source):
    """Queue-based Bellman-Ford. Practically bahut tez, par worst case wahi O(VE)."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    in_queue = {v: False for v in vertices}         # 3
    count = {v: 0 for v in vertices}                # 4
    queue = deque([source])                         # 5
    in_queue[source] = True                         # 6
    n = len(vertices)                               # 7

    while queue:                                    # 8
        u = queue.popleft()                         # 9
        in_queue[u] = False                         # 10
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 11
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 12
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 13
                if not in_queue[v]:                 # 14
                    queue.append(v)                 # 15
                    in_queue[v] = True              # 16
                    count[v] += 1                   # 17
                    if count[v] >= n:               # 18
                        return None                 # 19
    return dist                                     # 20

    1-2. Distances. 3. in_queue — node already queue mein hai ya nahi. Duplicate enqueues rokta hai. 4. count — har node kitni baar queue mein aayi. Negative cycle detection ke liye. 5-7. Queue setup. 8-10. Pop aur flag clear. 11-13. Relaxation. 14-16. Sirf tab enqueue karo jab already queue mein na ho. Ye SPFA ka core idea hai: Bellman-Ford har edge har pass mein check karta hai, chahe wo relax ho sakti ho ya nahi. SPFA sirf un nodes ko dobara process karta hai jinki distance actually badli. Ye "useless" relaxation attempts hata deta hai. 17-19. Agar koi node V ya zyada baar queue mein aayi → negative cycle. Kyunki bina cycle ke, ek node zyada se zyada V-1 baar relax ho sakti hai. 20. Return.

    SPFA practically 5-10x tez hai typical graphs par, par worst case wahi O(V·E) hai — aur adversarial inputs par wo worst case hit hota hai. Competitive programming mein iska "anti-SPFA test" famous hai.

    Passes:            V - 1
Har pass mein:     saare E edges check

TIME: O(V * E)

Negative cycle detection: ek aur O(E) pass
TOTAL: O(V * E)

Bellman-Ford:  O(V * E)

    Bellman-Ford Dijkstra se BAHUT dheema hai. Use sirf tab use karo jab negative weights hon.

    Early exit ke saath: 

    Actual passes = (longest shortest-path mein edges) + 1

Random graphs par ye typically log V ya usse kam hota hai
-> practically O(E log V) jaisa behaviour

Par WORST CASE (path graph, bad edge order) abhi bhi O(V·E)

parent:  O(V)

TOTAL AUXILIARY: O(V)

    Stability, in-place, adaptive¶

    Property Value Kyun
    Handles negative weights Haan — ye iska poora point hai Koi greedy finalisation nahi
    Detects negative cycles Haan V-th pass ka test
    Adaptive Haan, early exit ke saath Converge hote hi ruk jata hai
    Distributed-friendly Haan Har node sirf apne neighbours se baat karta hai — RIP routing protocol isi par bana hai

    Distributed property important hai: Bellman-Ford ko decentralised implement kiya ja sakta hai — har router sirf apne padosi routers se distance vectors exchange karta hai. Isi wajah se RIP (Routing Information Protocol) Bellman-Ford use karta hai, jabki OSPF Dijkstra use karta hai (par usko poora network topology chahiye).

    Kab use karna hai / kab nahi¶

    Use karo jab: - Negative edge weights hain — currency arbitrage, profit/loss networks, game scoring. - Negative cycle detect karna hai — arbitrage opportunities, infinite loops in systems. - Distributed setting — har node ko sirf local information chahiye (routing protocols). - Graph chhota hai aur simplicity chahiye.

    Mat use karo jab: - Saare weights non-negative hain → Dijkstra (bahut tez). - Unweighted → BFS. - Graph bada hai — O(V·E) prohibitive ho jata hai. - All-pairs chahiye → Floyd-Warshall (O(V³), jo V baar Bellman-Ford = O(V²E) se behtar hai dense graphs par), ya Johnson's algorithm (sparse graphs par).

    QA context: Ek test dependency graph jahan kuchh tests dusron ka setup time bachate hain (negative cost). Ya ek CI pipeline jahan cached artifacts negative time contribute karte hain. Aur negative cycle detection = "kya koi circular optimisation hai jo infinitely beneficial lagti hai" — jo aksar ek config bug hoti hai.

    Kitne tareeke se optimize¶

    # Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai
    1 Early exit (no changes in a pass) Typical graphs par 10-100x Ek boolean
    2 SPFA — sirf changed nodes ko re-process Practically 5-10x Worst case wahi; adversarial inputs par kharab
    3 SPFA + SLF (Small Label First) — chhoti distance wale ko front mein Aur 2x Deque manipulation
    4 SPFA + LLL (Large Label Last) Aur improvement Average maintain karna
    5 Edges ko topological order mein process karo (DAG par) O(V + E) — ek hi pass! Sirf DAGs par
    6 Johnson's algorithm all-pairs ke liye O(V·E + V² log V) — sparse par Floyd-Warshall se tez Complicated
    7 Yen's optimisation — edges ko do groups mein baanto ~2x kam passes Vertex ordering chahiye

    DAG shortest path — Bellman-Ford ka special case, O(V+E):

    def dag_shortest_path(graph, vertices, source):
    """DAG par shortest path, negative weights allowed. O(V + E)."""
    topo = topological_sort(graph, vertices)        # 1
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 2
    dist[source] = 0                                # 3
    for u in topo:                                  # 4
        if dist[u] == float('inf'):                 # 5
            continue                                # 6
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 7
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 8
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 9
    return dist                                     # 10
    1. Topological order nikaalo — O(V + E). 2-3. Distances.
    2. Topological order mein process karo. Ye kyun kaam karta hai? Topological order mein, jab hum u process karte hain, uske saare incoming edges already process ho chuke hain, yaani dist[u] final hai. To ek hi pass kaafi hai — V-1 passes ki zaroorat nahi! 5-6. Unreachable skip. 7-9. Relaxation.
    3. Return.

    Ye O(V + E) hai — Bellman-Ford ke O(V·E) se bahut tez, aur Dijkstra ke O(E log V) se bhi tez, aur negative weights bhi handle karta hai. Par sirf DAGs par. Agar aapka graph acyclic hai to ye hamesha best choice hai.

    Longest path in DAG: wahi algorithm, bas < ko > kar do aur inf ko -inf. (General graphs mein longest path NP-hard hai, par DAGs mein O(V+E)!)

    Interview answer: Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths and, unlike Dijkstra, handles negative edge weights. It relaxes every edge V-1 times. The bound is V-1 because any simple shortest path has at most V-1 edges, and each pass guarantees that at least one more edge of every shortest path has been correctly propagated.

    Its unique capability is detecting negative cycles. After V-1 passes all distances should be final, so if a V-th pass can still relax some edge, there must be a cycle with negative total weight — and in that case shortest paths are undefined, since you can go around the cycle repeatedly and drive the distance to negative infinity. That's why it's the algorithm behind currency arbitrage detection.

    The cost is speed: O(V·E) versus Dijkstra's O(E log V). On a sparse graph with a hundred thousand vertices that's 10^10 versus 1.7 million operations, so I'd only use it when negative weights are actually present. The standard optimisation is an early exit — if a full pass changes nothing, the distances have converged. On typical graphs that terminates in a handful of passes rather than V-1.

    Two special cases worth knowing. SPFA is a queue-based variant that only reprocesses nodes whose distance actually changed — practically five to ten times faster, though the worst case is unchanged. And on a DAG you don't need Bellman-Ford at all: process vertices in topological order and one pass suffices, giving O(V + E) with negative weights allowed, which beats both Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford.

    Cross-question: "Why exactly V-1 iterations?"

    Because a shortest path in a graph with V vertices can contain at most V-1 edges — more than that and some vertex repeats, which means a cycle, and if there's no negative cycle you can delete it without lengthening the path. Each pass over all edges guarantees that shortest paths using one more edge become correct, so after V-1 passes all shortest paths are correct. The V-th pass is the negative-cycle test.

    Cross-question: "Why does Bellman-Ford show up in routing protocols when Dijkstra is faster?"

    Because it's decentralised. Each relaxation only needs a node's own distance estimate and its direct neighbours' estimates — no node needs a global view of the topology. That's exactly the distance-vector model, and it's what RIP uses. Dijkstra needs the complete graph, which is why link-state protocols like OSPF have to flood topology information across the whole network first.

    Floyd Warshall¶

    Kya hai¶

    Floyd-Warshall saare jodo (all pairs) ke beech shortest path ek saath nikaalta hai — sirf teen nested loops mein.

    Real-world analogy: Ek airline ka route map. Aapko ek table chahiye jisme har shehar se har doosre shehar tak ka sabse sasta fare ho. Aap ek-ek karke shehar ko "hub" banate ho aur poochte ho: "Kya X se Y jaane mein is hub se hokar jaana sasta hai?" Har shehar ko ek baar hub banane ke baad, table complete ho jati hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    All-pairs shortest paths ke liye options:

    1. V baar Dijkstra chalao:
      O(V * E log V)
      Sparse (E=V):  V² log V
      Dense (E=V²):  V³ log V
      PAR negative weights handle nahi karta

2. V baar Bellman-Ford:
      O(V² * E)
      Dense: O(V⁴)   <- bahut dheema
      Negative weights handle karta hai

3. FLOYD-WARSHALL:
      O(V³)  hamesha
      Negative weights handle karta hai
      Negative cycle detect karta hai
      Code sirf 5 lines

    Dense graphs par Floyd-Warshall jeetta hai: V³ vs V³ log V. Aur uska code itna simple hai ki galti ki gunjaish hi nahi.

    Aur uska code kitna simple hai:

    for k in vertices:
    for i in vertices:
        for j in vertices:
            dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])

    Bas. Ye poora algorithm hai. Isse simple koi non-trivial graph algorithm nahi hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Core idea — "intermediate vertices" ka concept:

    dist[k][i][j] = i se j tak ki shortest distance, agar hum sirf
                {1, 2, ..., k} vertices ko INTERMEDIATE ki tarah use kar sakein

k = 0 (koi intermediate nahi): dist[0][i][j] = direct edge weight (ya inf)

Recurrence:
   dist[k][i][j] = min(
                       dist[k-1][i][j],                    <- k use NAHI kiya
                       dist[k-1][i][k] + dist[k-1][k][j]   <- k use kiya
                   )

Final answer: dist[V][i][j]  -- saare vertices intermediate ho sakte hain

    Diagram:

    Kya i se j jaane mein k se hokar jaana behtar hai?

        i ---------------> j
         \                ^
          \              /
           \            /
            \          /
             v        /
              k -----+

   Purana raasta:  dist[i][j]
   Naya raasta:    dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]

   Jo chhota ho wahi lo.

    Loop order kyun k bahar hai — ye SABSE IMPORTANT baat hai:

    SAHI:
   for k:       <- intermediate vertex BAHAR
      for i:
         for j:

GALAT:
   for i:
      for j:
         for k:    <- k andar

Kyun?  Kyunki recurrence ka structure hai "dist[k-1] se dist[k] banao".
       Jab hum k ka loop chalate hain, hum ye guarantee karte hain ki
       dist[i][k] aur dist[k][j] dono PICHHLE k values ke saath already
       optimal ho chuke hain.

       Agar k andar hoga, to hum dist[i][k] use karenge jo abhi tak
       compute hi nahi hua -> GALAT ANSWERS.

Ye ek line ka farak hai jo poore algorithm ko todta hai, aur interview mein
poochha jata hai.

    Space optimisation — 3D se 2D:

    Recurrence mein dist[k] sirf dist[k-1] par depend karta hai.
To hum 3D array ki jagah 2D use kar sakte hain, in-place update karte hue.

Kya ye safe hai?  Yaani kya dist[i][k] ya dist[k][j] is iteration mein badal sakte hain?

   dist[i][k] = min(dist[i][k], dist[i][k] + dist[k][k])
   dist[k][k] hamesha 0 hai (ya negative agar negative cycle ho)
   To dist[i][k] apne aap se update nahi hota  ->  SAFE  ✓

   Similarly dist[k][j]  ->  SAFE  ✓

Isliye 2D in-place kaam karta hai.  ->  O(V²) space

    Poora dry run¶

Edges:

    Verify kuchh entries: - dist[0][3] = 6: 0→1→2→3 = 3+2+1 = 6 ✓ - dist[1][0] = 9: 1→2→3→0 = 2+1+6 = 9 ✓ - dist[2][1] = 10: 2→3→0→1 = 1+6+3 = 10 ✓ - dist[2][0] = 7: 2→3→0 = 1+6 = 7 ✓

    Diagonal sab 0 hai — koi negative cycle nahi ✓

    Code¶

    def floyd_warshall(n, edges):
    """All-pairs shortest paths. O(V³) time, O(V²) space.
    n = vertices ki sankhya (0 se n-1)
    edges = [(u, v, weight), ...]"""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 2
    for i in range(n):                              # 3
        dist[i][i] = 0                              # 4
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 5
        dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)             # 6

    for k in range(n):                              # 7
        dk = dist[k]                                # 8
        for i in range(n):                          # 9
            dik = dist[i][k]                        # 10
            if dik == INF:                          # 11
                continue                            # 12
            di = dist[i]                            # 13
            for j in range(n):                      # 14
                nd = dik + dk[j]                    # 15
                if nd < di[j]:                      # 16
                    di[j] = nd                      # 17
    return dist                                     # 18


def has_negative_cycle(dist, n):
    """Diagonal par negative value = negative cycle."""
    return any(dist[i][i] < 0 for i in range(n))    # 19

    Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

    1. INF = float('inf') — ek variable mein, kyunki baar baar use hoga.

    2. [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)] — list comprehension, [[INF]*n]*n NAHI. Wahi 2D array trap — *n n references banata ek hi row ke.

    3-4. Diagonal 0. Har vertex se khud tak ki distance 0. Ye zaroori hai — warna line 15 mein dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] mein jab i == k ho to inf + something = inf aata aur koi path nahi milta.

    5-6. Direct edges. min(dist[u][v], w) use kiya, direct assignment nahi — kyunki parallel edges ho sakte hain (do vertices ke beech kai edges). Sabse chhoti chahiye. Agar aap dist[u][v] = w likhte to aakhri edge jeet jata, sabse chhota nahi.

    1. for k in range(n) — OUTER LOOP, intermediate vertex. Ye order critical hai — k bahar, i aur j andar.

    2. dk = dist[k] — row k ko ek local variable mein cache kar liya. Python mein dist[k][j] do lookups hai (dist[k] phir [j]). dk[j] sirf ek. Ye ~20-30% speedup deta hai — inner loop n³ baar chalti hai, to har micro-optimisation matter karti hai.

    3. for i in range(n) — source vertex.

    4. dik = dist[i][k] — ye value inner loop mein constant hai, to bahar nikal li. n³ se n² lookups.

    11-12. if dik == INF: continue — BAHUT bada optimisation. Agar i se k tak koi path hi nahi hai, to k ke through koi bhi path exist nahi karta. Poora inner j loop skip. Sparse graphs par ye 10x tak speedup de sakta hai.

    1. di = dist[i] — row i cache.

    2. for j in range(n) — destination vertex.

    3. nd = dik + dk[j] — i → k → j ka total.

    16-17. if nd < di[j]: di[j] = nd — relaxation. if check use kiya, min() nahi. di[j] = min(di[j], nd) bhi sahi hai par: - min() ek function call hai (Python mein overhead). - if version sirf tab write karta hai jab zaroorat ho. Inner loop mein ye ~15% farak deta hai.

    1. Return.

    2. Negative cycle detection: dist[i][i] < 0. Kyun kaam karta hai? dist[i][i] ka matlab hai "i se i tak wapas aane ki shortest distance". Normally wo 0 hai (kahin jaao hi mat). Agar wo negative hai, to iska matlab hai ki ek cycle exist karta hai jo i se shuru hokar i par wapas aata hai aur uska total weight negative hai — negative cycle.

    Path reconstruction ke saath:

    def floyd_warshall_with_paths(n, edges):
    """Distances + next-hop matrix path reconstruction ke liye."""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 2
    nxt = [[None] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 3
    for i in range(n):                              # 4
        dist[i][i] = 0                              # 5
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 6
        if w < dist[u][v]:                          # 7
            dist[u][v] = w                          # 8
            nxt[u][v] = v                           # 9

    for k in range(n):                              # 10
        for i in range(n):                          # 11
            if dist[i][k] == INF:                   # 12
                continue                            # 13
            for j in range(n):                      # 14
                nd = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]        # 15
                if nd < dist[i][j]:                 # 16
                    dist[i][j] = nd                 # 17
                    nxt[i][j] = nxt[i][k]           # 18
    return dist, nxt                                # 19


def reconstruct(nxt, u, v):
    """u se v tak ka path."""
    if nxt[u][v] is None:                           # 20
        return []                                   # 21
    path = [u]                                      # 22
    while u != v:                                   # 23
        u = nxt[u][v]                               # 24
        path.append(u)                              # 25
    return path                                     # 26

    1-5. Setup. 6-9. Direct edges. nxt[u][v] = v — "u se v jaane ke liye agla hop v hai" (direct edge). 10-17. Standard triple loop. 18. nxt[i][j] = nxt[i][k] — k NAHI, nxt[i][k]. Kyun? Kyunki nxt[i][j] "i se j jaane ke liye pehla hop" store karta hai, poora path nahi. Naya path i → ... → k → ... → j hai, aur uska pehla hop wahi hai jo i → ... → k ka pehla hop tha. Yaani nxt[i][k]. Agar aap nxt[i][j] = k likhte to reconstruction galat hoti — wo k ko direct hop maan leti jabki i se k tak bhi ek raasta hai. 19. Return. 20-21. No path. 22-25. Next-hop chain follow karo. 26. Path.

    Transitive closure (reachability) — Floyd-Warshall ka boolean version:

    def transitive_closure(n, edges):
    """Kaun se node se kaun sa node reachable hai. O(V³)."""
    reach = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]         # 1
    for i in range(n):                              # 2
        reach[i][i] = True                          # 3
    for u, v in edges:                              # 4
        reach[u][v] = True                          # 5
    for k in range(n):                              # 6
        for i in range(n):                          # 7
            if not reach[i][k]:                     # 8
                continue                            # 9
            for j in range(n):                      # 10
                if reach[k][j]:                     # 11
                    reach[i][j] = True              # 12
    return reach                                    # 13

    1-5. Boolean matrix, direct edges. 6-12. Same triple loop, par min ki jagah OR. reach[i][j] = reach[i][j] OR (reach[i][k] AND reach[k][j]) 8-9. k se i reachable nahi → skip poora inner loop. 13. Return.

    Ye "Warshall's algorithm" hai (Floyd ne shortest paths mein extend kiya). Iska use: - Dependency closure — "A par kya kya depend karta hai, indirectly bhi". - QA: "is module ko badalne se kaun se tests affect honge?"

    Bitset optimisation: Boolean version mein har row ko ek integer bana kar bitwise OR use kar sakte ho — 64x speedup:

    def transitive_closure_bitset(n, edges):
    """Bitset version — har row ek integer. ~64x tez."""
    reach = [1 << i for i in range(n)]              # 1
    for u, v in edges:                              # 2
        reach[u] |= 1 << v                          # 3
    for k in range(n):                              # 4
        bit_k = 1 << k                              # 5
        rk = reach[k]                               # 6
        for i in range(n):                          # 7
            if reach[i] & bit_k:                    # 8
                reach[i] |= rk                      # 9
    return reach                                    # 10
    1. Har row ek integer jisme bit j set hai agar j reachable hai. 1 << i = self-loop. 2-3. Direct edges — bit set karo. 4-6. k loop. 7-8. reach[i] & bit_k — kya i se k reachable hai? Ek bitwise AND, O(1).
    2. reach[i] |= rk — POORI ROW ek operation mein! Ye for j in range(n) loop ko ek single OR mein replace kar deta hai. Inner loop poori tarah gayab.
    3. Return.

    Complexity: O(V³/64) effectively — kyunki har OR 64 bits ek saath process karta hai (Python mein arbitrary precision integers hain to aur bhi zyada). n = 1000 par ye 100x+ tez hai.

    Complexity derive karke¶

    Teen nested loops, har ek n iterations:
   n * n * n = n³

TIME: O(V³)   -- hamesha, koi best/worst case nahi

    Comparison:

    Approach Sparse (E=V) Dense (E=V²) Negative weights?
    V × Dijkstra (heap) O(V² log V) O(V³ log V) Nahi
    V × Dijkstra (array) O(V³) O(V³) Nahi
    V × Bellman-Ford O(V³) O(V⁴) Haan
    Floyd-Warshall O(V³) O(V³) Haan
    Johnson's algorithm O(V² log V + VE) O(V³ log V) Haan

    Conclusion: - Sparse graph + negative weights → Johnson's (Bellman-Ford se reweight karo, phir V baar Dijkstra). - Dense graph → Floyd-Warshall. - Sparse + non-negative → V × Dijkstra.

nxt matrix:   O(V²) agar paths chahiye

TOTAL: O(V²)
