      - Sirf utne variables/rows rakho

    Order kyun matter karta hai step 3 mein: dp[i] ko dp[i-1] aur dp[i-2] chahiye. To loop i badhte hue chalna chahiye. Agar recurrence dp[i] ko dp[i+1] par depend karati hai to loop ULTA chalega. Ye har problem par sochna padta hai.

    Interview answer: I always develop a DP solution in four steps, and I'd walk through all four in an interview because each one shows a different insight.

    Start with the brute-force recursion. For climbing stairs it's climb(n) = climb(n-1) + climb(n-2) with climb(0) = 1 — you either took a one-step or a two-step to get here. That's O(2^n), which is unusable past about n = 35, but it's where the recurrence comes from and it's the part that actually requires thinking.

    Then memoise — literally one decorator, lru_cache — and it becomes O(n), because there are only n distinct states. That's a twelve-orders-of-magnitude improvement for one line.

    Then convert to tabulation: allocate an array, fill the base cases, and loop in an order where every state's dependencies are already computed. That removes Python's recursion limit, which caps the memoised version around n = 900, and it's faster because there are no function calls and the array access is cache-friendly.

    Finally, look at what the recurrence actually reads. Here it only reads the previous two values, so the whole array collapses to two rolling variables and space drops from O(n) to O(1). The one thing to be careful about is doing the update as a simultaneous tuple assignment, because updating them one at a time clobbers the value you still need.

    Fibonacci¶

    Kya hai¶

    F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1. DP ka "hello world".

    Real-world analogy: Khargoshon ki jodiyaan (Fibonacci ka original 1202 ka problem) — har mahine har vayask jodi ek nayi jodi paida karti hai, aur nayi jodi ek mahine mein vayask ho jati hai.

    Kyu hai¶

    Ye DP ka canonical example hai kyunki isme overlapping subproblems ekdum saaf dikhte hain, aur uska naive version spectacularly slow hai — jo memoisation ka motivation dikha deta hai.

    Poora dry run — fib(6) bottom-up¶

    i dp[i-2] dp[i-1] dp[i] = sum
    0 — — 0 (base)
    1 — — 1 (base)
    2 0 1 1
    3 1 1 2
    4 1 2 3
    5 2 3 5
    6 3 5 8

    fib(6) = 8 ✓

    Code¶

    def fib_naive(n):
    """O(1.618^n) -- exponential."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 1
        return n                                    # 2
    return fib_naive(n - 1) + fib_naive(n - 2)      # 3


def fib_dp(n):
    """O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 4
        return n                                    # 5
    a, b = 0, 1                                     # 6
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):                       # 7
        a, b = b, a + b                             # 8
    return b                                        # 9


def fib_matrix(n):
    """O(log n) via matrix exponentiation."""
    def mat_mult(A, B):                             # 10
        return [[A[0][0]*B[0][0] + A[0][1]*B[1][0],
                 A[0][0]*B[0][1] + A[0][1]*B[1][1]],
                [A[1][0]*B[0][0] + A[1][1]*B[1][0],
                 A[1][0]*B[0][1] + A[1][1]*B[1][1]]]

    def mat_pow(M, p):                              # 11
        result = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]                   # 12
        while p > 0:                                # 13
            if p & 1:                               # 14
                result = mat_mult(result, M)        # 15
            M = mat_mult(M, M)                      # 16
            p >>= 1                                 # 17
        return result                               # 18

    if n <= 1:                                      # 19
        return n                                    # 20
    return mat_pow([[1, 1], [1, 0]], n)[0][1]       # 21

    1-3. Naive. n <= 1 base case dono 0 aur 1 handle karta hai (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, dono return n se). 4-5. Base. 6. a = fib(i-2), b = fib(i-1). Initial: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1. 7-8. Rolling update, tuple assignment se simultaneous. 9. b mein fib(n).

    1. 2×2 matrix multiplication, hand-unrolled (loops se tez chhote matrices par). 11-18. Fast exponentiation on matrices.
    2. Identity matrix — multiplication ka 1. 13-17. Binary exponentiation: p ke har bit ke liye. p & 1 odd check, p >>= 1 halve. M = M*M har step par square. 19-21. [[1,1],[1,0]]^n ka [0][1] entry fib(n) hota hai. Kyun? Kyunki [[1,1],[1,0]] * [F(n), F(n-1)] = [F(n)+F(n-1), F(n)] = [F(n+1), F(n)]. Yaani wo matrix "ek Fibonacci step" hai. n steps = matrix ka n-th power.

    Complexity¶

    Version Time Space
    Naive recursion O(1.618^n) O(n)
    Memoised O(n) O(n)
    Bottom-up O(n) O(n)
    Rolling variables O(n) O(1)
    Matrix exponentiation O(log n) O(1)
    Binet's formula (float) O(1) O(1) — par precision issues n>70

    Ye derivation: naive ka 1.618^n golden ratio se aata hai — T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + 1 ka solution phi^n hai jahan phi = (1+sqrt(5))/2 = 1.618.

    Interview answer: Fibonacci is the standard demonstration of DP. The naive recursion is O(phi^n) where phi is the golden ratio — about 1.618 — because the recurrence for the call count is itself the Fibonacci recurrence. Memoising collapses it to O(n), since there are only n distinct arguments.

    The bottom-up version needs only the previous two values, so it's O(1) space with two rolling variables updated as a simultaneous tuple assignment. And there's a genuinely faster method: matrix exponentiation. The matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] raised to the n-th power has F(n) in it, and binary exponentiation computes that in O(log n) multiplications. That's the answer if someone asks for fib of a very large n.

    Binet's closed-form formula is O(1) but uses floating point, so it loses precision beyond about n = 70 — worth mentioning as a trap rather than a solution.

    Climbing Stairs¶

    Ye Fibonacci ka hi disguise hai — poori progression pehle wale section mein di gayi hai. Yahan uske variants aur unka state design.

    Variants¶

    Variant 1 — k steps allowed:

    def climb_k_steps(n, k):
    """Ek baar mein 1 se k tak steps. O(n*k) time, O(n) space."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 1
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        for step in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):        # 4
            dp[i] += dp[i - step]                   # 5
    return dp[n]                                    # 6

    1-2. Table, base case. 3. Har position. 4. min(k, i) — clamp. Agar i < k to aap i se zyada steps nahi le sakte (negative index aa jayega). Bina is clamp ke dp[-1] Python mein last element deta hai — silent wrong answer. 5. Sab valid steps se aane ke tareeke jodo. 6. Answer.

    Variant 2 — minimum cost climbing:

    def min_cost_climbing(cost):
    """Har seedhi ka cost hai. Minimum total cost. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    prev2, prev1 = 0, 0                             # 1
    for i in range(2, len(cost) + 1):               # 2
        current = min(prev1 + cost[i - 1],          # 3
                      prev2 + cost[i - 2])          # 4
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, current               # 5
    return prev1                                    # 6
    1. Dono base cases 0 — aap seedhi 0 ya 1 se free mein shuru kar sakte ho.
    2. Position 2 se n tak. 3-4. Do choices: ek step pehle se aao (cost[i-1] doge) ya do step pehle se (cost[i-2]). min kyunki hum cost minimise kar rahe hain (ways count karne mein + tha).
    3. Roll.
    4. Answer.

    Variant 3 — steps with forbidden positions:

    def climb_with_obstacles(n, blocked):
    """blocked = set of positions jahan nahi ja sakte."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 1
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        if i in blocked:                            # 4
            dp[i] = 0                               # 5
            continue                                # 6
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + (dp[i - 2] if i >= 2 else 0)   # 7
    return dp[n]                                    # 8

    1-3. Setup. 4-6. Blocked position → 0 ways, aur aage mat badho. continue zaroori hai warna line 7 use overwrite kar degi. 7. Conditional for i >= 2 — negative index se bachne ke liye. 8. Answer.

    Interview answer: Climbing stairs is Fibonacci with a different story: the number of ways to reach step n equals ways to reach n-1 plus ways to reach n-2, because your last move was either a one-step or a two-step. Base case is one way to be at step 0 — do nothing — which people often get wrong by writing zero, and then the whole answer collapses to zero.

    The variants are where the state design shows. Allowing steps of size one through k turns it into a sum over k previous states, so O(n·k). Adding a per-step cost changes the aggregation from sum to min, because you're now optimising rather than counting — that switch between sum and min or max is the single most common difference between "count the ways" and "find the best way" problems. And blocked positions are just a state that's forced to zero.

    House Robber¶

    Kya hai¶

    Ek line mein ghar hain, har ghar mein kuchh paisa. Aap do adjacent ghar nahi loot sakte (alarm baj jayega). Maximum kitna loot sakte ho?

    Real-world analogy: Ek conference mein back-to-back sessions attend nahi kar sakte (breaks chahiye). Har session ki value alag hai. Maximum value kaise nikaalein?

    Kyu hai¶

    Ye "include/exclude" DP pattern ka canonical example hai, jo bahut jagah aata hai — maximum independent set on a path, non-adjacent selection, scheduling with gaps.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Har ghar par DO CHOICES:
   1. LOOT karo:  nums[i] + best(i-2)     <- i-1 skip karna padega
   2. SKIP karo:  best(i-1)

dp[i] = max(nums[i] + dp[i-2], dp[i-1])

    Poora dry run¶

    nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]

    i nums[i] Rob: nums[i] + dp[i-2] Skip: dp[i-1] dp[i] = max
    0 2 2 + 0 = 2 0 2
    1 7 7 + 0 = 7 2 7
    2 9 9 + 2 = 11 7 11
    3 3 3 + 7 = 10 11 11
    4 1 1 + 11 = 12 11 12

    Answer: 12 (ghar 0, 2, 4 loote: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12) ✓

    Verify alternatives: [7, 3] = 10, [2, 9, 1] = 12, [7, 1] = 8, [2, 3] = 5. 12 maximum hai ✓

    Code¶

    def rob(nums):
    """Linear houses. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    rob_prev, skip_prev = 0, 0                      # 1
    for x in nums:                                  # 2
        rob_prev, skip_prev = skip_prev + x, max(rob_prev, skip_prev)   # 3
    return max(rob_prev, skip_prev)                 # 4


def rob_circular(nums):
    """Ghar CIRCLE mein hain -- pehla aur aakhri adjacent hain."""
    if len(nums) == 1:                              # 5
        return nums[0]                              # 6
    return max(rob(nums[:-1]), rob(nums[1:]))       # 7


def rob_tree(root):
    """Binary tree par house robber."""
    def solve(node):                                # 8
        if node is None:                            # 9
            return (0, 0)                           # 10
        lr, ls = solve(node.left)                   # 11
        rr, rs = solve(node.right)                  # 12
        rob_here = node.val + ls + rs               # 13
        skip_here = max(lr, ls) + max(rr, rs)       # 14
        return (rob_here, skip_here)                # 15
    return max(solve(root))                         # 16

    Line-by-line:

    1. Do states: rob_prev = "pichhla ghar loota tha to best", skip_prev = "pichhla ghar skip kiya tha to best". Dono 0 se shuru.
    2. Har ghar.
    3. Simultaneous update:
    4. rob_prev (naya) = skip_prev (purana) + x — is ghar ko lootne ke liye pichhla skip hona zaroori tha.
    5. skip_prev (naya) = max(rob_prev, skip_prev) — is ghar ko skip kiya, to pichhla kuchh bhi ho sakta tha. Tuple assignment se right side poori pehle evaluate hoti hai — critical.
    6. Dono states ka max — aakhir mein aap last ghar loot bhi sakte the aur nahi bhi.

    5-6. Single house. 7. Circular case ka trick: pehla aur aakhri ghar dono nahi loot sakte. To do cases: - nums[:-1] — aakhri chhod kar (pehla loot sakte ho) - nums[1:] — pehla chhod kar (aakhri loot sakte ho) Jo bada ho wahi answer. Ye ek elegant reduction hai.

    8-16. Tree version — har node do values return karta hai. 9-10. Null node → (0, 0). 11-12. Children ke results. lr = left ko rob kiya, ls = left ko skip kiya. 13. rob_here = is node ki value + dono children ko SKIP karna padega. 14. skip_here = har child ke liye best (rob ya skip, jo bhi bada). 15. Tuple return. 16. Root par max.

    Ye "har node se tuple return karo" pattern tree DP mein bahut common hai.

    Complexity¶

    Variant Time Space
    Linear O(n) O(1)
    Circular O(n) O(n) (slicing) ya O(1) with indices
    Tree O(V) O(height) recursion

    Interview answer: House robber is the canonical include-exclude DP. At each house you either rob it — adding its value to the best result from two houses back, since the adjacent one must be skipped — or skip it, keeping the best from one house back. So dp[i] = max(nums[i] + dp[i-2], dp[i-1]). Only two previous values are ever read, so it's O(n) time and O(1) space with two rolling variables.

    I find it clearer to track two named states — "best if I robbed the previous house" and "best if I skipped it" — because that generalises. The circular variant, where the first and last houses are adjacent, reduces to running the linear version twice: once excluding the last house and once excluding the first, then taking the max. And the tree variant returns a pair from each node — best-if-robbed and best-if-skipped — which is the standard shape for tree DP.

    Coin Change¶

    Kya hai¶

    Coins ki denominations di hain (unlimited supply). Ek target amount banane ke liye minimum kitne coins chahiye? (Ya: kitne alag tareeke hain?)

    Real-world analogy: Dukaandaar ko 87 rupaye ka change dena hai aur uske paas 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 ke note hain. Minimum kitne note dega?

    Kyu hai¶

    Ye unbounded knapsack ka simplest form hai, aur ye dikhata hai ki greedy kab fail hota hai:

    coins = [1, 3, 4],  amount = 6

GREEDY (sabse bada pehle):  4 + 1 + 1  =  3 coins
OPTIMAL (DP):               3 + 3      =  2 coins

GREEDY GALAT HAI.

(Indian/US currency par greedy kaam karta hai kyunki wo "canonical" system hai,
par arbitrary denominations par nahi.)

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    MINIMUM COINS:
   dp[amount] = 1 + min over coins c of dp[amount - c]

COUNT WAYS:
   dp[amount] = sum over coins c of dp[amount - c]     <- PAR ye PERMUTATIONS ginega!

   COMBINATIONS ke liye loop order badalna padta hai (neeche dekho)

    Poora dry run¶

    Minimum coins. coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. dp[0] = 0, baaki inf.

    amount coin 1 coin 3 coin 4 dp[amount]
    1 1 + dp[0] = 1 — (1<3) — 1
    2 1 + dp[1] = 2 — — 2
    3 1 + dp[2] = 3 1 + dp[0] = 1 — 1
    4 1 + dp[3] = 2 1 + dp[1] = 2 1 + dp[0] = 1 1
    5 1 + dp[4] = 2 1 + dp[2] = 3 1 + dp[1] = 2 2
    6 1 + dp[5] = 3 1 + dp[3] = 2 1 + dp[2] = 3 2

    Answer: 2 (3 + 3) ✓ Greedy ne 3 diya tha.

    Count ways (combinations). Same coins, amount 5. Loop coins bahar:

    After coin 1: dp = [1,1,1,1,1,1] (har amount sirf 1s se — ek tareeka) After coin 3: dp = [1,1,1,2,2,2] (3 ko 1+1+1 ya 3 — 2 tareeke) After coin 4: dp = [1,1,1,2,3,3] (4 ko 1111, 1+3, 4 — 3 tareeke)

    dp[5] = 3: 1+1+1+1+1, 1+1+3, 1+4 ✓

    Code¶

    def coin_change_min(coins, amount):
    """Minimum coins. O(amount * len(coins)) time, O(amount) space."""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dp = [INF] * (amount + 1)                       # 2
    dp[0] = 0                                       # 3
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):                  # 4
        for c in coins:                             # 5
            if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:    # 6
                dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1               # 7
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1  # 8


def coin_change_combinations(coins, amount):
    """Kitne alag COMBINATIONS (order matter nahi karta)."""
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)                         # 9
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 10
    for c in coins:                                 # 11
        for a in range(c, amount + 1):              # 12
            dp[a] += dp[a - c]                      # 13
    return dp[amount]                               # 14


def coin_change_permutations(coins, amount):
    """Kitne alag PERMUTATIONS (order matter karta hai)."""
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)                         # 15
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 16
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):                  # 17
        for c in coins:                             # 18
            if c <= a:                              # 19
                dp[a] += dp[a - c]                  # 20
    return dp[amount]                               # 21

    Line-by-line:

    1-2. INF sentinel — "abhi tak reachable nahi". 3. dp[0] = 0 — 0 amount ke liye 0 coins. Ye base case zaroori hai warna kuchh bhi compute nahi hoga. 4-5. Har amount, har coin. 6. c <= a — coin amount se bada nahi hona chahiye (negative index se bachao). dp[a-c] + 1 < dp[a] — improvement check. dp[a-c] INF ho sakta hai — INF + 1 Python mein inf hi rehta hai, jo < INF False deta. Safe. 7. Update. 8. INF matlab impossible → -1 return.

    9-13. COMBINATIONS — coins BAHAR ka loop. Ye order hi combinations vs permutations decide karta hai. Coin bahar hone se: hum pehle sirf coin-1 ke saath sab amounts fill karte hain, phir coin-3 add karte hain, etc. Ek combination sirf ek baar count hoti hai kyunki coins ka order fixed hai. 12. range(c, amount+1) — c se shuru (chhote amounts mein wo coin fit hi nahi hoti). 13. dp[a] += dp[a-c] — +=, = nahi. Hum ways jod rahe hain.

    15-20. PERMUTATIONS — amount bahar ka loop. Har amount ke liye saare coins try karte hain, to 1+3 aur 3+1 alag count hote hain. 19. Bounds check.

    Ye loop-order ka farak sabse zyada poochha jane wala DP detail hai.

    COMBINATIONS (coins outer):   {1,1,3} aur {1,3,1} ko EK maana
PERMUTATIONS (amount outer):  dono ALAG maane

Problem statement dhyaan se padho:
   "how many ways to make change"     -> usually COMBINATIONS
   "how many ordered sequences sum"   -> PERMUTATIONS

    Complexity¶

    Variant Time Space
    Minimum coins O(amount × coins) O(amount)
    Count combinations O(amount × coins) O(amount)
    Count permutations O(amount × coins) O(amount)

    Note: O(amount × coins) PSEUDO-POLYNOMIAL hai — amount input ki value hai, uske bits ki sankhya nahi. amount = 10^9 par ye chalega nahi.

    Interview answer: Coin change is the standard unbounded knapsack. For minimum coins, dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - c], with dp[0] = 0, giving O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) space.

    The important thing this problem demonstrates is that greedy fails. With coins 1, 3, 4 and a target of 6, greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 for three coins, while the optimum is 3 plus 3, two coins. Greedy happens to work on real currency systems because they're designed to be canonical, but not for arbitrary denominations.

    For the counting variant, the loop order determines the semantics and this trips a lot of people up. Coins in the outer loop counts combinations — 1+1+3 and 1+3+1 are the same. Amount in the outer loop counts permutations — they're different. Nothing else changes, just which loop is outside.

    One caveat on complexity: O(amount × coins) is pseudo-polynomial. The amount is a value, not an input size, so for a target of a billion this is infeasible even though it looks polynomial.

    Zero One Knapsack¶

    Kya hai¶

    n items hain, har ek ka weight aur value hai. Ek bag hai jiski capacity W hai. Har item ko ya to poora lo ya bilkul mat lo (0/1 — aadha nahi). Maximum total value?

    Real-world analogy: Aap trekking par ja rahe ho aur backpack mein 10 kg tak le ja sakte ho. Har cheez ka weight aur "usefulness" alag hai. Kya lekar jayein?

    Kyu hai¶

    Ye DP ka sabse important pattern hai — 2D state (item index, remaining capacity) ka canonical example. Iske variants har jagah aate hain: subset sum, partition equal subset, target sum, budget allocation.

    Greedy kyun fail hota hai: "value/weight ratio sabse acchi wali pehle lo" — ye fractional knapsack mein optimal hai, par 0/1 mein nahi:

    Capacity 10.  Items: (w=6, v=30), (w=5, v=20), (w=5, v=20)

Greedy by ratio:  item1 (ratio 5.0) lo  ->  4 kg bacha, kuchh fit nahi  ->  value 30
Optimal:          item2 + item3         ->  10 kg exactly              ->  value 40

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    dp[i][w] = pehle i items mein se, capacity w ke saath, maximum value

Har item par DO CHOICES:
   1. SKIP karo:  dp[i-1][w]
   2. LO (agar fit ho):  value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]

dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w],  value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]])

    Poora dry run¶

    weights = [1, 3, 4, 5], values = [1, 4, 5, 7], W = 7

    Table dp[i][w] — rows = items considered, columns = capacity:

    i \ w 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
    0 items 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
    +item1 (w1,v1) 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1
    +item2 (w3,v4) 0 1 1 4 5 5 5 5
    +item3 (w4,v5) 0 1 1 4 5 6 6 9
    +item4 (w5,v7) 0 1 1 4 5 7 8 9

    Answer: dp[4][7] = 9

    Kuchh cells ki calculation:

    • dp[2][4]: skip item2 → dp[1][4] = 1. Take item2 (w=3) → 4 + dp[1][1] = 4 + 1 = 5. max = 5 ✓
    • dp[3][7]: skip item3 → dp[2][7] = 5. Take item3 (w=4) → 5 + dp[2][3] = 5 + 4 = 9. max = 9 ✓
    • dp[4][7]: skip item4 → dp[3][7] = 9. Take item4 (w=5) → 7 + dp[3][2] = 7 + 1 = 8. max = 9 ✓

    Optimal selection: item2 (w=3, v=4) + item3 (w=4, v=5) = weight 7, value 9 ✓

    Code¶

    def knapsack_2d(weights, values, W):
    """0/1 knapsack, 2D table. O(nW) time, O(nW) space."""
    n = len(weights)                                # 1
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        wi, vi = weights[i - 1], values[i - 1]      # 4
        for w in range(W + 1):                      # 5
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]                 # 6
            if wi <= w:                             # 7
                take = vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi]       # 8
                if take > dp[i][w]:                 # 9
                    dp[i][w] = take                 # 10
    return dp[n][W]                                 # 11


def knapsack_1d(weights, values, W):
    """Space-optimised. O(nW) time, O(W) space."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 12
    for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):             # 13
        for w in range(W, wi - 1, -1):              # 14
            if dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]:             # 15
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 16
    return dp[W]                                    # 17


def knapsack_with_items(weights, values, W):
    """Value + kaun se items liye."""
    n = len(weights)                                # 18
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 19
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 20
        wi, vi = weights[i - 1], values[i - 1]      # 21
        for w in range(W + 1):                      # 22
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]                 # 23
            if wi <= w and vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi] > dp[i][w]:   # 24
                dp[i][w] = vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi]   # 25
    chosen = []                                     # 26
    w = W                                           # 27
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):                       # 28
        if dp[i][w] != dp[i - 1][w]:                # 29
            chosen.append(i - 1)                    # 30
            w -= weights[i - 1]                     # 31
    chosen.reverse()                                # 32
    return dp[n][W], chosen                         # 33

    Line-by-line:

    1-2. (n+1) × (W+1) table. +1 dono mein — row 0 = "koi item nahi", column 0 = "capacity 0". List comprehension, [[0]*(W+1)]*(n+1) NAHI. 3-4. Har item. i-1 indexing kyunki dp mein row i ka matlab "pehle i items", jo weights[i-1] tak hai. 5. Har capacity. 6. Default: SKIP — pichhli row ka same column. 7. wi <= w — item fit hota hai? 8. TAKE: item ki value + baaki capacity ka best (PICHHLI row se). dp[i-1][...] use kiya, dp[i][...] NAHI — kyunki 0/1 mein har item ek hi baar le sakte hain. dp[i] use karne se wo unbounded knapsack ban jata. 9-10. Max. 11. Answer.

    1. 1D table — sirf ek row.
    2. Har item.
    3. range(W, wi-1, -1) — ULTA (right to left)! Ye sabse critical line hai. Kyun ulta? Kyunki dp[w] ko dp[w - wi] chahiye jo pichhli item iteration ka hona chahiye. Agar hum seedha (left to right) chalte, to dp[w - wi] is item se already update ho chuka hota — yaani hum item ko do baar le lete → unbounded knapsack. Ulta chalne se dp[w - wi] abhi tak purana (pichhli item wala) hai. ✓ Ye ek line ka farak 0/1 aur unbounded knapsack ko separate karta hai. wi - 1 end (exclusive) — taaki w = wi tak jayein (w < wi par item fit nahi hoti). 15-16. Update.
    4. Answer.

    18-25. 2D version, items track karne ke liye (1D se items reconstruct nahi ho sakte). 26-31. BACKTRACK karke items nikaalo: 28. Aakhri item se ulta chalo. 29. dp[i][w] != dp[i-1][w] → item i LIYA gaya tha. Agar dono barabar hote to item skip kiya gaya tha (skip wali value hi final thi). 30-31. Item record, capacity kam karo. 32-33. Reverse aur return.

    Related problems (same pattern)¶

    def can_partition_equal_subset(nums):
    """Kya array ko do EQUAL SUM subsets mein baant sakte hain?"""
    total = sum(nums)                               # 1
    if total % 2 != 0:                              # 2
        return False                                # 3
    target = total // 2                             # 4
    dp = [False] * (target + 1)                     # 5
    dp[0] = True                                    # 6
    for x in nums:                                  # 7
        for s in range(target, x - 1, -1):          # 8
            if dp[s - x]:                           # 9
                dp[s] = True                        # 10
    return dp[target]                               # 11


def count_target_sum(nums, target):
    """+/- signs assign karke target banane ke kitne tareeke."""
    total = sum(nums)                               # 12
    if (total + target) % 2 != 0 or abs(target) > total:   # 13
        return 0                                    # 14
    s = (total + target) // 2                       # 15
    dp = [0] * (s + 1)                              # 16
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 17
    for x in nums:                                  # 18
        for j in range(s, x - 1, -1):               # 19
            dp[j] += dp[j - x]                      # 20
    return dp[s]                                    # 21

    1-3. Odd total → impossible (do equal integers ka sum even hota hai). 4. Target = aadha. 5-6. Boolean DP. dp[0] = True — 0 sum hamesha possible (kuchh mat lo). 7-8. Ulta loop — 0/1 knapsack pattern. 9-10. Agar s - x reachable hai to s bhi reachable hai. 11. Answer.

    12-15. Ye reduction sundar hai. Agar positive subset ka sum P aur negative ka N hai: P - N = target aur P + N = total. Dono jodo: 2P = total + target, to P = (total + target) / 2. Ab problem ban gaya: "kitne subsets ka sum P hai?" — jo standard knapsack counting hai. 13-14. Parity aur range checks — agar (total+target) odd hai to koi integer solution nahi. 16-20. Standard counting knapsack, ulta loop. 21. Answer.

    Complexity¶

    Version Time Space
    2D O(n·W) O(n·W)
    1D O(n·W) O(W)
    With item reconstruction O(n·W) O(n·W) (2D chahiye)

    Pseudo-polynomial: W ek value hai. W = 10^9 par ye chalega nahi, chahe n chhota ho. 0/1 knapsack NP-hard hai — koi truly polynomial algorithm nahi hai.

    Interview answer: 0/1 knapsack is the canonical two-dimensional DP. The state is dp[i][w] — the best value using the first i items with capacity w — and the recurrence is the classic take-or-skip: max of dp[i-1][w] and value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]. That's O(nW) time and O(nW) space.

    The space optimisation to O(W) is the part worth being careful about. You keep one row and iterate capacity from W downward. The reason it must go downward is that dp[w - weight] has to still hold the previous item's value; iterating upward would read a value already updated for the current item, which means taking that item twice — and that's exactly unbounded knapsack. So the direction of that single loop is the whole difference between the two problems.

    Greedy by value-to-weight ratio doesn't work here, though it is optimal for the fractional version, where you can take partial items. With capacity 10 and items of weight 6/value 30 and two of weight 5/value 20, greedy takes the best ratio first and gets 30, while the optimum is 40.

    A lot of problems reduce to this: subset-sum, partition into equal halves, and target-sum with plus-minus signs, which reduces algebraically to counting subsets that sum to (total + target)/2.

    Unbounded Knapsack¶

    Kya hai¶

    Wahi knapsack, par har item ki unlimited copies available hain.

    Real-world analogy: Ek vending machine se items khareedne hain budget ke andar, aur har item ka stock unlimited hai. Kya lein, aur kitne?

    Kyu hai¶

    Ye 0/1 knapsack se structurally alag hai aur uska ek line ka farak DP ka sabse elegant insight hai.

    0/1:        dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], v + dp[i-1][w - wt])
                                              ^^^^^ PICHHLI row -- item dobara nahi

UNBOUNDED:  dp[w]    = max(dp[w],      v + dp[w - wt])
                                              ^^^^ SAME row -- item dobara le sakte hain

    1D code mein ye farak sirf LOOP DIRECTION ka hai:

    0/1:        for w in range(W, wt-1, -1):    <- ULTA
UNBOUNDED:  for w in range(wt, W+1):        <- SEEDHA

    Poora dry run¶

    weights = [2, 3, 4], values = [3, 4, 5], W = 7

    1D table (seedha loop):

    After item dp[0] dp[1] dp[2] dp[3] dp[4] dp[5] dp[6] dp[7]
    init 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
    item1 (w2,v3) 0 0 3 3 6 6 9 9
    item2 (w3,v4) 0 0 3 4 6 7 9 10
    item3 (w4,v5) 0 0 3 4 6 7 9 10

    Answer: 10

    Item1 wali row ki calculation (w=2 se seedha): - dp[2] = max(0, 3 + dp[0]) = 3 - dp[4] = max(0, 3 + dp[2]) = 3 + 3 = 6 ← dp[2] already is item se update ho chuka! Yahi "item dobara" ka mechanism hai. - dp[6] = max(0, 3 + dp[4]) = 3 + 6 = 9 ← teen copies

    Item2 wali row: - dp[3] = max(3, 4 + dp[0]) = 4 - dp[5] = max(6, 4 + dp[2]) = max(6, 4+3) = 7 - dp[7] = max(9, 4 + dp[4]) = max(9, 4+6) = 10 ← item2 ek baar + item1 do baar = 4+3+3 = 10 ✓

    Code¶

    def unbounded_knapsack(weights, values, W):
    """Unlimited copies. O(nW) time, O(W) space."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 1
    for w in range(1, W + 1):                       # 2
        for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):         # 3
            if wi <= w and dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]: # 4
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 5
    return dp[W]                                    # 6


def unbounded_knapsack_item_outer(weights, values, W):
    """Same answer, items bahar. SEEDHA loop -- yahi 0/1 se farak hai."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 7
    for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):             # 8
        for w in range(wi, W + 1):                  # 9
            if dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]:             # 10
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 11
    return dp[W]                                    # 12


def rod_cutting(prices, n):
    """Rod ko tukdon mein kaato, maximum revenue. Unbounded knapsack ka classic."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 13
    for length in range(1, n + 1):                  # 14
        for cut in range(1, length + 1):            # 15
            if prices[cut - 1] + dp[length - cut] > dp[length]:   # 16
                dp[length] = prices[cut - 1] + dp[length - cut]   # 17
    return dp[n]                                    # 18

    Line-by-line:

    1-2. Table aur capacity loop. 3-5. Har item. dp[w - wi] SAME array se — jo is item se already update ho chuka ho sakta hai. Yahi unbounded ka mechanism hai. 6. Answer.

    7-12. Item-outer version. Line 9 mein range(wi, W+1) — SEEDHA. 0/1 mein ye range(W, wi-1, -1) (ulta) hota. Ek line ka farak, do alag problems.

    13-18. Rod cutting — ek rod ko tukdon mein kaat kar bechna hai, prices[i] = length i+1 ke tukde ka daam. 15. cut = pehla tukda kitna lamba. 1 se length tak — har possible pehla cut. 16-17. prices[cut-1] (us tukde ka daam) + dp[length-cut] (bache hue rod ka best). Ye unbounded knapsack hai jahan "weight" = length aur "value" = price.

    Complexity¶

    Problem Time Space
    Unbounded knapsack O(n·W) O(W)
    Rod cutting O(n²) O(n)
    Coin change (min) O(amount × coins) O(amount)

    Note: unbounded knapsack ka 1D version hamesha O(W) space leta hai — 0/1 ki tarah 2D version ki zaroorat hi nahi (kyunki hum same row use kar rahe hain by design).

    Interview answer: Unbounded knapsack is 0/1 knapsack with unlimited copies of each item. The recurrence changes from reading the previous row to reading the current one: dp[w] = max(dp[w], value + dp[w - weight]), where dp[w - weight] may already include this item.

    In the space-optimised one-dimensional code, that's expressed purely as loop direction. For 0/1 you iterate capacity downward so dp[w - weight] still holds the previous item's value; for unbounded you iterate upward so it holds the current item's value and the item gets reused. One line, two different problems — and it's a favourite interview question precisely because it looks like a typo.

    Coin change and rod cutting are both instances: coins are items with unlimited supply, and rod cutting is choosing the first cut length and recursing on the remainder. All three are O(n·W) pseudo-polynomial, so they're only tractable when the capacity or amount is bounded.

    Longest Common Subsequence¶

    Kya hai¶

    Do strings mein wo sabse lambi sequence dhoondhni hai jo dono mein usi order mein mile — par continuous hone ki zaroorat nahi. Analogy: do logon ki shopping list compare karo aur wo cheezein nikaalo jo dono ne usi order mein likhi hain, beech mein kuchh bhi extra ho to chalega.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Do pointers i, j — dono strings ke prefixes par. Agar a[i-1] == b[j-1], to wo character answer ka hissa hai: 1 + LCS(i-1, j-1). Agar match nahi, to ya to a ka character chhodo ya b ka — dono try karo aur max lo. State (i, j) baar baar repeat hoti hai, isliye table.

    Code¶

    def lcs_length(a, b):
    """LCS ki length. dp[i][j] = a ke pehle i aur b ke pehle j chars ka LCS."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 1
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 4
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                # 5
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1     # 6
            else:                                   # 7
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])   # 8
    return dp[n][m]                                 # 9


def lcs_string(a, b):
    """Actual subsequence nikaalo — table bana kar peeche chalo (backtrack)."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 10
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 11
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 12
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 13
            dp[i][j] = (dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]
                        else max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]))    # 14
    out = []                                        # 15
    i, j = n, m                                     # 16
    while i > 0 and j > 0:                          # 17
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                    # 18
            out.append(a[i - 1])                    # 19
            i -= 1                                  # 20
            j -= 1                                  # 21
        elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:          # 22
            i -= 1                                  # 23
        else:                                       # 24
            j -= 1                                  # 25
    return "".join(reversed(out))                   # 26

    Line-by-line:

    1-2. (n+1) x (m+1) table, row/col 0 = khaali string ka case = 0. Ye padding hi hai jo i-1 ko safe banata hai. 5-6. Match — dono taraf ek character kam karke diagonal se aao, +1. 8. Match nahi — diagonal mat lo, ya upar (a ka char chhoda) ya baayen (b ka char chhoda), jo bada ho. 9. Bottom-right cell = poori strings ka answer.

    10-14. Wahi table, ek line mein. 15-26. Backtracking. Bottom-right se shuru. Match mile to character le lo aur diagonal jao (19-21). Warna jis taraf ki value badi hai udhar jao (22-25) — kyunki wahi se ye value aayi thi. Aakhir mein reverse, kyunki hum peeche se aage bana rahe the.

    Compact dry run — a = "ABCD", b = "ACBD"¶

    – A C B D
    – 0 0 0 0 0
    A 0 1 1 1 1
    B 0 1 1 2 2
    C 0 1 2 2 2
    D 0 1 2 2 3

    Answer 3 — "ABD" (ya "ACD", dono valid; backtrack ek deta hai).

    Complexity¶

    Value Kyun
    Time O(n·m) Har cell exactly ek baar bharti hai, constant kaam per cell
    Space O(n·m), ya O(min(n,m)) Sirf pichhli row chahiye — length ke liye rolling array
    Backtrack ke saath O(n·m) space compulsory Path reconstruct karne ke liye poora table chahiye

    Note: agar sirf length chahiye, do rows kaafi hain. Agar string chahiye, poora table rakhna padega (ya Hirschberg's algorithm — O(n·m) time par O(min(n,m)) space, divide and conquer se; interview mein naam le dena hi kaafi hai).

    Interview answer: Longest common subsequence is the classic two-sequence DP. The state is dp[i][j] — the LCS length of the first i characters of A and the first j of B. If the current characters match, the answer is one plus the diagonal; if not, it's the max of dropping a character from either string. That's O(nm) time and O(nm) space, reducible to two rows if I only need the length.

    The reason it matters beyond the interview is that diff tools are built on it — git diff finds the LCS of two files and reports everything outside it as an insertion or deletion. In QA I've used the same idea for comparing ordered event streams: the LCS is the part that behaved as expected, and the gaps are exactly the regression.

    Two traps: LCS is not longest common substring — substring requires contiguity and has a different recurrence where a mismatch resets to zero rather than taking a max. And if the interviewer wants the actual subsequence rather than its length, I have to keep the whole table and backtrack from the bottom-right corner.

    Longest Increasing Subsequence¶

    Kya hai¶

    Ek array mein sabse lambi subsequence jiske elements strictly badhte jaayein (contiguous hona zaroori nahi). Analogy: saal bhar ke test-pass-count ka record hai; sabse lamba stretch dhoondho jisme har agli entry pichhli se behtar thi, beech ke bure mahine ignore karke.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    O(n²) version: dp[i] = index i par khatam hone wali LIS ki length. Har i ke liye peeche saare j dekho; jahan nums[j] < nums[i], wahan se extend kar sakte ho.

    O(n log n) version: ek tails array rakho jahan tails[k] = length k+1 wali kisi bhi increasing subsequence ka sabse chhota possible last element. Har naye number ke liye binary search se uski jagah dhoondho aur replace karo. tails ki length hi answer hai — par tails khud LIS nahi hai.

    Code¶

    from bisect import bisect_left


def lis_quadratic(nums):
    """O(n^2). dp[i] = i par khatam hone wali LIS ki length."""
    if not nums:                                    # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    dp = [1] * len(nums)                            # 3
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):                   # 4
        for j in range(i):                          # 5
            if nums[j] < nums[i] and dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]:   # 6
                dp[i] = dp[j] + 1                   # 7
    return max(dp)                                  # 8


def lis_nlogn(nums):
    """O(n log n). tails[k] = length k+1 wali LIS ka sabse chhota last element."""
    tails = []                                      # 9
    for x in nums:                                  # 10
        pos = bisect_left(tails, x)                 # 11
        if pos == len(tails):                       # 12
            tails.append(x)                         # 13
        else:                                       # 14
            tails[pos] = x                          # 15
    return len(tails)                               # 16

    Line-by-line:

    1. Har element akela ek LIS hai, isliye base 1. 5-7. Peeche ke har chhote element se extend karne ki koshish; best rakho.
    2. dp[-1] nahi, max(dp) — LIS kahin bhi khatam ho sakti hai. Ye common bug hai.

    9-16. Patience sorting. 11. bisect_left — pehli jagah jahan tails[pos] >= x. 12-13. x sabse bada hai — sequence lambi ho gayi. 14-15. Warna us length ka last element chhota kar do — future ke liye zyada room banta hai. Value badalti hai, length nahi. 16. tails ki length = LIS ki length.

    Strictly vs non-decreasing: bisect_left = strictly increasing. bisect_right use karo to non-decreasing (duplicates allowed) ho jaata hai. Ek function ka farak.

    Compact dry run — [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]¶

    x pos tails ke baad length
    10 0 [10] 1
    9 0 [9] 1
    2 0 [2] 1
    5 1 [2,5] 2
    3 1 [2,3] 2
    7 2 [2,3,7] 3
    101 3 [2,3,7,101] 4
    18 3 [2,3,7,18] 4

    Answer 4. Dhyaan do: final tails = [2,3,7,18] — ye ek valid LIS hai yahan, par hamesha nahi hoti. Actual sequence chahiye to har element ke saath uska predecessor index store karna padta hai.

    Complexity¶

    Version Time Space Kyun
    Quadratic O(n²) O(n) Har i ke liye i tak peeche dekha — 1+2+…+n = n²/2
    Binary search O(n log n) O(n) Har element par ek bisect = log n

    Interview answer: Longest increasing subsequence has two standard solutions and knowing both is usually the point of the question. The O(n squared) one defines dp[i] as the length of the LIS ending at index i, and for each i scans everything before it. The answer is the maximum over the whole dp array, not the last element — that's the most common bug.

    The O(n log n) one is patience sorting. I keep a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail value for an increasing subsequence of length k plus one. For each number I binary search for its position: if it's larger than everything I append and the answer grows, otherwise I overwrite that slot with a smaller value, which never shortens anything but leaves more room for future elements. The length of tails is the answer.

    The important caveat is that tails is not itself a valid LIS — it's a bookkeeping array that can hold values from incompatible subsequences. If I need the actual sequence I store a predecessor index alongside each element and walk back. Using bisect_left gives a strictly increasing subsequence; bisect_right allows equal values.

    Edit Distance¶

    Kya hai¶

    Ek string ko doosri banane ke liye kam se kam kitne single-character operations (insert, delete, replace) lagenge — Levenshtein distance. Analogy: spell-checker "recieve" dekh kar "receive" suggest karta hai kyunki dono ke beech distance sirf 2 hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    dp[i][j] = a ke pehle i aur b ke pehle j characters ke beech ki distance. Characters match karein to koi cost nahi, seedha diagonal. Warna teen choices — replace (diagonal), delete (upar), insert (baayen) — sabse sasti + 1.

    Code¶

    def edit_distance(a, b):
    """Levenshtein distance. O(n*m) time, O(m) space."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 1
    prev = list(range(m + 1))                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        curr = [i] + [0] * m                        # 4
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 5
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                # 6
                curr[j] = prev[j - 1]               # 7
            else:                                   # 8
                curr[j] = 1 + min(prev[j - 1],      # 9  replace
                                  prev[j],          # 10 delete
                                  curr[j - 1])      # 11 insert
        prev = curr                                 # 12
    return prev[m]                                  # 13

    Line-by-line:

    1. Base row: khaali a ko b banane ke liye j insertions — isliye 0,1,2,…,m.
    2. Base column: a ke i characters ko khaali string banane ke liye i deletions. 6-7. Match — cost zero. Diagonal se seedha copy. Ye +1 nahi hai, ye sabse zyada galat likhi jaane wali line hai.
    3. Replace — dono ka ek-ek character khatam, diagonal.
    4. Delete from a — a ka character chhoda, upar wali row.
    5. Insert into a — b ka character match kiya, current row ka baayan cell. 12-13. Rolling — sirf do rows chahiye kyunki har cell teen neighbours par depend karta hai jo sab pichhli ya current row mein hain.

    Compact dry run — a = "cat", b = "cut"¶

    – c u t
    – 0 1 2 3
    c 1 0 1 2
    a 2 1 1 2
    t 3 2 2 1

    Answer 1 — a ko u se replace karo. Cell (a,u) par teenon options ki cost 1+min(0,1,1)=1 thi, aur wahi aage chala.

    Complexity¶

    Value Kyun
    Time O(n·m) Har cell ek baar, constant 3-way min
    Space O(min(n,m)) Rolling rows; alignment chahiye to poora O(n·m)

    Variants jo poochhe jaate hain: operations ki alag-alag cost do to 1 + ki jagah cost_replace + likh do — structure same. Damerau-Levenshtein transposition (do adjacent characters swap) ko ek operation maanta hai aur ek chautha case add karta hai. LCS ka rishta: agar sirf insert aur delete allowed hon (replace nahi), to distance = n + m - 2*LCS(a,b).

    Interview answer: Edit distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another. The state dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i characters of A and the first j of B. On a character match it's a free diagonal move; on a mismatch it's one plus the cheapest of three neighbours — diagonal is a replace, the cell above is a delete, the cell to the left is an insert.

    The base cases carry real meaning: turning an empty string into a prefix of length j costs j insertions, which is why row zero counts upward. And the match case costs zero, not one — that's the bug interviewers watch for.

    It's O(n*m) in both time and space, and space drops to one row because every cell only depends on the previous row and the cell to its left. I keep the full table only when I need the alignment itself. Practically it's behind spell-checkers, fuzzy search and diff-style test assertions — in QA it's useful for asserting that an output is close enough to expected rather than byte-identical.

    Matrix Chain Multiplication¶

    Kya hai¶

    Matrices ki ek chain di hai; multiplication ka order aisa chuno ki total scalar multiplications kam se kam ho. Analogy: teen numbers ko multiply karne ka answer order se nahi badalta, par mehnat badalti hai — jaise 100 chhote packets pehle jodo ya bade wale, total same par time alag.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Matrix i ka dimension dims[i-1] x dims[i] hai. dp[i][j] = i..j chain ka minimum cost. Har possible last multiplication point k try karo: left chain ka cost + right chain ka cost + dono results ko multiply karne ka cost. Ye interval DP hai — chhoti lambaai pehle, badi baad mein.

    Code¶

    def matrix_chain(dims):
    """dims lambai n+1, n matrices. dp[i][j] = i..j ka min cost."""
    n = len(dims) - 1                               # 1
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for length in range(2, n + 1):                  # 3
        for i in range(1, n - length + 2):          # 4
            j = i + length - 1                      # 5
            dp[i][j] = float("inf")                 # 6
            for k in range(i, j):                   # 7
                cost = (dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]
                        + dims[i - 1] * dims[k] * dims[j])   # 8
                if cost < dp[i][j]:                 # 9
                    dp[i][j] = cost                 # 10
    return dp[1][n]                                 # 11

    Line-by-line:

    1. n matrices ke liye n+1 dimensions chahiye — chain valid tabhi hai jab adjacent dims match karein.
    2. Diagonal dp[i][i] = 0 — ek akeli matrix ko multiply karne ka cost zero.
    3. Length ke order mein bharo, index ke order mein nahi. dp[i][j] ko chhote intervals chahiye, isliye wo pehle ready hone chahiye. Yahi interval DP ki asli seekh hai. 4-5. Har starting point, aur usse length wala end.
    4. k = jahan chain toot rahi hai — A(i..k) * A(k+1..j).
    5. Left ka cost + right ka cost + final multiply: result matrices dims[i-1] x dims[k] aur dims[k] x dims[j] hain, to unhe multiply karne mein dims[i-1]*dims[k]*dims[j] lagte hain.
    6. Poori chain 1..n.

    Compact dry run — dims = [10, 30, 5, 60] (A:10x30, B:30x5, C:5x60)¶

    Interval k Cost Min
    [1,2] (AB) 1 10·30·5 = 1500 1500
    [2,3] (BC) 2 30·5·60 = 9000 9000
    [1,3] 1 0 + 9000 + 10·30·60 = 27000
    [1,3] 2 1500 + 0 + 10·5·60 = 4500 4500

    (AB)C = 4500 vs A(BC) = 27000 — 6x farak, sirf brackets se.

    Complexity¶

    Value Kyun
    Time O(n³) O(n²) intervals × har interval ke liye O(n) split points
    Space O(n²) Table

    Brute force Catalan number hota hai (~4ⁿ/n^1.5) — n=20 par arbon possibilities. DP usko 8000 operations mein le aata hai.

    Interview answer: Matrix chain multiplication asks for the cheapest parenthesisation of a chain of matrix products. Matrix multiplication is associative so the result never changes, but the cost does — dramatically. For three matrices of dimensions 10x30, 30x5 and 5x60, one grouping costs 4,500 scalar multiplications and the other 27,000.

    It's the canonical interval DP. The state is dp[i][j], the minimum cost of multiplying matrices i through j, and I try every split point k, adding the cost of the two halves plus the cost of the final multiply. The crucial implementation detail is loop order: I iterate by interval length rather than by index, because a longer interval depends on shorter ones that must already be solved.

    That's O(n cubed) time and O(n squared) space, against a Catalan-number brute force. The same pattern covers burst balloons, optimal binary search trees and polygon triangulation — once you recognise "choose a split point in a range", they're the same problem wearing different clothes.

    Palindrome Partitioning¶

    Kya hai¶

    Ek string ko aise tukdon mein kaato ki har tukda palindrome ho, aur kam se kam cuts lagein. Analogy: ek lambi ribbon ko aise kaatna hai ki har piece dono taraf se ek jaisa dikhe, aur kainchi kam se kam baar chale.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Do layers. Pehle ek is_pal[i][j] table banao — s[i..j] palindrome hai ya nahi, jo is_pal[i+1][j-1] par depend karta hai. Phir cuts[i] = s[0..i] ke liye minimum cuts — har j <= i par dekho ki agar s[j..i] palindrome hai to cuts[j-1] + 1.

    Code¶

    def min_cut(s):
    """Minimum cuts taaki har piece palindrome ho. O(n^2)."""
    n = len(s)                                      # 1
    is_pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]        # 2
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):                  # 3
        for j in range(i, n):                       # 4
            if s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or is_pal[i + 1][j - 1]):   # 5
                is_pal[i][j] = True                 # 6
    cuts = [0] * n                                  # 7
    for i in range(n):                              # 8
        if is_pal[0][i]:                            # 9
            cuts[i] = 0                             # 10
            continue                                # 11
        cuts[i] = i                                 # 12
        for j in range(1, i + 1):                   # 13
            if is_pal[j][i] and cuts[j - 1] + 1 < cuts[i]:   # 14
                cuts[i] = cuts[j - 1] + 1           # 15
    return cuts[n - 1]                              # 16


def all_partitions(s):
    """Saare palindromic partitions — backtracking, DP nahi."""
    res, path = [], []                              # 17

    def back(start):                                # 18
        if start == len(s):                         # 19
            res.append(path[:])                     # 20
            return                                  # 21
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):    # 22
            piece = s[start:end]                    # 23
            if piece == piece[::-1]:                # 24
                path.append(piece)                  # 25
                back(end)                           # 26
                path.pop()                          # 27

    back(0)                                         # 28
    return res                                      # 29

    Line-by-line:

    1. i ulta chalta hai — is_pal[i][j] ko is_pal[i+1][...] chahiye, jo badi i hai. Direction galat ho to table khaali padhega.
    2. s[i] == s[j] aur ya to lambaai 1-2 hai (j-i < 2) ya andar wala hissa palindrome hai.
    3. cuts[i] = prefix s[0..i] ka answer. 9-11. Poora prefix hi palindrome hai to zero cuts. Ye check zaroori hai warna cuts[-1] chahiye hota jo exist nahi karta.
    4. Worst case i cuts (har character alag). 13-15. Aakhri palindromic piece s[j..i] maano; usse pehle ka best cuts[j-1], plus ek cut.

    17-29. Saare partitions chahiye to DP nahi, backtracking — answers ki sankhya exponential hai (2^(n-1) tak), to koi polynomial algorithm ho hi nahi sakta.

    Compact dry run — s = "aab"¶

    i prefix is_pal[0][i]? cuts[i]
    0 a haan 0
    1 aa haan 0
    2 aab nahi j=2: s[2..2]="b" pal, cuts[1]+1 = 1 → 1

    Answer 1 — "aa" | "b".

    Complexity¶

    Task Time Space
    Min cuts O(n²) O(n²) palindrome table
    Min cuts, O(n) space O(n²) O(n) — har center se expand karo, table ke bina
    Saare partitions O(n · 2ⁿ) O(n) recursion depth

    Interview answer: Palindrome partitioning with minimum cuts is a two-stage DP, and saying so up front is half the answer. First I precompute an is-palindrome table for every substring, which is itself a DP: s[i..j] is a palindrome if the outer characters match and the inner substring already is. That table has to be filled with the start index moving backwards, because each entry depends on a larger start index.

    Then the cut DP: cuts[i] is the minimum cuts for the prefix ending at i. If the whole prefix is a palindrome the answer is zero; otherwise I try every position j where s[j..i] is a palindrome and take cuts[j-1] plus one. Both stages are O(n squared).

    If the question instead asks for all palindromic partitions rather than the minimum, DP is the wrong tool — the number of answers is exponential, so it's backtracking with a palindrome check at each extension. Recognising which of the two is being asked is the actual test: "count" or "minimum" means DP, "list them all" means backtracking.

    Matrix Path Problems¶

    Kya hai¶

    Grid par ek corner se doosre corner tak jaana hai — kitne raaste hain, ya sabse sasta raasta kaunsa hai. Analogy: sheher ka block-wise map; sirf right aur down ja sakte ho, aur har block par toll lagta hai.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Har cell tak pahunchne ke sirf do tareeke hain — upar se ya baayen se. Isliye dp[i][j] = f(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), jahan f counting ke liye sum hai aur cost ke liye min. Obstacles ka matlab sirf dp = 0 set karna hai.

    Code¶

    def unique_paths(m, n):
    """m x n grid mein top-left se bottom-right tak raaste. O(n) space."""
    row = [1] * n                                   # 1
    for _ in range(1, m):                           # 2
        for j in range(1, n):                       # 3
            row[j] += row[j - 1]                    # 4
    return row[n - 1]                               # 5


def unique_paths_obstacles(grid):
    """1 = obstacle. Blocked cell ke raaste zero."""
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])                  # 6
    row = [0] * n                                   # 7
    row[0] = 1 if grid[0][0] == 0 else 0            # 8
    for i in range(m):                              # 9
        for j in range(n):                          # 10
            if grid[i][j] == 1:                     # 11
                row[j] = 0                          # 12
            elif j > 0:                             # 13
                row[j] += row[j - 1]                # 14
    return row[n - 1]                               # 15


def min_path_sum(grid):
    """Har cell par cost; top-left se bottom-right tak minimum total."""
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])                  # 16
    dp = list(grid[0])                              # 17
    for j in range(1, n):                           # 18
        dp[j] += dp[j - 1]                          # 19
    for i in range(1, m):                           # 20
        dp[0] += grid[i][0]                         # 21
        for j in range(1, n):                       # 22
            dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j - 1])   # 23
    return dp[n - 1]                                # 24

    Line-by-line:

    1. Pehli row ke har cell tak sirf ek raasta (seedha right).
    2. row[j] += row[j-1] — row[j] abhi bhi pichhli row ki value hai (= upar se), aur row[j-1] already update ho chuka hai (= baayen se). Ek line mein 2D recurrence.
    3. Agar start hi blocked hai to zero raaste — ye edge case chhoot jaata hai. 11-12. Obstacle par count zero; aage ke cells apne aap sahi ho jaate hain.
    4. j > 0 guard — pehla column sirf upar se aata hai, jo row[j] mein pehle se hai.

    17-19. Pehli row ka prefix sum — sirf ek hi raasta hai, isliye saare costs jodo. 21. Har nayi row ka pehla cell: sirf upar se aa sakte ho. 23. min(dp[j], dp[j-1]) — dp[j] = upar wala (abhi tak update nahi hua), dp[j-1] = baayen wala (ho gaya). Plus current cell ka cost.

    Compact dry run — min_path_sum([[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]])¶

    Row dp ke baad
    init (row 0) [1, 4, 5]
    row 1 [2, min(4,2)+5=7, min(5,7)+1=6]
    row 2 [6, min(7,6)+2=8, min(6,8)+1=7]

    Answer 7 — raasta 1→3→1→1→1.

    Complexity¶

    Problem Time Space
    Unique paths O(m·n) O(n) rolling row
    Unique paths (formula) O(min(m,n)) O(1) — C(m+n-2, m-1)
    With obstacles O(m·n) O(n)
    Min path sum O(m·n) O(n)

    Note: bina obstacles wala unique paths asal mein combinatorics hai — total m+n-2 moves mein se m-1 down chunne hain. DP tab zaroori hota hai jab obstacles ya costs aa jaayein.

    Ek warning: agar movement chaaron directions mein allowed ho jaaye, to ye DP nahi rehta — cycles ban sakti hain, aur ye Dijkstra ban jaata hai. DP ko acyclic dependency chahiye.

    Interview answer: Grid path problems are the gentlest introduction to two-dimensional DP. Because you can only move right or down, every cell is reachable from exactly two predecessors, so dp[i][j] is a function of the cell above and the cell to the left — a sum when counting paths, a min when finding the cheapest one.

    All of them compress to a single row of size n, because I only ever need the previous row and the current row's left neighbour. In the one-dimensional form dp[j] still holds the value from above when I read it, and dp[j-1] has already been overwritten with the current row — so one line encodes the whole recurrence.

    Two things worth flagging. Without obstacles, unique paths is really a binomial coefficient — choose which m-1 of the m+n-2 moves go down — so the DP is unnecessary. And if the movement rules allow going up or left, it stops being a DP at all, because the dependency graph gains cycles; at that point it's a shortest-path problem and I'd reach for Dijkstra or BFS instead.

    How to Recognise a DP Problem¶

    Ye section aur agla — is poore Part ke sabse kaam ke do sections hain. Algorithm yaad rakhna aasan hai; pehchaanna ki problem DP hai, mushkil hai.

    Teen signals jo saath aane chahiye¶

    1. Optimisation ya counting ka shabd. "Minimum", "maximum", "longest", "how many ways", "is it possible". Agar problem saare answers maang rahi hai ("list all partitions"), to DP nahi — backtracking. DP ek number ya ek best answer deta hai.

    2. Choices ka sequence. Aap answer ko ek-ek decision karke bana sakte ho: ye item lo ya chhodo, yahan cut lagao ya nahi, ye character match karo ya skip. Agar ek hi formula se answer aa raha hai (jaise C(n, k)), DP ki zaroorat nahi.

    3. Overlapping subproblems. Recursion likho aur dekho ki wahi arguments dobara aa rahe hain ya nahi. Ye sabse zaroori signal hai — iske bina DP nahi hai, sirf divide and conquer hai.

    Merge sort mein sort(0,4) kabhi dobara call nahi hoti — isliye merge sort DP nahi hai, chahe wo optimal substructure rakhta ho. Fibonacci mein fib(3) teen baar aati hai — wahi DP banata hai.

    Practical test — 60 second mein¶

    1. Brute force recursion likho, bhale hi exponential ho. Sirf signature aur recurrence.
    2. Arguments ginno. Kitne alag (i, j, ...) combinations possible hain? Agar wo polynomial hain aur recursion tree exponential hai, to repeat ho rahe hain → DP.
    3. @lru_cache laga do. Agar kaam kar gaya, DP mil gaya. Bottom-up baad mein.

    Ye teesra step interview mein bilkul valid hai — top-down memo likh do, phir bolo "I can convert this to bottom-up and drop the recursion stack if you want."

    Kab DP nahi hai — worked counterexample¶

    Problem: "N cities, har pair ke beech distance, sabse chhota tour jo har city ek baar visit kare." (TSP)

    Ye optimisation hai, choices ka sequence hai, aur subproblems overlap bhi karte hain. Phir bhi standard DP fail ho jaata hai — kyunki state sirf "abhi kis city par hoon" nahi ho sakti; "kaunsi cities visit ho chuki hain" bhi state ka hissa hai. Aur wo ek subset hai, to states 2ⁿ · n ho jaate hain. Bitmask DP kaam karta hai par sirf n ≤ 20 tak. Seekh: DP tab tak useful hai jab tak state space polynomial hai — warna wo sirf brute force ka organised version hai.

    Doosra counterexample: "Array ko sort karo." Optimisation lagta hai, par yahan koi overlapping subproblem nahi — har subarray alag hai. Ye divide and conquer hai, DP nahi.

    Greedy vs DP — pehla filter¶

    Agar har step par ek local rule se optimal answer nikal aata hai (aur aap wo prove kar sakte ho), greedy kaafi hai — DP overkill hai. Agar local best baad mein galat sabit ho sakta hai (coin change [1,3,4], amount 6), to DP chahiye. Jab shaq ho, DP likho — wo hamesha sahi hoga, bas dhima hoga. Greedy tabhi likho jab exchange argument dimaag mein taiyaar ho.

    Interview answer: I look for three things together. First, the question asks for a minimum, a maximum, a count of ways, or a yes-no feasibility — not for the full list of solutions, which would mean backtracking instead. Second, the answer is built through a sequence of choices, so I can write a recurrence over "what do I do with the current element". Third, and most importantly, that recursion revisits the same arguments — without overlapping subproblems it's divide and conquer, not DP. Merge sort has optimal substructure but never repeats a subproblem, which is exactly why memoising it buys nothing.

    My practical method is to write the brute-force recursion first, count the distinct argument combinations, and if that count is polynomial while the recursion tree is exponential, memoise it. In an interview I'll write the top-down version with an lru_cache, confirm it's correct, and then offer to convert it to bottom-up to remove the recursion stack.

    The limit worth naming is when the state has to include a set rather than an index — travelling salesman, for example. The DP is correct but the state space is two to the n, so it's only a practical answer for small inputs.

    How to Define the State¶

    State galat define kar di to baaki sab bekaar hai. Ye sabse zyada slip yahin hoti hai.

    State kya hoti hai¶

    State = minimum information jo aapko chahiye taaki aage ke decisions le sako, bina ye jaane ki aap yahan tak pahunche kaise. Isi ko "Markov property" kehte hain. Agar aage ka answer past ke kisi detail par depend karta hai jo state mein nahi hai, to state incomplete hai.

    Teen sawaal poochho¶

    1. Main abhi kahan hoon? — index, position, remaining capacity. Ye lagbhag hamesha state ka hissa hota hai. 2. Aage ka faisla kis cheez par depend karta hai? — bacha hua budget, pichhla element, kitne transactions ho chuke. Har aisi cheez ek dimension hai. 3. Kya main state ko chhota kar sakta hoon? — agar ek dimension ki value sirf 2-3 ho sakti hai (bought/not bought), to wo boolean flag hai, poora array nahi.

    Do standard shapes¶

    Shape Matlab Kahan
    dp[i] = i tak ka answer (prefix) i ke baad ki cheezein irrelevant Coin change, climbing stairs
    dp[i] = i par khatam hone wala answer i mandatory hai answer mein LIS, max subarray, house robber ke variants

    Ye do alag cheezein hain aur inko mila dena classic bug hai. Prefix wale mein answer dp[n] hota hai; "ending at i" wale mein max(dp) hota hai. LIS mein dp[-1] return karna isi confusion se aata hai.

    Worked example — state galat se sahi tak¶

    Problem: stock prices ka array, do transactions tak allowed, maximum profit.

    Attempt 1: dp[i] = day i tak ka max profit. Fail — kyunki aage ka faisla is baat par depend karta hai ki kitni transactions bachi hain aur abhi stock haath mein hai ya nahi. Ye dono information dp[i] mein nahi hai.

    Attempt 2: dp[i][k] = day i tak, k transactions use karke max profit. Abhi bhi fail — "stock haath mein hai ya nahi" missing hai. Agar haath mein hai, to aaj bech sakta hoon; nahi hai to sirf khareed sakta hoon. Do bilkul alag situations, ek hi state.

    Attempt 3: dp[i][k][holding] jahan holding ∈ {0, 1}. Ab complete hai. Transitions: dp[i][k][0] = max(dp[i-1][k][0], dp[i-1][k][1] + price[i]) (hold karo ya becho), dp[i][k][1] = max(dp[i-1][k][1], dp[i-1][k-1][0] - price[i]) (hold karo ya khareedo).

    Seekh: state tab tak badhao jab tak transition deterministic na ban jaaye. Agar transition likhte waqt aapko "par ye to depend karta hai ki…" bolna pad raha hai, wahi missing dimension hai.

    State chhoti rakhne ke tareeke¶

    • Symmetry — dp[i][j] mein agar sirf j - i matter karta hai, to ek dimension kaafi hai.
    • Rolling — agar sirf pichhli row chahiye, dp[i] ki jagah do arrays.
    • Bitmask — subset chahiye aur n chhota hai (≤ 20) to integer mein pack karo.
    • Normalise — dp[remaining] aksar dp[used] se chhota hota hai agar capacity bandhi hai.

    Interview answer: The state is the smallest amount of information that makes the rest of the decisions independent of how I got there. I build it by asking two questions: where am I, and what else does the next decision depend on. Each thing in that second answer becomes a dimension.

    The test I apply is whether I can write the transition without saying "but that depends on". The stock-trading problem is the clearest example — dp[day] is not enough, dp[day][transactions used] is still not enough, and only dp[day][transactions][holding] makes the transition deterministic, because whether I currently own the stock decides which moves are even legal.

    The other distinction I'm careful about is prefix states versus ending-at states. dp[i] meaning "best answer using the first i elements" gives the answer at dp[n]; dp[i] meaning "best answer that ends at i" gives the answer as the max over the whole array. Longest increasing subsequence is the ending-at kind, and returning dp of the last index instead of the maximum is the single most common bug in that problem.

    Part 6: Greedy Algorithms¶

    Greedy sabse aasan likhne wali cheez hai aur sabse mushkil prove karne wali. Code aksar paanch line ka hota hai. Interview mein sawaal ye nahi hota ki "greedy likh sakte ho" — sawaal ye hota hai ki "ye greedy sahi kyun hai?" Isliye is Part mein do sections code se pehle aate hain: correctness kaise sabit karte hain, aur exchange argument kya hai.

    What Makes Greedy Provably Correct¶

    Do conditions — dono chahiye¶

    1. Greedy choice property. Ek globally optimal solution aisa maujood hai jo pehli greedy choice ko include karta hai. Dhyaan do: ye nahi kaha ki "greedy choice hamesha optimal solution mein hoti hai" — kaha ye hai ki koi ek optimal solution use include karta hai. Ye farak chhota lagta hai par proof ka poora dhaancha isi par khada hai.

    2. Optimal substructure. Pehli choice lene ke baad jo bachta hai, wo usi problem ka chhota version hai, aur uska optimal solution poore ka optimal solution banata hai.

    DP mein optimal substructure hota hai par greedy choice property nahi hoti — isliye DP saare options try karta hai. Greedy mein dono hote hain, isliye wo ek option try karke aage badh jaata hai. Yahi poora farak hai.

    Proof ka standard structure¶

    Greedy correctness ke do standard proofs hote hain:

    Exchange argument (agla section) — optimal solution lo, usse greedy jaisa banao bina kharaab kiye. Sabse zyada use hota hai.

    Greedy stays ahead — induction se dikhao ki har step k par greedy ka partial solution kisi bhi doosre solution ke partial solution se kam se kam utna hi accha hai. Activity selection ke liye: greedy ke pehle k activities ka finish time har doosre valid choice ke k-th finish time se <= hota hai. Agar greedy har jagah aage hai, to wo peeche kaise reh sakta hai.

    Matroid — jab greedy hamesha kaam karta hai¶

    Formally, greedy hamesha optimal hota hai agar problem ek matroid hai — do properties: subsets of a valid set are valid (hereditary), aur agar ek valid set doosre se bada hai to bade wale se ek element utha kar chhote wale mein daala ja sakta hai (exchange property). Kruskal's MST isi wajah se kaam karta hai — forests ek matroid banate hain. Interview mein ye naam le dena bohot achha signal hai, par baaki sab problems ke liye exchange argument hi likhna padega.

    Ek chhota worked proof — fractional knapsack¶

    Claim: highest value/weight ratio wala item pehle poora bharna optimal hai. Proof: maano optimal solution O mein us item (ratio r_max) ka x weight hai jabki hum y > x bhar sakte the. To O mein kisi doosre item ka y - x weight hai jiska ratio r < r_max. Us y - x weight ko hata kar highest-ratio item se badal do. Weight same rahega, value badhegi ya barabar rahegi ((y-x)·r_max >= (y-x)·r). Matlab O se buri nahi, aur ab wo greedy choice include karti hai. Isliye greedy choice safe hai. ∎

    Red flags — greedy shayad galat hai¶

    • Choices ek doosre ko constrain karti hain (0/1 knapsack — ek item lene se capacity kam hoti hai jo baad ke better combos rok deti hai).
    • Answer mein combination matter karti hai, individual elements nahi (coin change).
    • Aapko "yahan lena behtar hai ya wahan" ka trade-off dikh raha hai jiska jawaab aage ke data par depend karta hai.

    Interview answer: A greedy algorithm is correct when two properties hold. The greedy choice property says there exists an optimal solution that contains the first greedy choice — note that it's "there exists", not "every optimal solution contains it", and that phrasing is what makes the proof work. Optimal substructure says that after making that choice, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem.

    Dynamic programming needs only the second property, which is why it explores all the choices. Greedy has both, so it can commit to one and never look back — that's the entire difference between the two paradigms.

    To prove it I use one of two arguments. The exchange argument takes an arbitrary optimal solution and transforms it step by step into the greedy one without ever making it worse. "Greedy stays ahead" uses induction to show the greedy partial solution is at least as good as any other after every step. If I can't sketch one of those in a couple of sentences, I don't trust the greedy and I write the DP instead — a correct slow answer beats a fast wrong one.

    The Exchange Argument¶

    Kya hai¶

    Greedy ko prove karne ka sabse standard tareeka: koi bhi optimal solution lo, aur usme ek-ek badlaav karke usse greedy solution bana do — har badlaav se answer kharaab nahi hona chahiye. Analogy: aap keh rahe ho "tumhara jo bhi best plan hai, main usme ek cheez badal doonga jisse wo mera plan jaisa ho jaayega aur utna hi accha rahega — matlab mera plan bhi best hai."

    Template — chaar steps¶

    1. Maano O ek optimal solution hai jo greedy G se alag hai.
    2. Pehli jagah dhoondho jahan dono alag hain (ye zaroori hai — "pehli" se induction chalta hai).
    3. O mein us jagah swap karo taaki wo G se match kar jaaye.
    4. Dikhao ki swap ke baad O abhi bhi valid hai aur utna hi accha ya behtar hai.

    Nateeja: G jitne bhi points par O se alag tha, sab badle ja sakte hain bina kharaab kiye — matlab G bhi optimal hai. ∎

    Step 4 ke do hisse dono zaroori hain. Sirf "value kharaab nahi hui" kaafi nahi — swap ke baad solution feasible bhi rehna chahiye (constraints toote nahi).

    Worked example — activity selection¶

    Greedy: sabse pehle khatam hone wali activity chuno.

    Proof: maano O optimal hai aur usme pehli activity a1 hai, jabki greedy g1 chunta hai jiska finish time sabse kam hai. To finish(g1) <= finish(a1).

    Ab O mein a1 ko hata kar g1 daal do. Valid hai kya? O ki doosri activity a2 ka start time >= finish(a1) >= finish(g1) hai — to g1 uske saath clash nahi karti. Count badla? Nahi, ek hataayi ek daali — count same. Matlab naya solution bhi optimal hai aur greedy choice include karta hai. Yahi induction har step par lagao. ∎

    Worked example 2 — job sequencing (deadline wala)¶

    Greedy: profit ke ghatte order mein jobs dekho, har job ko uske deadline ke sabse late khaali slot mein daalo.

    Exchange: maano O mein job x (profit 100) reject hai par job y (profit 40) accept hai, aur x ka koi valid slot y ke slot se compatible tha. y hata kar x daal do — deadline abhi bhi satisfy hoti hai (kyunki hum y ka slot use kar rahe hain jo x ke deadline ke andar tha), aur profit 60 badh gaya. Matlab O optimal tha hi nahi — contradiction. Isliye greedy ka "zyada profit pehle" sahi hai.

    "Sabse late slot" wala hissa alag se justify hota hai: late slot bharne se pehle wale slots khaali rehte hain, jo tight deadline wali jobs ke liye bache rehte hain. Early slot bharna kabhi behtar nahi ho sakta.

    Jab exchange argument fail hota hai — counterexample¶

    0/1 knapsack, ratio ke hisaab se greedy. Items: (w=10, v=60), (w=20, v=100), (w=30, v=120). Capacity 50. Ratios: 6, 5, 4.

    Greedy: item1 (10, 60) + item2 (20, 100) = 30 weight, 160 value. Bacha 20 weight, item3 (30) fit nahi hota. Total 160. Optimal: item2 + item3 = 50 weight, 220 value.

    Exchange kyun fail hua? Kyunki O mein se item3 hata kar item1 daalne se weight badalta hai — hum "ek ke badle ek" swap nahi kar sakte, kyunki items indivisible hain aur weights alag hain. Exchange argument tabhi chalta hai jab swap feasibility todhe bina ho sake. Fractional knapsack mein ye chalta hai kyunki wahan hum exactly y-x weight exchange kar sakte hain.

    Yahi ek line yaad rakhne layak hai: greedy tab tootta hai jab swap karne par feasibility ya to tootti hai ya usse compensate karne mein value girti hai.

    Interview answer: The exchange argument is how I prove a greedy is optimal. I take an arbitrary optimal solution, find the first place where it differs from the greedy choice, and swap that element for the greedy one. Then I show two things: the modified solution is still feasible, and it's no worse than before. Repeating that transforms any optimal solution into the greedy one without loss, so the greedy must itself be optimal.

    For activity selection, the greedy picks the earliest finishing activity. If an optimal solution starts with a different activity, that one finishes no earlier, so replacing it with the greedy choice can't create a conflict with whatever came next, and the count is unchanged. Induction does the rest.

    Where it fails is just as instructive. In 0/1 knapsack the swap isn't weight-neutral — exchanging one item for another changes how much capacity is left, so feasibility breaks and the argument collapses. That's precisely why fractional knapsack is greedy and 0/1 is DP: divisibility is what makes the exchange legal.

    Activity Selection¶

    Kya hai¶

    Start-end times wali activities di hain; maximum kitni activities kar sakte ho bina overlap ke. Analogy: ek conference room hai aur bees meeting requests — sabse zyada meetings kaise fit karein.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Finish time se sort karo, aur har wo activity utha lo jiska start pichhli chuni hui activity ke finish ke baad ho. Intuition: jaldi khatam hone wali activity sabse zyada baaki time chhodti hai, aur count maximise karna hai — duration se koi matlab nahi.

    Code¶

    def activity_selection(intervals):
    """(start, end) list se maximum non-overlapping activities."""
    if not intervals:                               # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 3
    chosen = [order[0]]                             # 4
    last_end = order[0][1]                          # 5
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 6
        if s >= last_end:                           # 7
            chosen.append((s, e))                   # 8
            last_end = e                            # 9
    return chosen                                   # 10


def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals):
    """Kam se kam kitne intervals hataane padenge taaki koi overlap na bache."""
    if not intervals:                               # 11
        return 0                                    # 12
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 13
    kept, last_end = 1, order[0][1]                 # 14
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 15
        if s >= last_end:                           # 16
            kept += 1                               # 17
            last_end = e                            # 18
    return len(intervals) - kept                    # 19

    Line-by-line:

    1. key=x[1] — end time se sort. Start se sort karna galat hai (neeche counterexample), duration se sort karna bhi galat hai.
    2. last_end hi poori state hai — pichhli chuni gayi activity ka end. Isse zyada kuchh yaad rakhne ki zaroorat nahi, aur yahi greedy ko O(n) banata hai.
    3. s >= last_end — agar meetings back-to-back allowed hain ([1,3] aur [3,5] clash nahi). Agar strict gap chahiye to s > last_end. 11-19. Same algorithm, ulta sawaal. "Kitne hataao" = total minus "kitne rakh sakte ho". Interview mein ye do problems alag lagti hain, hain ek hi.

    Compact dry run — [(1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)]¶

    Sort by end: (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)

    Activity s >= last_end? Chuna? last_end
    (1,4) — (pehla) haan 4
    (3,5) 3 >= 4? nahi nahi 4
    (0,6) 0 >= 4? nahi nahi 4
    (5,7) 5 >= 4? haan haan 7
    (3,9) nahi nahi 7
    (5,9) nahi nahi 7
    (6,10) nahi nahi 7
    (8,11) 8 >= 7? haan haan 11

    Answer 3: (1,4), (5,7), (8,11).

    Galat greedy — counterexample¶

    Start time se sort: (0, 100), (1, 2), (3, 4). Start se chalne par (0,100) pehle aayegi aur baaki dono block ho jaayengi → answer 1. Sahi answer 2.
