    For binomial coefficients I precompute factorials and their inverses. The neat part is that I only need one modular exponentiation, for the largest inverse factorial, and then walk backwards multiplying by i to get the rest — linear overall, with constant-time queries after that.

    One language detail: Python's modulo always returns a non-negative result for a positive modulus, so subtraction is safe. In C++ or Java I'd have to add the modulus back before reducing.

    Permutations and Combinations¶

    Kya hai¶

    Counting ke do basic sawaal — arrangements (order matter karta hai) aur selections (order matter nahi karta) — aur unhe generate karne ke tareeke. Analogy: podium par teen log kis order mein khade hain = permutation; team mein kaun kaun hai = combination.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    P(n, r) = n! / (n-r)! — pehli jagah ke liye n options, doosri ke liye n-1, aur aage. C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r! — kyunki har selection r! alag orders mein ginn li gayi thi, us overcounting ko divide kar do. Generate karne ke liye backtracking; difference sirf itna hai ki combinations mein aage se hi chalte hain (start index), permutations mein saare bache hue elements try karte hain.

    Code¶

    from math import comb, perm, factorial


def permutations_of(items):
    """Saare arrangements — backtracking, used flags ke saath."""
    res, path = [], []                              # 1
    used = [False] * len(items)                     # 2

    def back():                                     # 3
        if len(path) == len(items):                 # 4
            res.append(path[:])                     # 5
            return                                  # 6
        for i in range(len(items)):                 # 7
            if used[i]:                             # 8
                continue                            # 9
            used[i] = True                          # 10
            path.append(items[i])                   # 11
            back()                                  # 12
            path.pop()                              # 13
            used[i] = False                         # 14

    back()                                          # 15
    return res                                      # 16


def combinations_of(items, r):
    """r size ke saare subsets — start index se aage hi chalo."""
    res, path = [], []                              # 17

    def back(start):                                # 18
        if len(path) == r:                          # 19
            res.append(path[:])                     # 20
            return                                  # 21
        for i in range(start, len(items)):          # 22
            path.append(items[i])                   # 23
            back(i + 1)                             # 24
            path.pop()                              # 25

    back(0)                                         # 26
    return res                                      # 27


def all_subsets(items):
    """Power set — bitmask se, recursion ke bina."""
    n = len(items)                                  # 28
    out = []                                        # 29
    for mask in range(1 << n):                      # 30
        out.append([items[i] for i in range(n)
                    if mask & (1 << i)])            # 31
    return out                                      # 32

    Line-by-line:

    7-9. Saare indices try karo, jo already use ho chuke unhe skip. Isliye order matter karta hai. 10-14. Choose → recurse → un-choose. Backtracking ka core; path.pop() aur used[i] = False ka jodi hona zaroori hai warna state leak ho jaayegi.

    22-24. range(start, ...) aur back(i + 1) — yahi ek line permutations ko combinations banati hai. Hum kabhi peeche nahi jaate, isliye [1,2] aur [2,1] dono nahi bante. Repetition allowed ho to back(i) likh do.

    30-31. Bitmask power set. mask ka har bit batata hai ki wo element liya ya nahi. 2^n subsets, aur recursion ki zaroorat nahi. Sirf n <= 20 tak practical.

    Compact dry run — combinations_of(['a','b','c'], 2)¶

    Call path Action
    back(0), i=0 [a] recurse
    back(1), i=1 [a,b] record
    back(1), i=2 [a,c] record
    back(0), i=1 [b] recurse
    back(2), i=2 [b,c] record
    back(0), i=2 [c] back(3) — kuchh nahi

    [['a','b'], ['a','c'], ['b','c']] — C(3,2) = 3 ✓

    Complexity¶

    Task Time Space
    C(n,r) value (math.comb) O(min(r, n-r)) O(1)
    Generate permutations O(n · n!) O(n) recursion + O(n·n!) output
    Generate combinations O(r · C(n,r)) O(r) recursion
    Power set O(n · 2ⁿ) O(n·2ⁿ) output

    Ek zaroori baat: ye "algorithms" nahi hain jinme optimise karne ki gunjaish ho — output ka size hi exponential hai, to koi bhi correct solution utna hi time lega. Agar interviewer "optimise karo" bole, matlab wo generate karna nahi, count karna chahta hai (formula) — ya pruning chahta hai (jaise N-Queens mein).

    Duplicates handle karna¶

    Agar input mein duplicates hain aur unique results chahiye: pehle sort karo, phir loop mein if i > start and items[i] == items[i-1]: continue. Ye same level par same value ko dobara choose hone se rokta hai — bina set banaye.

    Formulas jo yaad rakhne layak hain¶

    Cheez Formula
    Permutations of n n!
    r out of n, ordered n! / (n-r)!
    r out of n, unordered n! / (r!·(n-r)!)
    With repetition, ordered n^r
    With repetition, unordered C(n+r-1, r) (stars and bars)
    Subsets of n 2^n
    Pascal's rule C(n,r) = C(n-1,r-1) + C(n-1,r)

    Pascal's rule hi DP hai — "ye element liya ya nahi liya" — aur wahi 0/1 knapsack ka bhi skeleton hai.

    Interview answer: Permutations count arrangements where order matters, combinations count selections where it doesn't, and the relationship is that combinations divide out the r factorial orderings of each selection.

    Generating them is backtracking, and the difference between the two is a single line. For permutations I loop over all indices and track which are used; for combinations I pass a start index and recurse with i plus one, so I never look backwards and never produce the same set in a different order. Both follow choose, recurse, un-choose.

    The complexity is output-bound — there are n factorial permutations, so no algorithm can be faster than that. If an interviewer asks me to optimise a generator, what they actually want is either a counting formula instead of enumeration, or pruning as in N-Queens where I abandon branches early.

    For handling duplicates I sort first and skip a value if it equals the previous one at the same recursion level, which avoids building a set of results afterwards. And Pascal's rule — C(n,r) equals C(n-1,r-1) plus C(n-1,r) — is literally the take-it-or-leave-it DP recurrence, which is a nice bridge back to knapsack.

    Random Numbers and Reservoir Sampling¶

    Kya hai¶

    Ek stream se k random items uniformly chunna, jab aapko pehle se pata hi nahi ki stream mein kitne items hain — aur poora data memory mein nahi aa sakta. Analogy: nadi ke kinare baithe ho, machhliyan behti ja rahi hain, aap sirf ek balti (k size) rakh sakte ho — par har machhli ka chunne ka chance barabar hona chahiye.

    Kaise kaam karta hai¶

    Pehli k items seedha reservoir mein daal do. Uske baad i-th item (0-indexed) ke liye 0 se i ke beech ek random number j nikaalo; agar j < k to reservoir ke j-th slot ko replace kar do. Isse har item ka final probability exactly k/n nikalta hai, chahe n kitna bhi ho.

    Code¶

    import random


def reservoir_sample(stream, k):
    """Stream se k uniform random items. O(n) time, O(k) space."""
    reservoir = []                                  # 1
    for i, item in enumerate(stream):               # 2
        if i < k:                                   # 3
            reservoir.append(item)                  # 4
        else:                                       # 5
            j = random.randint(0, i)                # 6
            if j < k:                               # 7
                reservoir[j] = item                 # 8
    return reservoir                                # 9


def reservoir_one(stream):
    """k = 1 ka simple case — sabse aasan proof."""
    chosen = None                                   # 10
    for i, item in enumerate(stream):               # 11
        if random.randint(0, i) == 0:               # 12
            chosen = item                           # 13
    return chosen                                   # 14


def fisher_yates(arr):
    """Uniform shuffle, O(n). Har permutation equally likely."""
    a = list(arr)                                   # 15
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, 0, -1):              # 16
        j = random.randint(0, i)                    # 17
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]                     # 18
    return a                                        # 19


def weighted_choice(items, weights):
    """Weight ke hisaab se ek item — prefix sum + binary search."""
    from bisect import bisect_left                  # 20
    cum, total = [], 0                              # 21
    for w in weights:                               # 22
        total += w                                  # 23
        cum.append(total)                           # 24
    r = random.uniform(0, total)                    # 25
    return items[bisect_left(cum, r)]               # 26

    Line-by-line:

    3-4. Pehle k items bina soche le lo — abhi tak n <= k hai to sab chahiye. 6. randint(0, i) — inclusive dono taraf, matlab i+1 possible values. 7-8. Probability k/(i+1) ki j < k ho. Aur agar replace hua to kaunsa purana item nikla ye bhi uniform hai. Yahi do baatein mil kar uniformity dete hain.

    10-14. k=1 ka version — i-th item ko 1/(i+1) probability se lo. Proof: i-th item survive karta hai agar wo chuna jaaye (1/(i+1)) aur uske baad koi na chune (i+1/i+2 · i+2/i+3 · … · n-1/n). Product telescope ho kar 1/n deta hai. Har item ke liye same. ∎

    16-18. Fisher-Yates. Peeche se chalo, aur har i ke liye 0..i mein se koi bhi swap karo. randint(0, i) hi sahi hai — randint(0, n-1) GALAT hai aur wo biased shuffle deta hai (n^n outcomes ko n! permutations par map karta hai, jo evenly divide nahi hote). Ye interview mein poochha jaata hai.

    20-26. Weighted sampling — prefix sums banao, ek uniform random point chuno, binary search se dekho wo kis bucket mein gira.

    Compact dry run — k = 1, stream [A, B, C]¶

    i item randint(0,i)==0 ki prob chosen ban-ne ki final prob
    0 A 1/1 = 1.0 1 × (1/2 nahi) × (2/3 nahi) = 1/3
    1 B 1/2 1/2 × 2/3 = 1/3
    2 C 1/3 1/3

    Teenon exactly 1/3 — aur ye bina n = 3 jaane hua.

    Complexity¶

    Value Kyun
    Time O(n) Har item par ek RNG call + shayad ek assignment
    Space O(k) Sirf reservoir — stream ki lambaai se independent
    Fisher-Yates O(n) time, O(1) extra In-place
    Weighted choice O(n) setup, O(log n) per query Prefix sums reusable

    QA mein kahan kaam aata hai¶

    • Production logs se sample — 50 GB log file se 1000 representative lines, ek pass mein.
    • Test data selection — 10 million rows ke DB dump se uniform sample, bina ORDER BY RANDOM() (jo poora table sort karta hai).
    • Flaky test triage — CI history stream karke random failures ka unbiased sample.
    • Load test payloads — real traffic ka uniform sample, memory blow-up ke bina.

    Interview answer: Reservoir sampling picks k uniformly random items from a stream of unknown length using O(k) memory and one pass. I fill the reservoir with the first k items, then for the i-th item I draw a random index between zero and i and replace that slot if the index is below k.

    The proof is cleanest for k equals one: the i-th item is chosen with probability one over i plus one, and survives if nothing after it is chosen, which is a telescoping product that collapses to exactly one over n. Every item gets the same probability, and crucially n never appears in the algorithm — only in the proof.

    The related algorithm is Fisher-Yates for shuffling: walk backwards and swap each position with a random index in the remaining prefix. The classic bug is drawing from the full range each time instead of the shrinking one — that produces n to the n equally likely outcomes mapped onto n factorial permutations, which can't be uniform because the counts don't divide evenly.

    In QA I use reservoir sampling to pull a representative sample of lines from log files far larger than memory, which is much cheaper than an order-by-random over a full table.

    Algorithm Decision Guide¶

    Interview mein problem sunne ke baad pehle 60 second mein ye decide karna hota hai ki kaunsa family hai. Ye guide usi ke liye hai.

    Keywords se algorithm tak¶

    Problem mein ye dikhe Socho ye
    "sorted array" Binary search
    "kth largest / smallest" Heap (O(n log k)) ya quickselect (O(n) avg)
    "top k frequent" Counter + heap
    "shortest path, unweighted" BFS
    "shortest path, weighted, non-negative" Dijkstra
    "shortest path, negative weights" Bellman-Ford
    "all pairs shortest" Floyd-Warshall
    "minimum cost to connect all" MST — Kruskal ya Prim
    "prerequisites / build order / dependency" Topological sort
    "are these connected / groups" Union-Find ya DFS
    "minimum / maximum / how many ways" DP
    "all possible combinations / list every" Backtracking
    "maximum non-overlapping" Greedy, end se sort
    "merge overlapping" Greedy, start se sort
    "contiguous subarray" Sliding window ya Kadane
    "substring with condition" Sliding window + hashmap
    "pattern in text" KMP / Z / built-in in
    "palindrome" Two pointers, expand-from-centre, Manacher
    "anagram / frequency" Counter
    "cycle in linked list" Floyd's tortoise-hare
    "next greater / smaller" Monotonic stack
    "sliding window max" Monotonic deque
    "prefix / autocomplete" Trie
    "range sum queries" Prefix sums ya Fenwick tree
    "n <= 20 aur subsets" Bitmask DP
    "minimum in stream / running median" Two heaps

    Constraints se complexity tak¶

    Constraint Target
    n ≤ 10 O(n!) — permutations
    n ≤ 20–25 O(2ⁿ) — bitmask, subsets
    n ≤ 500 O(n³) — Floyd-Warshall, matrix chain
    n ≤ 5000 O(n²) — quadratic DP
    n ≤ 10⁶ O(n log n) — sorting, heap, KMP
    n ≤ 10⁸ O(n) — single pass
    n ≤ 10¹⁸ O(log n) — binary search, math, fast pow

    Decision flow — text mein¶

    1. Kya answer ek single number hai (min/max/count)? → DP ya greedy. Agar exchange argument nahi bana pa rahe → DP.
    2. Kya saare answers chahiye? → Backtracking. Complexity output-bound hogi.
    3. Kya data mein structure hai (sorted, tree, graph)? → Us structure ka algorithm.
    4. Kya "contiguous" shabd hai? → Sliding window / prefix sums. "Subsequence" hai to DP.
    5. Kya har element ko sirf ek baar chhoo sakte ho (streaming)? → Reservoir, running aggregates, heaps.
    6. Kuchh nahi mil raha? → Brute force likho, uski complexity bolo, phir bottleneck dhoondh kar optimise karo. Ye galat jawaab nahi hai — ye process hai jo interviewer dekhna chahta hai.

    QA/SDET-specific mapping¶

    Real kaam Algorithm
    Flaky test dependency order Topological sort
    Test suite ko parallel workers mein baantna Greedy bin packing (LPT)
    Duplicate bug reports dhoondhna Edit distance / shingling + hashing
    API response diff LCS (difflib)
    Log file se sample lena Reservoir sampling
    Retry backoff schedule Fast exponentiation ka intuition
    Test selection by dependency graph BFS/DFS reachability
    Coverage overlap dhoondhna Set operations / interval merging

    Sawaal poochhne ke liye — jo aap interviewer se poochh sakte ho¶

    1. Input size ki range kya hai? (Complexity target isse decide hoti hai.)
    2. Duplicates ho sakte hain?
    3. Input sorted hai kya? Ya main sort kar sakta hoon?
    4. Kya main input modify kar sakta hoon (in-place allowed)?
    5. Multiple valid answers ho sakte hain, ya exactly ek?
    6. Empty input / single element par kya expected hai?
    7. Memory constraint hai kya?
    8. Kya ye ek baar chalega ya baar baar (preprocessing worth hai kya)?

    In sawaalon ka poochhna hi points deta hai — chahe jawaab kuchh bhi ho.

    Common Misconceptions Corrected¶

    # Jo log maante hain Sach
    1 "Quick sort hamesha merge sort se tez hai" Average par haan, worst case O(n²) hai. Merge sort guaranteed O(n log n) hai aur stable bhi
    2 "O(1) ka matlab instant" O(1) ka matlab input size se independent — wo constant 10 seconds bhi ho sakta hai
    3 "Big-O actual speed batata hai" Big-O growth rate batata hai. n=100 par O(n²) aksar O(n log n) se tez chalta hai (constants)
    4 "Binary search sirf arrays par chalta hai" Answer par bhi chalta hai — koi bhi monotonic predicate
    5 "Recursion iteration se hamesha dhimi hai" Overhead hai, par tail-call/memo ke saath farak minimal. Clarity ki value bhi hai
    6 "DP matlab hamesha 2D table" State ki dimensions problem decide karti hai — 1D, 3D, bitmask sab hote hain
    7 "Memoisation aur tabulation same hai" Same complexity, par memo sirf zaroori states compute karta hai; tabulation sab karta hai. Sparse states par memo tez
    8 "Greedy tez hai isliye behtar hai" Greedy aksar galat hota hai. Proof ke bina greedy = guess
    9 "Dijkstra negative weights handle kar leta hai" Nahi. Ek baar node finalise hone ke baad revisit nahi hota. Negative ke liye Bellman-Ford
    10 "BFS hamesha shortest path deta hai" Sirf unweighted (ya equal-weight) graphs par
    11 "Hash table hamesha O(1) hai" Average O(1). Worst case O(n) collisions se. Aur hashing khud O(key length) hai
    12 "Python list append O(n) hai kyunki resize hota hai" Amortised O(1) — doubling strategy se
    13 "in list par aur set par same hai" List O(n), set O(1). Ye sabse zyada dekha jaane wala real bug hai
    14 "String concatenation sasta hai" Loop mein += O(n²) hai — strings immutable hain. join use karo
    15 "Sorting hamesha O(n log n) hai" Comparison-based sorting ke liye. Counting/radix O(n) hain (assumptions ke saath)
    16 "Heap sorted hota hai" Nahi — sirf heap property (parent vs children). Poora order nahi hota
    17 "Balanced BST aur heap same cheez hain" BST inorder sorted deta hai; heap sirf min/max deta hai. Alag use cases
    18 "Merge sort in-place ho sakta hai" Theoretically haan, par practically nahi — in-place merge complexity aur constants dono badha deta hai
    19 "Space complexity mein output count hota hai" Convention: auxiliary space ginte hain, output nahi
    20 "Recursion stack space free hai" Har frame memory leta hai — O(depth). Deep recursion Python mein RecursionError deta hai (default limit 1000)
    21 "Tail recursion Python mein optimise hoti hai" Nahi hoti. CPython jaanbujh kar TCO nahi karta
    22 "Amortised aur average same hai" Amortised = worst-case sequence ka average. Average = probabilistic. Amortised stronger guarantee hai
    23 "Two pointers sirf sorted arrays par" Sliding window, fast/slow, linked lists — sab jagah
    24 "Backtracking aur DFS alag hain" Backtracking = DFS on implicit tree + pruning + state undo
    25 "n log n se behtar sorting impossible hai" Comparison-based ke liye impossible. Radix sort O(dn) hai
    26 "Union-Find ka find O(1) hai" O(alpha(n)) hai — practically constant, par technically nahi
    27 "Floyd-Warshall Dijkstra se bura hai" All-pairs ke liye O(V³) aksar V baar Dijkstra se behtar hai (code simpler, constants kam)
    28 "DP hamesha optimal solution deta hai" Tabhi jab optimal substructure ho. Galat state = galat answer, chahe table bhar gaya ho
    29 "Bigger O hamesha bura hai" O(2ⁿ) with n=15 theek hai; O(n²) with n=10⁶ nahi. Constraints dekho
    30 "Interview mein optimal solution zaroori hai" Nahi. Working solution + honest complexity + optimisation ka raasta — ye zyada important hai

    Teen misconceptions jo sabse mehngi padti hain¶

    Ek — "greedy sahi lag raha hai to sahi hoga." Coin change [1,3,4] par 6. Proof ke bina greedy mat likho.

    Do — "hash lookup O(1) hai to loop ke andar list mein in karna bhi theek hai." for x in big_list: if x in other_list — ye O(n·m) hai. set bana lo, O(n+m) ho jaayega. Ye QA scripts mein sabse common performance bug hai.

    Teen — "recursion depth ki fikar nahi." 10,000 nodes ki linked list par recursive traversal Python mein crash karti hai. Production code mein iterative likho, ya sys.setrecursionlimit badalne ke bajaay algorithm badlo.

    Interview answer: The corrections I'd most want to be judged on are these. Big-O describes growth, not speed — an O(n squared) algorithm with small constants beats an O(n log n) one on small inputs, and the constraints tell me which regime I'm in. Hash lookups are average O(1), not guaranteed, and the most expensive real bug I see is checking membership against a list inside a loop, which is quadratic and fixed by building a set once.

    On paradigms: greedy is a guess until I can give an exchange argument, Dijkstra genuinely cannot handle negative weights because it finalises nodes permanently, and BFS gives shortest paths only when edges are unweighted. And amortised is a stronger claim than average — it bounds any sequence of operations, not an expected case.

    Finally, on the interview itself: a working solution with an honest complexity analysis and a stated path to optimisation is worth more than a half-finished optimal one. Getting to correct first and then improving is the process I'd follow on the job, and it's the process I follow at the whiteboard.
